title: Dried tangerine peel polysaccharide (DTPP) alleviates hepatic steatosis by suppressing TLR4/MD-2-mediated inflammation and endoplasmic reticulum stress
chunk_text: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is a complex pathogenic metabolic syndrome characterized by increased inflammation and endoplasmic reticulum stress. In recent years, natural polysaccharides derived from traditional Chinese medicine have shown significant anti-inflammatory effects, making them an attractive therapeutic option. However, little research has been conducted on the therapeutic potential of dried tangerine peel polysaccharide (DTPP) — one of the most important medicinal resources in China. The results of the present study showed that DTPP substantially reduced macrophage infiltration in vivo and suppressed the expression of pro-inflammatory factors and endoplasmic reticulum stress-related genes. Additionally, surface plasmon resonance analysis revealed that DTPP had a specific affinity to myeloid differentiation factor 2, which consequently suppressed lipopolysaccharide-induced inflammation via interaction with the toll-like receptor 4 signaling pathway. This study provides a potential molecular mechanism underlying the anti-inflammatory effects of DTPP on NAFLD and suggests DTPP as a promising therapeutic strategy for NAFLD treatment.

In recent years, natural polysaccharides derived from traditional Chinese medicine have shown significant anti-inflammatory effects, making them an attractive therapeutic option. However, little research has been conducted on the therapeutic potential of dried tangerine peel polysaccharide (DTPP) — one of the most important medicinal resources in China. The results of the present study showed that DTPP substantially reduced macrophage infiltration in vivo and suppressed the expression of pro-inflammatory factors and endoplasmic reticulum stress-related genes. Additionally, surface plasmon resonance analysis revealed that DTPP had a specific affinity to myeloid differentiation factor 2, which consequently suppressed lipopolysaccharide-induced inflammation via interaction with the toll-like receptor 4 signaling pathway. This study provides a potential molecular mechanism underlying the anti-inflammatory effects of DTPP on NAFLD and suggests DTPP as a promising therapeutic strategy for NAFLD treatment. chunk_text: e demonstrated that toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) activation regulates inflammation and ER stress in NAFLD [4,5]. TLR4 is a receptor present in different types of liver cells, such as hepatocytes, stellate cells, and Kupffer cells. It can be activated by microbial products such as lipopolysaccharide (LPS) [6] and endogenous free fatty acids (FFAs) [7]. Upon activation, TLR4 triggers the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, which contribute to the recruitment of immune cells, particularly macrophages, to the liver, thus intensifying the inflammatory response [8]. Moreover, recent research has shed light on the regulatory role of TLR4 in ER stress. ER stress occurs when there is an imbalance between the folding demand of proteins and the capacity of the ER to fold them properly. This triggers the activation of the unfolded protein response (UPR), which restores ER homeostasis. Unresolved UPR can cause liver cell injury and promote inflammation. TLR4 activation has been shown to enhance ER stress in the liver, thereby further exacerbating the inflammatory response and contributing to the progression of NAFLD [9]. Inhibition of the TLR4 signaling pathway has been shown to prevent inflammatory responses and liver damage in experimental models [10,11]. However, the development of specific inhibitors to completely block TLR4 signaling remains a challenge [12], and potential inhibition of TLR4 should be carefully evaluated to prevent unwanted consequences on immune system function. Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM)-derived polysaccharides possess a wide range of biological functions [13,14], and are known for their significant anti-inflammatory properties [15]. Recent studies have also demonstrated their potential role in alleviating hepatic steatosis. For instance, Astragalus polysaccharides (APS) — the main bioactive constituent isolated from the root of Astragalus membranaceus —reduced hepatic ER stress and restored glucose homeostasis in a diabetic mouse model [16]. Compared with commonly used anti-inflammatory drugs such as aspirin, acetaminophen, piroxicam, and ketorolac, TCM polysaccharides serve as a safe, effective, and long-lasting therapeutic approach [17]. Although studies have demonstrated the excellent therapeutic efficacy of TCM polysaccharides, their underlying molecular mechanisms are yet to be fully understood. Dried tangerine peel (DTP), also known as pericarpium citri reticulatae or “Chenpi” in TCM, has gained significant recognition and application [18]. Recent studies have highlighted its remarkable anti-inflammatory properties [19]. Additionally, DTP is effective in regulating abnormal lipid metabolism, thereby benefiting metabolic disorders [20]. However, the therapeutic potential of dried tangerine peel polysaccharide (DTPP) — a crucial component of DTP — in the treatment of hepatic steatosis remains largely unexplored. MD-2 directly recognizes the lipid A domain of LPS, which is required for TLR4 activation. Previously evidence showed that pro-inflammatory cytokines were not induced by LPS in MD-2-/- mice, suggesting that the TLR4-MD-2-LPS complex is essential for the activation of downstream signaling pathway [26]. Although several natural and synthetic chemicals have been developed to neutralize MD-2, none have reached clinical trials or have been applied for the treatment of NAFLD. The mechanism of targeting MD-2 in NAFLD remains elusive. In the current study, DTTP was isolated from mature tangerine peel following 5 years of storage. ER stress and inflammation are recognized as interconnected processes that play vital roles in the development of NAFLD. Our results revealed a reduction in IRE1α, a critical signaling molecule linking ER stress and NF-κB-mediated inflammation [31]. The expression of ER stress-associated genes such as Chop, GRP78, and xbp1s was decreased in LPS-treated macrophages and oleic acid-treated hepatocytes [32]. Besides, DTPP treatment significantly diminished oleic acid-stimulated lipid accumulation in hepatocytes, demonstrating great potential in preventing and treating NAFLD-related inflammation. To evaluate the effectiveness of DTPP as a potential therapy for NAFLD in living organisms, we established a Casper zebrafish model of NAFLD using a high-fat diet. Zebrafish offer a cost-effective and less labor-intensive alternative to rodents, which are commonly used to establish NAFLD models [33,34]. Recent studies have shown that zebrafish have highly c

title: Dried tangerine peel polysaccharide (DTPP) alleviates hepatic steatosis by suppressing TLR4/MD-2-mediated inflammation and endoplasmic reticulum stress
chunk_text: a cost-effective and less labor-intensive alternative to rodents, which are commonly used to establish NAFLD models [33,34]. Recent studies have shown that zebrafish have highly conserved lipid metabolism, making them a suitable model organism for research on NAFLD [35]. During NAFLD development, resident liver macrophages may differentiate into a pro-inflammatory phenotype, triggering the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines and reactive oxygen species [36]. Moreover, macrophages from monocytes can migrate from the peripheral blood to the liver, exacerbating liver injury and abnormal lipid metabolism [37]. To visualize and simulate these symptoms, we utilized Casper zebrafish with the MPEG: EGFP transgenic line, where macrophages are labeled with green fluorescence [38]. The results showed that DTPP reduced macrophage infiltration into the liver and normalized lipid metabolism disorders. To verify the effect of DTPP on TLR4/MD-2 in vivo, the gene expressions of liver tissue from NAFLD zebrafish model were analyzed by RNA-seq. We identified several genes associated with inflammation, as detailed in the Supplementary Materials (Fig. S3). Notably, nearly half of these pro-inflammatory genes exhibited downregulation following DTPP treatment. Prior research has highlighted the role of MyD88 and TRAF6 in the TLR4 signaling pathway, which can lead to an accumulation of unfolded proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), thereby inducing an ER stress response [39]. As shown in Fig. S4, we have also summarized the genes relevant to the TLR4 signaling pathway. Genes such as MyD88

chunk_text: smic reticulum (ER), thereby inducing an ER stress response [39]. As shown in Fig. S4, we have also summarized the genes relevant to the TLR4 signaling pathway. Genes such as MyD88, Traf6, Mapk6, and Mapk9 were all downregulated post-DTPP treatment, suggesting that the therapeutic efficacy of DTPP persists in vivo. Although further studies are needed to investigate the specific molecular mechanisms by which DTPP exerts its effects, expecially for the PERK and ATF6 pathways in future studies to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the effects of DTPP on ER stress response. The establishment of a high-quality NAFLD model using Casper zebrafish provides a valuable tool for understanding the pathogenesis of NAFLD and evaluating potential therapeutic interventions. 5 Conclusion In summary, The present study provides the first evidence that DTPP suppresses LPS-induced inflammation by interfering with the TLR4/MD-2 signaling pathway and alleviates ER stress, thereby mitigating hepatocellular lipid accumulation and ultimately ameliorating hepatic steatosis. Our findings contribute to a better understanding of the pharmacological potential of DTPP and underscores its therapeutic potential in NAFLD treatment. title: Citri Reticulatae Pericarpium (Chenpi): A multi-efficacy pericarp in treating cardiovascular diseases
chunk_text: Citri Reticulatae Pericarpium (CRP) has been utilized as a versatile medicinal herb with wide cardiovascular benefits in Asian nations for centuries. Accumulating evidence suggests that CRP and its components are effective in preventing cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) such as atherosclerosis, myocardial infarction, myocardial ischemia, arrhythmia, cardiac hypertrophy, heart failure, and hypertension. Studies show that the two most bioactive components of CRP are flavonoids and volatile oils. The cardiovascular protective effects of CRP have attracted considerable research interest due to its hypolipidemic, antiplatelet activity, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects. Hereby, we provide a rigorous and up-to-date overview of the cardiovascular protective properties and the potential molecular targets of CRP, and finally highlight the pharmacokinetics and the therapeutic potential of the main pharmacologically active components of CRP to treat CVDs.

title: Citri Reticulatae Pericarpium (Chenpi): A multi-efficacy pericarp in treating cardiovascular diseases
chunk_text: 3 4 https://orcid.org/0000-0001-7272-6917 Citri Reticulatae Pericarpium (CRP) has been utilized as a versatile medicinal herb with wide cardiovascular benefits in Asian nations for centuries. Accumulating evidence suggests that CRP and its components are effective in preventing cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) such as atherosclerosis, myocardial infarction, myocardial ischemia, arrhythmia, cardiac hypertrophy, heart failure, and hypertension. Studies show that the two most bioactive components of CRP are flavonoids and volatile oils. The cardiovascular protective effects of CRP have attracted considerable research interest due to its hypolipidemic, antiplatelet activity, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects. Hereby, we provide a rigorous and up-to-date overview of the cardiovascular protective properties and the potential molecular targets of CRP, and finally highlight the pharmacokinetics and the therapeutic potential of the main pharmacologically active components of CRP to treat CVDs. CRP remains a prevalently used traditional Chinese medicine with abundant resources and easy accessibility. Approxima

chunk_text: ion, generally referred to as Chenpi in Chinese ( Fig. 1) [1]. CRP remains a prevalently used traditional Chinese medicine with abundant resources and easy accessibility. Approximately 140 chemical compounds have been extracted and identified from CRP, including flavonoids, volatile oils, and alkaloids, with flavonoids regarded as the most important bioactive ingredients [2]. CRP extracts, enriched with polymethoxy flavonoids, have been identified as a prospective therapeutic treatment for metabolic disorders and circulatory system diseases due to their remarkable anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and anti-apoptotic activity [3,4]. CRP is commonly used to treat vomiting, nausea, and anemia in traditional Chinese medicine [5]. Flavonoids and volatile oils in CRP are regarded as major constituents, including hesperidin, hesperetin, naringin, and naringenin. These ingredients act separately or in concert to counteract lipid peroxidation, thrombosis, inflammatory responses, as well as endothelial dysfunction [4]. Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) are a category of illnesses that involve the heart and its developed vascular system. Coronary heart disease, stroke, peripheral vascular disease, heart failure, and aneurysm are examples of CVDs [6], the majority of which are intimately associated with the onset and progression of atherosclerosis [7]. Despite recent advances in therapeutic strategies, CVDs continue to be the primary cause of death globally, and their morbidity and mortality are rising annually [8,9]. Therefore, elucidating the pathologies of CVDs and investigating potentia

chunk_text: ue to be the primary cause of death globally, and their morbidity and mortality are rising annually [8,9]. Therefore, elucidating the pathologies of CVDs and investigating potential novel treatments is hence a vital matter. Multiple epidemiological studies reveal a positive association between the citrus flavonoids’ consumption and the cardiovascular mortality reduction [10,11]. In vitro and in vivo investigations have also identified CRP and its main active components to be effective in the treatment of CVDs [12–14]. However, a systematic overview of the cardiovascular protective properties and the underlying mechanisms of CRP in CVDs is scant so far. In this review, the physiologically active compounds from CRP and its cardiovascular effects, potential molecular targets and therapeutic utility were comprehensively summarized and discussed, to provide a deeper understanding of the traditional medicine CRP from “modern” biomedical perspectives, and highlight the superiority of applying CRP and derivatives clinically as promising therapeutics against CVDs and metabolic diseases. 2 Main physiologically active compounds CRP contains categories of chemical components, primarily volatile oils, flavonoids, alkaloids, as well as trace amounts of other elements. Among the active ingredients of CRP, flavonoids are the most well studied and can be extracted in high quantities from CRP [15]. 2.1 Flavonoids As a major class of physiologically active components of CRP, Citrus flavonoids encompass several subgroups of flavonoids, such as C- or O-glycosylated flavones, O-glycosylated flav

Fig. 2 illustrates the structural formulae of several major flavonoid compounds in CRP. Harvest timing and storage time have great influence on the amount of its bioactive flavonoids. According to previous studies, total flavonoids rose as storage duration increased [17,18]. The Chinese Pharmacopeia specifies hesperidin as the index ingredient of CRP and proposes that the percentage content of hesperidin in CRP must not be less than 3.5 %. Accumulating evidence from cellular, animal, and epidemiological studies suggests that regular flavonoid consumption is associated with a reduced risk of CVDs, via its lipid-lowering, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and anti-thrombotic properties, which contributes significantly to the overall health benefits associated with citrus fruit ( Fig. 3) [19]. 2.2 Volatile oil Volatile oil, another prominent active substance in CRP [20], has been shown to possess antioxidant, antibacterial, expectorant, asthma relief, digestive fluid promotion, intestinal gas elimination, coronary artery dilation, and anti-cholestatic effects [21]. Monoterpenes and sesquiterpenes comprise the main components of CRP volatile oil [22] ( Fig. 4). Similar to flavonoids, the volatile oil content and composition vary depending on harvesting period, storag

chunk_text: erpenes comprise the main components of CRP volatile oil [22] ( Fig. 4). Similar to flavonoids, the volatile oil content and composition vary depending on harvesting period, storage time, and extraction methods. CRP had the highest average yield of volatile oil (∼8.94 % in CRP) in September. Although the components of volatile oil with different origins are basically the same, the composition of these components is quite different. For example, with the delay of the harvesting period, the content of limonene increased; nevertheless, the content of β-pinene and α-pinene decreased [23]. Cui et al. investigated the volatile oil content of CRP at various harvest and storage times and discovered that the hydroxyl radical scavenging/reducing ability, and the antioxidant effect of the volatile oils were proportional to the volume fraction of volatile oil [24]. Based on a previous study, the volatile oil content of CRP decreased after steaming (by 1.13 %−1.06 %); however, the total number of volatile oil species did not alter after steaming [25]. 2.3 Alkaloids CRP contains over twenty different alkaloid components. Synephrine, the most widely reported alkaloid, exhibits both vasoconstrictive and expansion effects in the trachea and bronchi. In terms of its properties as a sympathomimetic agent, synephrine (Fig. 4) is characterized by quick action and rapid elimination [26]. It can also increase metabolism by improving fat oxidation. Therefore, this ingredient was commonly used in nutritional supplements for appetite control, weight loss, and mental focus [27]. 2.4 Other chemical co

Therefore, this ingredient was commonly used in nutritional supplements for appetite control, weight loss, and mental focus [27]. 2.4 Other chemical components CRP also contains a significant quantity of the essential nutrients required for human survival, including polyphenols, pectin (15 %−30 %), and inositol [28] (Fig. 4). Additionally, CRP has a high concentration of vitamin C, protein, and carotenoids; in fact, its nutrient density is higher than that of fruit juice. All of these substances are necessary for the human body to function properly. Limonin (Fig. 4) is also widely studied and belongs to the metabolites of the citrus family [29], which has a wide range of pharmacological actions, spanning anti-cancer, anti-inflammatory, anti-oxidation, and liver protection properties [30]. Furthermore, CRP contains many trace elements such as Mg, Mn, Na, Fe, Ti, Cr, K, Sr, Ca, Mo, Cu, Zn, etc. 3 Pharmacokinetics of CRP Bioavailability is a critical consideration in evaluating CRP's bioeffect. The pharmacokinetics of all four main active ingredients in CRP (naringin ( Table 1), naringenin ( Table 2), hesperidin, and hesperetin) have been well investigated. Naringin can be promptly absorbed by oral administration (p.o.) and was detectable in rats in 15 min [31]. In studies with rabbits, oral naringenin was significantly more rapidly absorbed with a higher Cmax but a much shorter residence time compared to naringin [32]. Naringin showed the highest accumulation in the lung, followed by the liver, kidney and muscle, while naringenin showed the highes

chunk_text: shorter residence time compared to naringin [32]. Naringin showed the highest accumulation in the lung, followed by the liver, kidney and muscle, while naringenin showed the highest accumulation in the liver, followed by the kidney, lung and heart [33]. Compared to adult rats, naringenin had a significantly longer Tmax and T1/2, but its Cmax and AUC were relatively higher in aged rats. This may be due to the fact that age affects gastrointestinal tract and hepatorenal function [33,34]. Additionally, even though naringin had a considerable first-pass effect in rats and dogs, the area under the curve (AUC) of naringenin administered by p.o. was significantly higher than intravenous administration (i.v.). This finding suggests that extensive glucuronidation of naringenin occurred during the first pass at gut wall [34–36]. Besides, the pharmacokinetic behavior of naringenin followed linear pharmacokinetics, while the relationship between the dosage and AUC seemed nonlinear [37]. Studies in rats and healthy volunteers indicated that hesperidin has limited bioavailability and must be converted to hesperetin by the colonic microflora before it can be absorbed by colonocytes [38–40]. In contrast, hesperetin is directly and rapidly absorbed by intestinal cells [39,41]. Expectantly, studies have been done to improve the bioavailability of hesperidin are also becoming available. An extensive nine-step fermentation procedure increased the bioactivity of hesperidin, according to Li et al. [42]. The absorption of hesperidin was also dramatically boosted in rats after administration of he

The absorption of hesperidin was also dramatically boosted in rats after administration of hesperidin treated with BglA protein (a protein produced by yeast isolated from CRP). Furthermore, the bioavailability of hesperidin and hesperetin is susceptible to various physiological conditions. Brand et al. [43] identified that concomitant administration of hesperetin with other flavonoids increased the bioavailability of hesperetin. Silberberg et al. [44] discovered that the bioavailability of hesperidin and naringenin was lower in tumor-bearing rats relative to healthy rats. Additionally, hesperetin and hesperidin also exerted effects on the bioavailability of other drugs. For example, hesperetin and hesperidin inhibited cytochrome P450 and improved the bioavailability of some drugs such as diltiazem [45] and verapamil [46]. 4 Cardiovascular actions and molecular targets of CRP A number of recent pharmacological studies indicate that the active components in CRP, especially flavonoids, have protective effects on CVDs, including anti-hypolipidemia, anti-thrombosis, and anti-atherosclerosis. CRP exerts its cardioprotective effect by altering the functions of multiple vascular cells, immune cells and molecular targets associated with CVDs ( Fig. 5). 4.1 Hypolipidemic effects A key contributor to both the initiation and the progression of atherosclerosis is a condition known as dyslipidemia [47]. Studies have illustrated that most of the ingredients of CRP (mainly flavonoids) have the effect of

chunk_text: d the progression of atherosclerosis is a condition known as dyslipidemia [47]. Studies have illustrated that most of the ingredients of CRP (mainly flavonoids) have the effect of lowering blood lipid levels. Emerging evidence indicated that CRP lowered the levels of triglycerides, total cholesterol, and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol [48]. Mechanistically, CRP mainly prevents hyperlipidemia by intervening in the metabolic pathways of taurine and hypotaurine metabolism, fatty acid biosynthesis, as well as arginine and proline metabolism [49]. Additionally, multiple lines of investigations indicate a central role of naringenin and naringin in the hypolipidemic effect of CRP. In vivo, naringenin may promote hypolipidemic and anti-obesity actions through activating transcription factor peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-α (PPAR-α) and subsequently upregulating its target genes for fatty acid oxidation [50]. Naringin, a natural antioxidant, is capable of lowering plasma cholesterol and partially altering the antioxidant status [51]. The cholesterol-lowering effect of naringin, as well as its suppressive effect on aortic fat accumulation, was very likely due to lowering the acyl-coenzyme a-cholesterol acyltransferase (ACAT) activity and increasing the sterol excretion in reaction to cholesterol feeding [52]. ATP-binding cassette transporter 1 (ABCA1) plays a pivotal role in cholesterol and HDL metabolism. Hesperetin was found to promote Apolipoprotein-I-mediated cholesterol efflux from macrophages by increasing ABCA1 expression via the activation of liver X receptor

title: Citri Reticulatae Pericarpium (Chenpi): A multi-efficacy pericarp in treating cardiovascular diseases
chunk_text: HDL metabolism. Hesperetin was found to promote Apolipoprotein-I-mediated cholesterol efflux from macrophages by increasing ABCA1 expression via the activation of liver X receptor α (LXRα) and PPARγ [53]. Together, CRP maintains lipid homeostasis by: (1) activating PPARα transcription factor; (2) inhibiting ACAT activity; (3) inhibiting adipogenesis and lipogenesis; and (4) promoting cholesterol efflux. As such, CRP could serve as an effective therapeutic agent for the treatment of metabolic diseases due to abnormal lipid metabolism. 4.2 Anti-oxidative effects Excess free radicals, including reactive oxygen species (ROS), which are caused by the disruption of the balance between the oxidation and antioxidant systems and are beyond the body’s scavenging capacity, are harmful to cells and tissues [54]. Therefore, oxidative stress is a response that sets in motion a variety of destructive processes [55]. In modern society, the morbidity rate of myocardial ischemia and reperfusion has been markedly increased. Oxidative stress places a high emphasis on this pathological process [56]. Besides, oxidative stress is tightly associated with the high-risk factors of atherosclerosis, such as smoking and obesity. Excessive ROS production during the oxidative stress and oxidation of low-density lipoproteins (LDL) is considered to be one of the initiators of atherosclerosis [57]. Several key studies have confirmed that CRP possesses a potent anti-oxidative effect. CRP can scavenge radicals, hydrogen peroxide and chelate ferrous ions [58]. A number of researchers have also proposed that C

title: Citri Reticulatae Pericarpium (Chenpi): A multi-efficacy pericarp in treating cardiovascular diseases
chunk_text: med that CRP possesses a potent anti-oxidative effect. CRP can scavenge radicals, hydrogen peroxide and chelate ferrous ions [58]. A number of researchers have also proposed that CRP is beneficial in protecting against hydroxyl-induced DNA damage, and that its antioxidant capacity is primarily due to flavonoids, in particular hesperidin and narirutin. Mechanically, these protective effects are linked to radical-scavenging, which entails donating hydrogen atoms (H·) and donating electrons (e) [59]. In a sequence of antioxidant tests, CRP and the main active compounds in CRP (hesperidin, tangeretin and nobiletin) exhibited antioxidant capacity to some degree, which have the effect of scavenging of 2,2-Diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH), hydroxyl radicals, superoxide anion, and hydrogen peroxide [60]. In addition, Wang et al. demonstrated that hesperetin has a protective function against lead-induced oxidative damage in the liver and kidney of rats via its antioxidant activity [61]. Taken together, CRP could be a promising therapeutic candidate for the suppression of oxidative stress. 4.3 Anti-inflammatory effects Increased permeability of endothelial tissue as well as influx of blood leukocytes into the interstitial space characterize inflammation, which ultimately leads to swelling. Mounting studies have illustrated that inflammation plays a crucial role in atherosclerotic plaque progression, vulnerability, and thrombogenicity. CRP possesses powerful anti-inflammatory properties through inhibiting inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS)-mediated NO production [62] and decreasin

chunk_text: bility, and thrombogenicity. CRP possesses powerful anti-inflammatory properties through inhibiting inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS)-mediated NO production [62] and decreasing the secretion of pro-inflammatory factors including tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), interleukin-1β (IL-1β)[63], and interleukin-6 (IL-6) [64]. In addition, CRP is capable of suppressing the activity of cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) [65,66]. CRP exhibited stronger nitric oxide (NO), iNOS, and COX-2 inhibitory efficacy compared to other equivalent mixtures of flavonoids. Chen et al. [67] also pointed out that nobiletin content was positively connected with anti-inflammatory activity and therefore can be a good chemical marker for evaluating the anti-inflammatory impact of CRP from various sources. Noteworthy, oral intake of hesperidin improves endothelial dysfunction and reduces circulating markers of inflammation [68]. Similarly, hesperetin and its principal circulating plasma metabolites effectively inhibited the migration of TNF-α-inflamed human aortic endothelial cells (HAECs) in vitro [69]. This was accompanied and perhaps mediated by a considerable decrease in plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1) levels. Clinically, hesperidin could be used as an anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory agent in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) patients [70]. Mechanistically, the anti-inflammatory effect of hesperidin may be mediated by significant inhibition of IL-1β-induced phosphorylation of c-Jun N-terminal kinases (JNK) and induction of matrix metalloproteinases-3 (MMP-3) and IL-6 [70]. Hesperetin-7-O-glucuronide works similar to hesperetin [71]. In another study, naringin attenuated the generation of chemokines, such as IL-8, MCP-1 and macrophage inflammatory protein-1α (MIP-1α), by interfering with the nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells (NF-κB) and mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling pathways, which partially accounts for its anti-inflammatory effects [72]. Collectively, the evidence suggests that CRP protects against inflammation by inhibiting iNOS and COX-2 production and reducing the expression of inflammatory factors and chemokines. 4.4 Vasodilatory and vasoprotective effects It is clear from persuasive evidence that the endothelium is essential to maintain proper coronary arterial function. Endothelial dysfunction, generally manifested as impairment of endothelium-dependent vasodilation, is a significant contributor to CVDs [73]. Endothelial cells synthesize and release a number of cytokines, such as prostacyclin and NO, which are vital in modulating vascular tone and controlling platelet and leukocyte adhesion, aggregation, and migration [74]. NO appears to be a key element in maintaining normal vascular homeostasis and protecting vessels from atherogenic process-induced injuries [19,75]. A novel role of hesperetin in endothelial cells sheds light on the improvement of endothelial dysfunction in the exploratory clinical trial conducted by Rizza et al. Th

chunk_text: es [19,75]. A novel role of hesperetin in endothelial cells sheds light on the improvement of endothelial dysfunction in the exploratory clinical trial conducted by Rizza et al. The vasoprotective properties of hesperetin may account for the cardiovascular benefits of citrus consumption [68]. Yamamoto et al. demonstrated that glucosyl-hesperidin (G-hesperidin, a water-soluble derivative of hesperidin) ingestion improved acetylcholine induced endothelium-dependent vasodilation in spontaneously hypertensive rats [76]. G-hesperidin was administered to spontaneously hypertensive rats for 8 weeks and was able to reduce pressure parameters as well as improve endothelial response [77]. In addition, they also demonstrated that G-hesperidin and its derivatives induced vasodilatation through enhanced NO production by endothelial cells. In a recent study, hesperetin has also been found to promote vasodilation by activating voltage-operated calcium channels and potassium currents on isolated coronary arteries of rodents [78]. Moreover, the naturally-occurring flavonoid (+/-)-naringenin had a vasorelaxant effect on endothelium-denuded vessels due to the activation of large-conductance calcium-dependent potassium channels (BK channels) in myocytes [79]. Consequently, the vasodilatory and endothelial protective properties of CRP are possibly linked to an increase in NO production. 4.5 Anti-platelet activity and anti-thrombogenic effect Under pathologic situations like atherosclerosis, vascular injury frequently causes hyperactive platelet activation, leading to occlusive thrombus formatio

chunk_text: anti-thrombogenic effect Under pathologic situations like atherosclerosis, vascular injury frequently causes hyperactive platelet activation, leading to occlusive thrombus formation, myocardial infarction, and stroke [80]. Platelets are involved in the processes of hemostasis, thrombosis, and inflammation [81,82]. Citrus flavonoids can modulate blood platelet function involved in the inhibition of clot formation, which is a reversible process. Additionally, citrus flavonoids are thought to prevent platelet aggregation primarily through three pathways: mobilization of intracellular Ca2+, attenuation of activator-induced αIIbβ3 receptor activation, and stimulation of MAPKs and phospholipases [83]. The anti-platelet action of naringenin, naringin, and esculetin isolated from citrus fruits was revealed by Zaragozá et al. [84]. For instance, naringin inhibited platelet aggregation by 90 %, whereas naringenin only inhibited platelet aggregation by 50 %. Two citrus flavonoids, naringenin and hesperidin, were also discovered to bind to and block the αIIbβ3 receptor. The primary ligand of the αIIbβ3 receptor is fibrinogen, which plays a prominent role in platelet activation and aggregation. Among the two flavonoids, the occupancy of the αIIbβ3 receptor is significantly higher in naringin [84]. In addition, hesperidin was able to suppress collagen-, arachidonic acid-, adenosine diphosphate- (ADP) and thrombin-induced rat platelet aggregation both in vitro and in vivo. Naringin, but not ADP, also prevented platelet aggregation induced by collagen, arachidonic acid, or thrombin. In viv

chunk_text: in-induced rat platelet aggregation both in vitro and in vivo. Naringin, but not ADP, also prevented platelet aggregation induced by collagen, arachidonic acid, or thrombin. In vivo, the oral administration of hesperidin extended mouse tail vein bleeding time in a dose-dependent manner. In light of these findings, it appears that hesperidin possesses anti-platelet activity and may be advantageous for individuals at high risk of CVDs [85]. However, the precise chemical mechanism underlying the anti-platelet actions of citrus fruit flavonoids is still incompletely understood and merits further investigation. 4.6 Modulatory effects on neutrophils Neutrophils are a type of polymorphonuclear leukocytes that serve as the first line of defense for our immune system. Despite their critical role in innate immunity, neutrophil activation is not always beneficial. Accumulating evidence indicates that neutrophils play an important role in the progression of CVDs, such as atherosclerosis, thrombosis, and acute coronary syndromes (ACS) [86]. Flavonoids (hesperidin and naringin) inhibited the synthesis of platelet-activating factor (PAF), a strong inflammatory lipid necessary for neutrophil activation and chemotaxis [87] in H2O2-treated endothelial cells [88] and decreased neutrophil infiltration in a rat air pouch model [89]. In view of the significant role of neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) in CADs [90,91], the potential effect of CRP flavonoids on NET formation remains to be studied further. 5 Therapeutic effects of CRP in CVDs Numerous in vivo and in vitro studies provided evidenc

chunk_text: , the potential effect of CRP flavonoids on NET formation remains to be studied further. 5 Therapeutic effects of CRP in CVDs Numerous in vivo and in vitro studies provided evidence demonstrating that CRP was effective in preventing and treating CVDs [92–94]. 5.1 Atherosclerosis Atherosclerosis, a chronic inflammatory disease of vascular system, is one of the leading causes of other CVDs. Atherosclerosis causes narrowing of the arteries, which disrupts the basic structural elements of the blood vessels, leading to a partial or complete obstruction of the arteries. Ischemic heart failure, stroke, and myocardial infarction can all be caused by atherosclerosis of the coronary artery, which results in irregular blood flow. In experimental animal models, citrus flavonoids are able to prevent the formation of atherosclerosis. Assini et al. demonstrated that naringenin attenuated inflammation and adipose tissue expansion in LDLr-/- mice fed with cholesterol-enriched diets, thus showing a significant protective effect against atherosclerosis [95]. Similar findings were recently observed that naringenin also decreased plasma levels of non-high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, endothelial dysfunction biomarker expression, monocyte adhesion to endothelial cells, and smooth muscle cell proliferation [96]. Naringin has also exhibited potential protective effects against atherosclerosis development, especially for diet-induced atherosclerosis [97]. The anti-atherosclerosis capabilities of naringin include hypocholesterolemic and high density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) elevating prop

title: Citri Reticulatae Pericarpium (Chenpi): A multi-efficacy pericarp in treating cardiovascular diseases
chunk_text: for diet-induced atherosclerosis [97]. The anti-atherosclerosis capabilities of naringin include hypocholesterolemic and high density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) elevating properties [52]. Additionally, Choe et al. revealed that naringin attenuated atherosclerosis plaques partly by lowering cholesterol and inhibiting ICAM-1 expression, thereby inhibiting macrophage infiltration [98]. Further research revealed that naringin represses cell invasion and migration via inhibition of PI3K/AKT/mTOR/p70S6K pathway, and suppresses MMP-9 expression via inactivation of the transcription factors NF-kB and activator protein-1 (AP-1) in TNF-α-induced vascular smooth muscle cells [99], which provides a theoretical basis for the preventive use of naringin for atherosclerosis. Collectively, these findings point to the possibility that CRP could represent as a feasible therapy option for atherosclerosis and atherosclerotic CVDs. 5.2 Myocardial ischemia and arrhythmias Myocardial ischemia is a pathological state in which blood perfusion to the heart is reduced and results in a lower supply of oxygen to the heart and aberrant energy metabolism in myocardium [100]. Cardiac arrhythmias are irregularities or disruptions in the normal activation or beating of the heart myocardium. Patients generally experience dizziness, palpitations, rapid heartbeat, and weakness [101]. In an induced myocardial I/R injury rat model, hesperidin was shown to alleviate arrhythmias and infarct size. Hesperidin significantly increased the tissue nitrite, antioxidant level and reduced inflammation, arrhythmias and

title: Citri Reticulatae Pericarpium (Chenpi): A multi-efficacy pericarp in treating cardiovascular diseases
chunk_text: hesperidin was shown to alleviate arrhythmias and infarct size. Hesperidin significantly increased the tissue nitrite, antioxidant level and reduced inflammation, arrhythmias and apoptosis ratio. Overall, hesperidin has a protective effect against arrhythmias and apoptosis caused by focal myocardial ischemia [102]. Selvaraj et al. evaluated the cardioprotective efficacy of hesperidin in rats with isoproterenol-induced myocardial ischemia and found that hesperidin was effective in improving cardiac function and inhibiting myocardial injury [103]. According to this research, the cardioprotective impact of hesperidin on ischemic rats could be mediated by its anti-lipid peroxidative and antioxidant characteristics. In a rat model of acute infarction, naringenin exerted anti-ischemic effects through activation of BK channels and significantly reduced I/R-induced cardiac injury [104]. In addition, Zhang et al. demonstrated that pretreatment of nobiletin (30 mg/kg, i.v.) improved myocardial I/R injury by downregulating the myocardial expression of ERS-related signal molecules, but activating the pro-surviving PI3K/AKT pathway [105]. In summary, citrus flavonoids as main active component of CRP are highly promising therapeutic agents in controlling arrhythmias and myocardial ischemia. 5.3 Heart failure Heart failure is referred to a complex clinical illness defined by abnormal changes in the structure or function of heart [106]. Heart failure occurs when the heart is unable to pump blood effectively owing to weakening or stiffness of the heart muscle, resulting in symptoms such as

title: Citri Reticulatae Pericarpium (Chenpi): A multi-efficacy pericarp in treating cardiovascular diseases
chunk_text: function of heart [106]. Heart failure occurs when the heart is unable to pump blood effectively owing to weakening or stiffness of the heart muscle, resulting in symptoms such as diminished energy, trouble breathing, weight gain, and swelling of the legs or abdomen [107]. In an aortic banding (AB) model [108], hesperetin protects against cardiac remodeling caused by pressure overload through suppressing cardiac hypertrophy, fibrosis, oxidative stress, and myocyte apoptosis. The inactivation of PKCα/βII-AKT, JNK and transforming growth factor β1 (TGFβ1) signaling pathways was responsible for the inhibitory action of hesperetin on cardiac remodeling. The cited data indicates that hesperidin may be an effective treatment for heart failure. In an established senescent model of myocardial cells, naringenin showed potential anti-aging effects, as evidenced by decreased radical oxidative species (ROS) production, and increased mitochondrial metabolic activity and calcium-buffering capacity [109], indicating that Naringenin might play a protective role in age-associated cardiometabolic disorders, including heart failure. Overall, the above studies supported the idea that hesperidin and naringenin from CRP had anti-heart failure effects both in vivo and in vitro. 5.4 Pathological cardiac hypertrophy One of the most important risk factors for heart failure is pathological cardiac hypertrophy, characterized by hypertrophic growth in ventricular dimensions coupled with myocardial fibrosis and dysfunction [110,111]. At the molecular level, PPAR-γ is one of the essential inhibitors of

title: Citri Reticulatae Pericarpium (Chenpi): A multi-efficacy pericarp in treating cardiovascular diseases
chunk_text: d by hypertrophic growth in ventricular dimensions coupled with myocardial fibrosis and dysfunction [110,111]. At the molecular level, PPAR-γ is one of the essential inhibitors of cardiac hypertrophy development [112]. Interestingly, CRP prevented Angiotensin II (Ang II)-induced pathological cardiac hypertrophy, as indicated by enhancing cardiac function, reducing hypertrophic growth and minimizing cardiac fibrosis via upregulation of PPARγ expression [113]. In line with this finding, Bhargava et al. [114] found that in male albino Wistar rats, hesperidin inhibited oxidative stress and apoptosis, improved cardiac hemodynamics and mitigated cardiac hypertrophy by increasing PPAR-γ expression. These studies consistently emphasized the vital role of PPAR-γ in CRP-mediated attenuation of pathological cardiac hypertrophy. 5.5 Hypertension Hypertension is primarily manifested by elevated arterial pressure in the body circulation, which is a significant etiology and risk contributor to the availability of a wide range of CVDs and cerebrovascular diseases [115–117]. Hypertension negatively impacts the structure and function of vital organs such as the heart, brain, and kidneys, ultimately leading to organ failure [118,119]. There is a substantial causal association between blood pressure levels and the morbidity and mortality of CVDs [120]. Prior research found that a single oral administration or intraperitoneal injection of G-hesperidin reduced systolic blood pressure in a dose-dependent manner. This effect was significantly blocked by an endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS)

chunk_text: ritoneal injection of G-hesperidin reduced systolic blood pressure in a dose-dependent manner. This effect was significantly blocked by an endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) inhibitor NG-nitro-L-arginine methyl ester (L-NAME). Specifically, the hypotensive effect of hesperetin was associated with NO-mediated vasodilation in spontaneously hypertensive rats (SHRs) [77]. Another study revealed that taking G-hesperidin on a sustained basis lowered oxidative stress in SHRs by reducing the expression of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate oxidase (NOX) in the vasculature, hence alleviating endothelial dysfunction and hypertension [76]. Furthermore, in stroke-prone spontaneously hypertensive rats, hesperidin modulated NO synthesis and protected the endothelial function from ROS [121]. In addition, blood pressure and heart rate decreased in SHRs under the treatment of hesperidin and glucosyl hesperidin, suggesting that hesperidin and glucosyl hesperidin exhibited an anti-hypertensive impact on hypertensive animals [122]. Thus, it appears that CRP represents a viable pharmacological candidate of hypertension in the clinic. 6 Conclusions and perspectives In this paper, the chemical composition and experimental research of CRP are refined and summarized by evaluating the literature published in recent years. The CRP has a great amount of production and is very easily obtainable. Besides, CRP contains multiple active components including flavonoids, volatile oils, and alkaloids. Citrus flavonoids can regulate the occurrence and progression of CVDs through a diverse range

chunk_text: ntains multiple active components including flavonoids, volatile oils, and alkaloids. Citrus flavonoids can regulate the occurrence and progression of CVDs through a diverse range of mechanisms and multiple pathways, including improving lipid metabolism, reducing inflammatory responses, suppressing oxidative stress, controlling thrombosis, protecting blood vessels, and inhibiting neutrophil chemotaxis. Due to the abundance of its targets and cardiovascular protective effects, as well as plentiful chemicals it includes, CRP is capable of protecting against CVDs efficiently in multiple points. Additional work is needed to explain the specific mechanism of the major components of CRP for the precise prevention and treatment of CVDs. As a flavonoid component unique to CRP, hesperidin possesses potent anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties. Since inflammation and oxidative stress play a significant role in the development of CVDs, hesperidin, the major bioactive component of CRP, has great application potential. Compared with the expensive medications and the other traditional medicine for the treatment of CVDs, CRP is a commonly used herb with wide distribution, abundant resources, easy cultivation, high medicinal value, less toxic, and edible, which offers a great deal of potential for exploitation as a cardiovascular drug. New mechanisms for the treatment of CVDs of citrus flavonoids also continue to be of significant interest in future studies. For example, the CRP flavonoid quercetin is a newly found ferroptosis inhibitor also with exceptionally high antioxidant prope

title: Citri Reticulatae Pericarpium (Chenpi): A multi-efficacy pericarp in treating cardiovascular diseases
chunk_text: inue to be of significant interest in future studies. For example, the CRP flavonoid quercetin is a newly found ferroptosis inhibitor also with exceptionally high antioxidant properties [123], which provides an impetus to further explore the potential effect of CRP on other non-apoptotic programs of death, such as pyroptosis, necroptosis, and recently reported cuproptosis [124] in CVDs. Furthermore, CRP flavonoids have also been demonstrated to modulate protein degradation through the cellular mitophagy pathway [125,126]. Thus, is it realistic to assume that CRP may regulate proteotoxic stress to limit cuproptosis [127]? Citrus flavonoids have a limited solubility and absorption rate since they are weakly acidic or alkaline. However, modification of dosage forms can markedly enhance their absorption. For example, glycosylation of flavonoids was able to increase their water solubility and bioactivity while lowering their toxic effects. Besides, creating solid lipid nanoparticles of citrus flavonoids can also improve their absorption [128,129]. Methods such as molecular modifications, multiple active substance complexation, and targeted positioning might be explored to increase the absorption qualities of citrus flavonoids in the gastrointestinal system and successfully improve their bioavailability. Collectively, comprehensively reviewing the literature can provide a more detailed summary of the various chemical constituents of CRP and their pharmacological activities in CVDs. This will be helpful to facilitate the development of CRP in both basic research and clinical use,

This will be helpful to facilitate the development of CRP in both basic research and clinical use, which is envisioned to have a broader application prospect. title: Effects of aging on the fine structure, chain conformation, and morphology of Chenpi polysaccharides
chunk_text: The aging process endows Chenpi (Pericarpium Citri Reticulatae) with unique value and efficacy. This study investigated the dynamic changes in the fine structure, chain conformation, and morphology of water-soluble polysaccharides from Chenpi over time. In the initial storage period of Chenpi (1 year), Chenpi polysaccharides (CP) exhibited a triple-helical structure, with chains entangled and aggregated into rough spherical conformations. Galacturonic acid (GalA, 47.78 mol%) was the predominant monosaccharide. However, AFM results indicated aggregation phenomena in 15-year CP. Additionally, CP viscosity decreased while thermal stability improved, reflecting the natural structural transformation of CP. This study provides scientific evidence supporting the application of Chenpi in the food and pharmaceutical industries.

Thermal analysis and rheological measurements provided further insight into the structural characteristics of CP. As Chenpi aged, the extraction yield of CP increased significantly, which may have been related to reduced polysaccharide viscosity, smaller molecular size, and a lower degree of methyl esterification. In addition, total sugar content slightly declined, while total protein content initially decreased and then increased. Table 1 revealed that the main components of CP include GalA, Ara, and Gal, followed by Glc and Rha, reflecting the characteristic structure of pectin. Although the aging process did not alter the types of monosaccharides in the polysaccharides, it significantly affected the relative content of monosaccharides as well as the associated structural and functional properties. As aging progressed, the content of GalA significantly decreased from 47.78 mol% in the first year to 23.61 mol% in the fifteenth year, indicating the gradual breakdown of the HG domain in the polysaccharide backbone. The molar percentage of HG further revealed that the degradation rate of CP was relatively slow during the initial storage period (18.5 %) but accelerated to 25.9 % in the later stages. Due to the mild storage conditions of Chenpi, this aging process differed from the typical β-elimination reactions induced by high temperatures or alkaline conditions and was more likely triggered by specific enzymes produced by microorganisms. chunk_text: rvations from AFM. 4 Conclusion This study investigated the dynamic changes in the structure, chain conformation, and morphology of water-soluble CP over time. The results showed that during the initial aging period (1 year), the primary monosaccharide of CP was GalA (47.78 mol%), and the main structural domain was HG (44.56 mol%). As aging progressed, CP molecules degraded at a gradually decreasing rate, primarily in the HG region, which decreased to 20.01 mol% by 15 years. Additionally, the molecular sizes (Mw, Mn, Rg, and particle size) continuously decreased, accompanied by a reduction in the DE and a weakening of the semicrystalline structure. Some neutral sugars gradually integrated into the polysaccharide side chains during degradation, forming dense molecular layers, and ultimately leading to RG-I becoming the main structural domain (69.42 mol%), with Ara gradually becoming the main monosaccharide (41.38 mol%). These analyses were supported by data from FT-IR, NMR, and monosaccharide composition. Results of SEC-MALLS, AFM, and TEM showed that CP from different years exhibited spherical conformations, but the formation mechanisms varied. During the initial aging period, CP possessed a triple-helical structure, with some flexible chains entangled to form rough spheres. As aging progressed, the aggregates dissociated, and polysaccharide side chains accumulated, resulting in smooth spheres with clear boundaries. The reduction in molecular size and the accumulation of highly branched side chains made the molecular conformation more compact, increasing single-molecule den

By 15 years, CP15 was completely degraded, losing the triple-helical structure entirely, with uniform molecular sizes all below 20 nm, and AFM results indicated that 15-year CP showed aggregation phenomena. Besides, the viscosity of CP decreased, and thermal stability improved, reflecting the natural structural transformation of CP. This study not only provided new insights into the effects of aging on CP but also offered essential theoretical support for the further development and utilization of Chenpi's functional properties and physiological activities. title: Accurate and visualiable discrimination of Chenpi age using 2D-CNN and Grad-CAM++ based on infrared spectral images
chunk_text: Dried tangerine peel (“Chenpi”), has numerous clinical and nutritional benefits, with its quality being significantly influenced by its storage age, referred to as “Chen Jiu Zhe Liang” in Chinese. Concequently, the rapid and accurate identification of Chenpi's age is important for consumers. In this study, Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) was employed to capture spectral images of Chenpi. These FTIR images were then analyzed using a two-dimensional convolutional neural networks (2D-CNN) model, achieving a discrimination accuracy of 97.92%. To address the “black box” nature of the 2D-CNN, Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping Plus Plus (Grad-CAM++) was utilized to highlight the important regions contributing to the model's performance. Additionally, six other machine learning models were developped using features identified by the 2D-CNN to validate their effectiveness. The results demonstrated that the combination of FTIR spectral images and 2D-CNN provides a highly effective method for accurately determining the age of Chenpi.

Dried tangerine peel (“Chenpi”), has numerous clinical and nutritional benefits, with its quality being significantly influenced by its storage age, referred to as “Chen Jiu Zhe Liang” in Chinese. Concequently, the rapid and accurate identification of Chenpi's age is important for consumers. In this study, Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) was employed to capture spectral images of Chenpi. These FTIR images were then analyzed using a two-dimensional convolutional neural networks (2D-CNN) model, achieving a discrimination accuracy of 97.92%. To address the “black box” nature of the 2D-CNN, Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping Plus Plus (Grad-CAM++) was utilized to highlight the important regions contributing to the model's performance. Additionally, six other machine learning models were developped using features identified by the 2D-CNN to validate their effectiveness. The results demonstrated that the combination of FTIR spectral images and 2D-CNN provides a highly effective method for accurately determining the age of Chenpi. Keywords FTIR

By addressing these objectives, this study aims to provide a reliable and interpretable solution for Chenpi age identification, benefiting the food industry in quality control and increasing consumer confidence in Chenpi products. 2 Sample and data description In this study, 39 Chenpi samples were purchased from ten different companies located in Jiangmen, Guangdong Province, China, specifically sourced from the Xinhui region. These samples were harvested in the years 2014, 2016, 2018 and 2020. Detailed information of the Chenpi samples is summarized in Table S1 (Supporting information). Notably, the production of Xinhui Chenpi follows the traditional process of sun-drying fresh citrus peels and then storing them in a ventilated and dry environment to mature. In order to minimise the influence of unknown external factors on the analysis results, all samples were subjected to experimental analysis as soon as possible after purchase. FTIR data were collected from the 39 Chenpi samples in the mid-infrared spectral range of 400–4000 cm−1 (FTIR, Nicolet iS5, Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc., USA). The samples were pre-treated, milled and remov

chunk_text: om the 39 Chenpi samples in the mid-infrared spectral range of 400–4000 cm−1 (FTIR, Nicolet iS5, Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc., USA). The samples were pre-treated, milled and removed by a 60 mesh sieve. The FTIR spectrum of the Chenpi powder was measured by potassium bromide (KBr, purchased from Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China) pellet method. The samples were weighted 1 mg and mixed with 100 mg of KBr uniformly, pressed it into a transparent flake for measurement. The accompanying OMNIC software was used for infrared spectroscopy analysis. The objective of this study was to accurate classify and analyze these samples based on their harvest year. Each sample was measured six times, generating a total of 234 spectral data from the original 39 samples. The data were organized into a data matrix of size 234 × 7468. 3 Methodology 3.1 Deep learning 3.1.1 Two-dimensional convolutional neural networks FTIR spectral classification using 2D-CNN involves treating spectral data as two-dimensional images, extracting spatial and spectral features through convolution and pooling, and progressively learning abstract features to achieve accurate classification. This approach has high potential in infrared spectral tasks due to its ability to handle complex features, improve classification accuracy, and reduce overfitting. By carefully designing the network structure and appropriately adjusting the parameters, these advantages can be fully utilized to enhance spectral analysis. This paper introduces a 2D-CNN model specially designed for FTIR spectral image processing

chunk_text: ing the parameters, these advantages can be fully utilized to enhance spectral analysis. This paper introduces a 2D-CNN model specially designed for FTIR spectral image processing tasks. The model employs three successive convolutional layers to extract hierarchical features from the input images. Each convolutional layer consists of convolution operations followed by batch normalization, ReLU activation, and maximum pooling. This design not only enhances feature extraction capabilities but also reduces the model's parameter count, thereby improving computational efficiency. Starting with a three-channel input image, the initial convolutional layer progressively transforms it into feature maps with 16, 32, and 64 channels, respectively. These feature maps are further compressed through fully connected layers, enabling the mapping from high-dimensional data to the final classification predictions. The output layer utilizes the log softmax function to generate probabilities for each category, making the model suitable for multi-category classification tasks. The structured 2D-CNN architecture exemplifies the efficacy of deep learning in image recognition and classification. By stacking convolutional layers, the model extracts intricate details from input images, enabling precise classification. The architectural diagram of the 2D-CNN structure was illustrated in Fig. 1 . 3.1.2 Visualization method The 2D-CNN is often considered as a “black box” model in deep learning. chunk_text: he 2D-CNN is often considered as a “black box” model in deep learning. To gain deeper insights into the decision-making process of the 2D-CNN model and validate its interpretability, we employed the Grad-CAM++ method for model visualization in this study. Grad-CAM++ is an advanced version of the Grad-CAM technique, which generates class activation maps by leveraging gradient information to highlight the image regions the model focuses on when recognizing target categories (Moujahid et al., 2022). In the present study, we first propagated the input images through the trained 2D-CNN model to obtain its predictions. Subsequently, we used the Grad-CAM++ method to compute the gradients of the output layer with respect to the convolutional feature maps, generating class activation maps based on these gradients. Finally, these maps were overlaid onto the original images to create intuitive heatmaps, revealing the critical regions the model relies on during classification decisions. By utilizing Grad-CAM++ for visualization, we not only validated the model's performance on specific tasks but also uncovered its internal mechanisms, providing a clearer understanding of the model's behavior. This visualization method provides strong support for interpreting deep learning models, thereby enhancing their transparency and credibility. 3.1.3 Data augmentation Deep learning models relys on large datasets for effective training, and data augmentation (DA) techniques can be used to enhance model performance by increasing the diversity of instances through synthesized data (Shorten & Khoshgof

DT is a popular supervised learning method used for both classification and regression problems. The algorithm works by recursively splitting the dataset into smaller subsets based on the value of the most informative feature at each step. It selects a feature as the current node and calculates its information gain or entropy. The feature with the highest information gain or entropy is chosen for the split. This process repeats until the stopping condition is met (Kim, 2016). In this study, grid search was employed to tune the hyperparameters of the decision tree model, and each parameter configuration was evaluated using 4-fold cross-validation. The optimal settings were determined to be a maximum depth of 3, a minimum number of samples required to split an internal node of 2, and a minimum number of samples required to be at a leaf node of 4. XGBoost is an advanced implementation of gradient boosting that has gained widespread recognition for its high performance in both classification and regression tasks. It enhances model accuracy through the integration of multiple weak classifiers (typically decision trees) into a single strong learner (Qiu et al., 2022). XGBoost introduces additional regularization terms and penalty functions in its objective function to control model complexity and assess overfitting risks, making it more robust than standard gradient boosting. Model hyperparameters were initially adjusted using the training set. The accuracy or loss on the validation set was then used to further tune the hyperparameters, helping to accelerate the model's convergence. Finally, the test set was used to evaluate the model's performance. Evaluating the performance of a classifier model is crucial. Common evaluation metrics include classification accuracy, precision, recall, and F1_score (Adegun et al., 2023). The metrics were definedas follows: Accuracy measures the proportion of correct predictions out of the total number of cases examined, providing an overall evaluation of the model's classification performance. It is calculated as: (1) Accracy = TP + TN TP + TN + FP + FN where, TP (True Positives) is the number of samples correctly predicted as positive, FP (False Positives) is the number of negative samples incorrectly predicted as positive, TN (True Negatives) is the number of samples correctly predicted as negative, and FN (False Negatives) is the number of positive samples incorrectly predicted as negative. Precision measures

The results reveal a significant overlap in the spectral features among Chenpi samples from different years, which propose a challenge for differentiating the sample classes using conventional methods such as cosine similarity or Euclidean distance. To overcome this limitation and improve the classification accuracy, we constructed a 2D-CNN specifically designed for spectral image classification. This model's performance was then compared with traditional machine learning methods that utilize spectral data. The analysis and validation process for the 2D-CNN model is illustrated in Fig. 2 . 4.2 Deep learning classification results 4.2.1 Classification results of 2D-CNN Plotting the loss value and accuracy curves of datasets is an essential method for evaluating the learning progress and detecting overfitting or underfitting in a deep learning model (Zhao et al., 2021). The loss curves indicate a trend of convergence and reduction, suggesting that the learning process is been optimized. Meanwhile, the accuracy curves show the model's performance improvements on both the training and validation sets, highlighting its ability to learn and generalise. As shown in Fig. 3a, the training and validation loss and accuracy for the 2D-CNN model demonstrate a clear reduction in training loss and a corresponding increase in accuracy over the epochs, reflecting the model's learning efficiency (Dong, 2024), which is a positive outcome. After evaluating the relationship between the number of iterations and the model's runtime, we identified the optimal parameter settings for the 2D-CNN model as follows: “epoch” at 50, “learning rate” at 0.008, and “batchsize” at 12. Then, the 2D-CNN model was established using the optimized parameters (as depicted in Step 1 in Fig. 2). The classification results for the test set are illustrated in Fig. 4a and Fig. 4b. The model achieved impressive performance on the test set, misclassifying only one out of 47 samples. The final evaluation metrics on the test set obtain an accuracy of 97.92%, precision of 98.12%, recall of 97.91%, and F1_score of 97.92% (Table 1 ). These results highlight the robustness and precision of the 2D-CNN architecture in making accurate predictions, validating its potential for application in classification tasks. Moreover, the high accuracy and consistency across multiple evaluation metrics suggest that the 2D-CNN model is well-suited for applications that require precise and reliable classification. While the performance of a model often depends on the richness of the provided information (Luo et al., 2022), excessive augmentation can lead to information loss, making it challenging for the model to learn effective features. Additionally, it increases computational demands, prolongs training time and escalates resource costs. Therefore, it is crucial to carefully selected appropriate augmentation methods. To explore the impact of different augmentation strategies, we randomly performed combinations of 3, 7, and all 10 augmentation methods, resulting in datasets of different sizes (Table 1). These datasets were also split into training, validation and test sets, and 2D-CNN models were established accordingly. Among them, the model utilizing the three augmentation (3-DA) methods achieved the highest classification accuracy. The corresponding training and validation loss and accuracy for this model are presented in Fig. 3b. In constrast, the models based on 7-DA and 10-DA combinations, although benefiting from larger data sizes, exhibited a significant drop in model performance. When comparing the accuracy before (Fig. 4a and Fig. 4b) and after augmentation (Fig. 4c and Fig. 4d), it was found that the model's accuracy remained consistent, suggesting that the original data was sufficiently diverse and representative, providing the important features needed for the model to learn effectively. Consequently, we opted to use the original data for subsequent analyses. 4.2.2 Visualization of 2D-CNN identified features The Grad-CAM++ algorithm is employed to generate a heatmap of the gradients of the weights in the final convolutional layer, thus providing a visual representation of the network model's decision-making process (as illustrated in Step 2 of Fig. 2). On the Grad-CAM++ heatmap, the darker red areas indicate the features that are most critical for category localisation. In this study, these features were visualized, and the results for Chenpi samples from four different years are displayed in Fig. 6a. It is evident that the highlighted areas vary across different years, reflecting how the model's focus shifts based on the imput spectral images. This visualization enhances the transparency and interpretability of the model's decisions, allowing us to intuitively grasp the key features the model focuses on when distinguishing between categories. To address this, we extend our research by appliying the six aforementioned machine learning methods in conjunction with different variable selection methods to establish discriminant models. 4.3 Machine learning modelling results At first, six machine learning models were established without applying any feature selection techniques. As can be seen from Table 2, models such as XGBoost and DT showed high accuracy values of 93.62% and 91.49%, respectively, demonstrating their strong performance in the classification task. Similarly, the LR, KNN, and PLS-DA models also performed relatively well, with accuracy values of 87.13%, 87.23% and 85.21%, respectively, indicating their ability to handle the dataset effectively despite the presence of potentially irrelevant features. However, GBDT model had a lower accuracy of 70.21%, indicating that the model might be negatively affected by irrelevant or redundant variables. This observation underscores the importance of feature selection in enhancing model performance by eliminating noise and focusing on the most informative variables. The results presented in Table 2 indicated that the introduction of feature selection had a significant impact on model performance. Specifically, AdaBoost feature selection markedly improved the classification accuracy of GBDT, DT and XGBoost models, maintained the accuracy of KNN, while slightly decreased the accuracy for LR and significantly for PLS-DA. On the other hand, Boruta feature selection improved the accuracy of GBDT, LR and DT models, while reduced the accuracy of KNN, PLS-DA and XGBoost models. These results highlight the importance of integrating machine learning algorithms with appropriate feature selection methods to improve classification accuracy. Finally, the results of six models based on three feature selection methods were compared (Fig. S3). The comparsion reveals that models such as GBDT, LR, KNN, and PLS-DA built on 2D-CNN identified features exhibit higher accuracy than those established using other two feature selection methods (Fig. S3a). This demonstrates the superior ability of 2D-CNN to extract relevant and informative features, thereby enhancing the performance of these models compared to Adaboost and Boruta. In addition, the accuracy of the DT model remains unchanged regardless of the feature selection method, while the XGBoost model established on 2D-CNN identified features achieves better accauacy with Boruta and lower with AdaBoost. Moreover, the features identified by the 2D-CNN were visualized using the Grad-CAM++ technique, which helps to avoid the “black box” phenomenon commonly associated with deep learning models. To further validate the effectiveness of the features identified by the 2D-CNN, they were input into six different machine learning methods to establish classification models. The results indicated that the 2D-CNN model established on the FTIR spectral images not only outperformed other used methods but also demonstrated that the features selected by 2D-CNN show good interpretability and classification accuracy across various machine learning models. Therefore, our research lays a solid foundation for further research and the optimisation of deep learning based feature extraction methods. title: FT-NIR combined with machine learning was used to rapidly detect the adulteration of pericarpium citri reticulatae (chenpi) and predict the adulteration concentration
chunk_text: Pericarpium citri reticulatae (PCR) has been used as a food and spice for many years and is known for its rich nutritional content and unique aroma. However, price increases are often accompanied by adulteration. In this study, two kinds of adulterants (Orange peel-OP and Mandarin Rind-MR) were identified by chromaticity analysis, FT-NIR and machine learning algorithm, and the doping concentration was predicted quantitatively. The results show that colorimetric analysis cannot completely differentiate between PCR and adulterants. Using spectral preprocessing combined with machine learning algorithms, PCR and two adulterants were successfully distinguished, with classification accuracy reaching 99.30 % and 98.64 % respectively. After selecting characteristic wavelengths, the R2 P of the adulterated quantitative model is greater than 0.99. Generally, this study proposes to use FT-NIR to study the adulteration of PCR for the first time, which fills the technical gap in the adulteration research of PCR, and provides an important method to solve the increasingly serious adulteration problem of PCR.

It can be clearly seen with the naked eye that the surface colors of the three pure samples are significantly different. However, when PCR powder is mixed with different proportions (10 %, 20 %, 30 %, 40 %, 50 %) of OP and MR, the surface color of the sample will change to a certain extent. Specifically, when the adulteration ratio is low, the color is basically similar to that of PCR powder. As the adulteration ratio gradually increases, the color of the sample gradually changes to the adulterants, which makes it difficult for us to distinguish it with the naked eye. In order to further study the color changes of PCR and its adulterants, we used colorimetric analysis technology to measure the colors of three pure samples and two adulterants with different proportions, and obtained the color values L⁎, a⁎ and b⁎. In CIELAB chromaticity space, they represent brightness value, red-green value and yellow-blue value respectively. Among the three pure samples, PCR has the lowest L⁎ value and b⁎ value, and the highest a⁎ value (Fig. 1B). As the adulteration ratio increases, whether it is adulterated with OP powder (Fig. 1C) or MR powder (Fig. 1D), the L⁎ and b⁎ values of the sample gradually increase, and the a⁎ value gradually decreases. In order to further distinguish PCR and adulterants, we used PCA and t-SNE to perform visual analysis on the original NIR spectral information. Principal component analysis (PCA) is a widely used linear dimensionality reduction technique that transforms original variables into new variables that are linear combinations of the original variables. In contrast, t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) is a nonlinear dimensionality reduction technique that can map high-dimensional data to a low-dimensional space while retaining the local structure of the data (Yan et al., 2022). It can be seen from the PCA plots of the three pure samples (Fig. 2D) that principal components 1 and 2 contributed 87.9 % and 10.2 % to the variance respectively, and the first two principal components accounted for more than 98 % of the variance, which shows that the PCA model captures most of the information in the NIR spectrum. The visualization results show that the three pure samples can be clearly distinguished, and the samples adulterated with OP (Fig. 2E) and MR (Fig. 2F) can also be distinguished from pure PCR, but the adulterants in adjacent proportions are closer. All in all, through PCA and t-SNE visual analysis, it can be seen that PCR and adulterants with different proportions have obvious clustering trends, so it is necessary to combine spectral preprocessing and classification models to distinguish them. 3.2.2 Machine learning discriminant analysis based on spectral preprocessing In order to find out the difference between PCR and adulterants, we further preprocessed the spectra and developed five machine learning algorithms for differentiation. SVM takes the optimal hyperplane as the core to maximize the distance between different categories of points and the hyperplane (Amirvaresi & Parastar, 2021). RF make predictions by building multiple decision trees and combining them. GBM iteratively train a series of decision trees to gradually improve the performance of the overall model (Sun et al., 2021). KNN calculates the distance between the unknown sample and all samples in the training set, then selects the K closest samples to predict by voting or averaging. PLS-DA uses dimensionality reduction technology to find a new feature space that can distinguish different categories to the greatest extent, and then uses this new feature space for classification and prediction. title: Efficiency of four different dietary preparation methods in extracting functional compounds from dried tangerine peel
chunk_text: Dried tangerine peel (DTP) is an excellent plant resource that has been used as ingredients for both food and traditional Chinese medicine. In this study, the efficiency of four different dietary preparation methods (i.e. soaking, boiling, steaming, and ethanol extraction) in extraction of functional compounds (i.e. flavonoids and essential oil constituents) from DTP was evaluated systematically for the first time. To conduct a comprehensive evaluation of the extraction of the functional compounds, a synthetic evaluation model based on a weighting method was established. The optimum conditions of each dietary preparation method (e.g., time, temperature, solid-liquid ratio, etc.) were determined by response surface methodology. Ethanol extraction showed the best extraction efficiency, followed by soaking, boiling, and steaming. Additionally, different DTP extracts were shown to be clearly distinguished by electronic eye and electronic tongue. This research provides essential findings for the effective dietary instruction of DTP consumption.
