Hebei 057250 China ⁎ Corresponding authors. Dried tangerine peel (DTP) is an excellent plant resource that has been used as ingredients for both food and traditional Chinese medicine. In this study, the efficiency of four different dietary preparation methods (i.e. soaking, boiling, steaming, and ethanol extraction) in extraction of functional compounds (i.e. flavonoids and essential oil constituents) from DTP was evaluated systematically for the first time. To conduct a comprehensive evaluation of the extraction of the functional compounds, a synthetic evaluation model based on a weighting method was established. The optimum conditions of each dietary preparation method (e.g., time, temperature, solid-liquid ratio, etc.) were determined by response surface methodology. Ethanol extraction showed the best extraction efficiency, followed by soaking, boiling, and steaming. Additionally, different DTP extracts

Additionally, different DTP extracts were shown to be clearly distinguished by electronic eye and electronic tongue. This research provides essential findings for the effective dietary instruction of DTP consumption. Chemical compounds studied in this article Hesperidin (PubChem CID: 10621) Nobiletin (PubChem CID: 72344) Tangeretin (PubChem CID: 68077) β-Myrcene (PubChem CID: 31253) d-Limonene (PubChem CID: 440917) γ-Terpinene (PubChem CID: 7461) o-Cymene (PubChem CID: 10703) Caryophyllene (PubChem CID: 5281515) α-Farnesene (PubChem CID: 5281516) Methyl methanthranilate (PubChem CID: 6826) Keywords Dried tangerine peel Dietary preparation methods Flavonoids Essential oil Synthetic evaluation 1 Introduction Citrus is a major fruit crop with a production worldwide of approximately 98 million tons in 2017 (USDA data). Citrus fruit is widely consumed fresh and is appreciated for its characteristic sour-sweet flavors (Azimi & Fatemi, 2018). In addition, almost 28% of all citrus fruit are processed into juice or other commercial products. Citrus peel is the major byproduct produced in the citrus processing industry. Recently citrus peel has drawn attention for its functional and medicinal effects (Cypriano, Silva, & Tasic, 2018; Duan et al., 2017). Thereinto, dried tangerine peel (DTP) is prepared from the dried ripe peel of Citrus Reticulata Blanco and its cultivars with a long natural aging and storing process in East Asia (Fu et al., 2

chunk_text: aration methods, i.e., soaking, boiling, steaming and ethanol extraction. 2.2.1 Soaking The soaking of DTP was executed in a stainless steel container in which one gram of the DTP sample was soaked in hot water. The container was immediately covered with a sealing film when soaking. The sample was soaked with different time (1, 2, 4 and 8 min), temperature (50, 60, 70, 80, 90 and 100 °C), solid-liquid ratio (1:15, 1:20, 1:25, 1:30 and 1:35 g/mL) and soaking times (1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6), respectively. After being soaked, the DTP was removed and the soaking extracts were immediately centrifuged at 10000 rpm for 3 min for further analysis. 2.2.2 Boiling One gram of the DTP sample was placed in 30 mL of boiling water in a stainless steel container. The samples were continuously heated by an induction cooker (C21-SDHC8E15J, Hangzhou, China) at 1200 W, and followed by DTP removal at 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 min, respectively. The boiled DTP extracts were obtained after centrifugation. 2.2.3 Steaming One gram of the DTP sample was placed on a steamer rack, within a stainless steel container. Under the steamer rack, 30 mL boiling water was used to steam the DTP sample in a sealed container for the duration of steaming. The DTP samples were heated by an induction cooker for 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 min; once the DTP was removed, the steamed extracts were prepared after centrifugation. 2.2.4 Ethanol extraction The ethanol extraction of DTP was implemented on a reflux system. One gram of the DTP sample was extracted with ethanol in a round-bottom flask, and the flask was heated in an oil bath. T

After being extracted, the DTP was removed and the ethanol extracts were immediately centrifuged for further analysis. 2.3 LC-MS analysis of flavonoids Identification of flavonoid constituent in the DTP extracts was performed on an Agilent Technologies HPLC system (1290 Infinity II) coupled with a Thermo Fisher Scientific mass spectrometer (Q-Exactive Focus). A ZORBAX Eclipse Plus-C18 column (50 mm × 2.1 mm i.d., 1.8 μm, Agilent Technologies) was used to separate compounds with 0.1% (v/v) formic acid in ultrapure water as mobile phase A and acetonitrile as mobile phase B at a flow rate of 0.4 mL/min. The following elution program was set up: from 9% B to 50% B in 10 min, to 100% B in 1 min and a plateau of 100% B in 4 min. The other parameters were as follows: temperature 25 °C; UV detection at 280 nm and 330 nm; and injection volume 10 μL. MS data was acquired using electrospray ionization (ESI) in a positive ionization mode. The parameters were set as follows: sheath gas flow rate, 25 L/min; Aux gas flow rate, 8 L/min; capillary temperature, 320 °C; Aux gas heater temperature, 350 °C; S-lens RF level, 50.0; nebulizer gas pressure, 45 psi; dry gas flow, 6.00 L/min; electrospray voltage, 4000 V; target mass, m/z 40

Quantification by HPLC was performed with the method mentioned above using calibration curves obtained by injecting known concentrations of flavonoids (hesperidin, nobiletin and tangeretin) as external standards; their standard curves were plotted as follows: y = 0.144x + 0.0885 (R2  = 0.9954), y = 0.1921x–0.2151 (R2  = 0.9991) and y = 0.2441x–3.1003 (R2  = 0.9964), respectively, with linearity ranges of 0.1–100 μM. 2.4 HS-SPME–GC–MS analysis of essential oil Essential oil in the DTP extracts was firstly isolated and concentrated by Headspace solid phase micro-extraction (HS-SPME), and then analyzed by gas chromatography coupled with a mass spectrometer (GC–MS QP 2010 plus, Shimadzu, Japan). For the HS-SPME procedure, 1 mL of ten-fold diluted extract samples and 1 μL of internal standard (0.95 mg/mL cyclohexanone) were placed together in a vial. The vial was sealed immediately with a PTFE-silicon septum (Supelco, Bellefonte, PA, USA) and heated at 60 °C for 30 min on a heating platform. A 65 μm polydimethylsiloxane–divinylbenzene (PDMS/DVB) SPME fibre (Supelco Inc., Bellefonte, PA, USA) was extended through the needle to place the stationary phase in contact with the headspace of the sample in the vial. After 40 min, the fibre was pulled out from the vial and inserted into the injection port (at 200 °C) of the GC system to desorb the analytes from the fibre for 2 min. GC–MS analysis was performed according to our previous study with some modifications (Yang, Zhao, et al., 2017). The GC oven temperature was programmed from 40 °C for 1 min, to 120 °C at the speed of 3 °C/min and held for 2 min, then to 230 °C at the speed of 5 °C/min and held for 3 min. The essential oil compounds were identified by comparing their retention time, linear retention indices (Kovats indices) and mass spectra with those in the NIST 11 databases. Based on the peak-area ratios relative to that of the internal standard (cyclohexanone), the relative content of each essential oil compound in the samples were obtained as cyclohexanone equivalents by the GC peak area (Yang, Zhao, et al., 2017; Zheng, Zeng, Peng, Wu, & Su, 2018). 2.5 Extraction efficiency determination The flavonoids and essential oil compounds in the DTP sample were quantified in order to calculate their extraction efficiency of different dietary preparation methods. To guarantee a full and effective extraction of flavonoids, DTP powder was extracted with both ethyl acetate and distilled water. Specifically, 0.5 g of DTP powder was extracted with 25 mL ethyl acetate in a 50-mL tube, and broken at 8000 rpm/min for 3 min with a high-speed blender (ULTRA-TURRAX T25 digital, IKA, Germany). With the help of Yet Another Analytic Hierarchy Process (YAAHP) software (v0.6.0), this hierarchical structure of the model was divided into three layers: the first layer was the objective layer, which had only one element, and was used to analyze the preset goal of the problem, namely the synthetic evaluation of DTP extracts by different dietary preparation methods. The second layer was the intermediate criterion layer, which included the 4 dietary preparation methods affecting the synthetic evaluation of DTP extracts. The four indices were recorded as c1, c2, c3, and c4 for soaking, boiling, steaming, and ethanol extraction, respectively. The third layer was the project layer, which contained the major flavonoids and essential oil compounds (Calabrese, Costa, Levialdi, & Menichini, 2016; Jiang et al., 2018). Relative priorities are assigned for these flavonoids and essential oil compounds based on their content and function using the scale from 1 to 9 (1 = extremely important, 5 = neither important nor important, and 9 = extremely not important). The weighting factors of the flavonoids and essential oil compounds were assigned by matrix analysis, and then a synthetic evaluation model for DTP extracts was established according to the following Eq. (2). This model can provide detailed solutions for the optimization of the dietary preparation methods for DTP. 2.7 Response surface optimization For single factor tests, one gram of the DTP sample was soaked in ultrapure water with different soaking time (1, 2, 4 and 8 min), temperature (50, 60, 70, 80, 90 and 100 °C), solid-liquid ratio (1:15, 1:20, 1:25, 1:30 and 1:35 g/mL), and extraction times (1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6). Notably, the extraction efficiencies of these three flavonoids exhibited the same variation tendencies (Table S2). The increasing trends involved two stages: hot water permeates rapidly in one stage into the cellular structure of DTP, resulting in the dissolution of flavonoids into the hot water; the other stage consists of the external diffusion of flavonoids through the porous structures of DTP into the water. chunk_text: tial oil compounds in DTP affected by four different dietary preparation methods were evaluated synthetically for the first time. Two evaluation methods are adopted herein that include the extraction efficiency of each functional compound and the synthetic evaluation of these components based on the weighting factors method. Single factor tests and RSM were applied to optimize the soaking, boiling, steaming and ethanol extraction of DTP. Our results show that soaking time of 4 min, temperature of 80 °C, solid-liquid ratio of 1:31 g/mL and extraction for two times are the optimum conditions for soaking; similarly, extraction time of 4 min, ethanol content of 60% and solid-liquid ratio of 1:30 g/mL are the optimum conditions for ethanol extraction. The synthetic evaluation of flavonoids and essential oil compounds according to the four dietary preparation methods show that the highest level was obtained by ethanol extraction, followed by soaking, boiling, and steaming. Furthermore, electronic eye and electronic tongue are effective tools for the discrimination of different extract samples of DTP. These significant findings offer important information that can improve the effective utilization of citrus peel resources and aid in the selection of the most effective preparation method for the consumption of DTP. title: Classification of Pericarpium Citri Reticulatae (Chenpi) age using surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy
chunk_text: Pericarpium Citri Reticulatae (PCR) is used in food and medical herbal formula, and its quality is determined by its age. Raman spectroscopy is a laser technology for molecular fingerprinting. The feasibility of using surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) to determine the PCR age was investigated. The Raman peaks were acquired using a Raman spectrometer with a 785 nm diode laser and were analyzed using principal component analysis (PCA) followed by linear discriminant analysis (PCA–LDA). There were six major peaks at 600, 730, 990, 1370, 1607, and 1742 cm−1 in the SERS spectra, and their intensity, especially the peak at 1607 cm−1, was inversely correlated with the PCR age. The different ages of PCR could be correctly classified with over 90 % accuracy by using PCA-LDA based on the SERS spectra. In conclusion, a Raman spectrometer may be used as a novel method to identify the age of PCR products.

chunk_text: medical herbal formula, and its quality is determined by its age. Raman spectroscopy is a laser technology for molecular fingerprinting. The feasibility of using surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) to determine the PCR age was investigated. The Raman peaks were acquired using a Raman spectrometer with a 785 nm diode laser and were analyzed using principal component analysis (PCA) followed by linear discriminant analysis (PCA–LDA). There were six major peaks at 600, 730, 990, 1370, 1607, and 1742 cm−1 in the SERS spectra, and their intensity, especially the peak at 1607 cm−1, was inversely correlated with the PCR age. The different ages of PCR could be correctly classified with over 90 % accuracy by using PCA-LDA based on the SERS spectra. In conclusion, a Raman spectrometer may be used as a novel method to identify the age of PCR products. As a precious ingredient, Chenpi has been included in food (Liu, Wang, & Zhang, 2015) and in traditional herbal medicinal formula mainly for the treatment of digestive and respiratory diseases such as chronic atrophic gastritis, exogenous cough, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, type 2 diabetes with secondary const

Biosensing techniques are detection systems typically consisting of a recognition component that interacts with the analyte of interest, a biotransducer or biosensor component (i.e. optical biosensors, electronic biosensors, and magnetic biosensors) that produces a measureable signal proportional to the contraction of target analyte, and an electronic system for signal application and reading (Bhalla, Jolly, Formisano, & Estrela, 2016). A variety of biosensor applications have been found in many different fields including disease detection and food quality monitoring (Bhalla et al., 2016; Qin, Wang, Gao, & Yao, 2022). Among these applications, antigen–antibody-based Western blots or the Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, pregnancy test, and glucose monitoring are the most important examples of biosensor devices developed as of today. When a monochromatic light hits a substance, it generates two scattering processes (elastic and inelastic); one is elastic scattering without photo energy change, and the other is inelastic (Raman) scattering with the energy change (Raman & Krishnan, 1928). Raman spectroscopy is based on the inelastic scattering as a biosensor for substances analysis. Surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) is a combination of the Raman spectroscopy and nanotechnology. With metal nanoparticles (NPs) such as gold (AuNPs) and silver nanoparticles (AgNPs), the Raman scattering or signal can be enhanced by 7 – 10 folds of magnitude when the analyte is near or ab

In both cases, the signal was weak but was largely enhanced by the addition of Ag NP. 2 Materials and methods 2.1 Standard materials and extract preparation PCR materials with different ages (from 1 to 40 years old) were purchased from Jiangmen Xinbaotang Co. ltd. (Guangdong, China). Each age group consisted of 15 PCR samples from different producers as follows: 1 year old that were collected in 2018, 10 years old in 2008, 20 years old in 1998, 30 years old in 1988, and 40 years old in 1978. The experiments of this study were performed and finished in Dr. Caigan Du’s laboratory at the University of British Columbia in 2019. The ingredient of PCR was extracted with ethanol for SERS analysis. In brief, the PCR materials were grinded in liquid nitrogen to a fine powder with a pestle, followed by removal of the coarse parts using a 100-mesh sieve. The ingredients (samples) were extracted by ethanol maceration, in which 0.5 g of PCR powder was suspended in 10 mL of ethanol (from 50 % to 100 %) and incubated at 60 °C for 12 h. The insoluble particles in the extraction solution were pelleted by centrifugation at 1000 × g for 15 min, and the supernatant (PCR extract) was stored at −80 °C until it was used in the experiment. One milliliter (mL) of PCR extract was evaporated with nitrogen, and the remaining was dissolved in 80 µL of dH2O for each SERS determination. 2.2 Preparation of silver nanoparticles (Ag NP) Ag NP were routinely used in the studies with Raman spectroscopy in our laboratory and were prepared

chunk_text: 2O for each SERS determination. 2.2 Preparation of silver nanoparticles (Ag NP) Ag NP were routinely used in the studies with Raman spectroscopy in our laboratory and were prepared as previously described (Zong et al., 2021). Briefly, a mixture containing 90 mL of 1.11 mmol/L AgNO3 solution, 5 mL of 60 mmol/L hydroxylamine hydrochloride solution and 4.5 mL of 0.1 mol/L NaOH was stirred at 25 °C in the darkness for 3 h. The Ag NP was pelleted by centrifugation at 13,000 × g for 12 min. The resultant Ag NP (5 µL) and the PCR extract (5 µL) were mixed at 1:1 ratio. The mixture droplets were air-dried on an aluminum plate at 25 °C for 60 min to produce the aggregation of the AgNPs with the ingredients in the PCR extract. Very occasionally a ring-like pattern formed (coffee-ring effect) on the surface after the evaporation of the mixture solution. This coffee-ring effect occurred when the non-volatile solutes such as a metal NPs-containing suspension was dried on the solid surface (Ma & Hao, 2011; Mampallil & Eral, 2018). This ring could affect SERS readout but could be significantly prevented by drying the sample at a cold temperature (He, Guo, & Li, 2019). In our experiments, if there was the “coffee ring effect” or crystals formation in the sample preparation, the extract/AgNPs was prepared again until the absence of the crystal effect. 2.3 SERS measurements SERS spectra of the AgNP/PCR aggregation were acquired with a Raman spectrometer (Aura™, Verisante Technology, Vancouver, BC Canada) that was equipped with a 785 nm diode laser for Raman excitation as described previously

SERS signals were measured under the 150 mW excitation laser power with one second of an integration time and a spectral resolution of 8 cm−1 in the wavenumber range of 499 – 1799 cm−1. Further, three sets of SERS spectra that covered the whole sample area on the aluminum slide were generated per sample, and the mean of these three spectra was used in the subsequent data analysis. 2.4 Data analysis The fluorescence background of the SERS spectrum was removed using a fifth-order polynomial fitting algorithm prior to the data acquisition as described before (Zhao, Lui, McLean, & Zeng, 2007). The differences between the groups and the correlation of Raman peak intensity at 1607 cm−1 with the corresponding PCR age were statistically analyzed using GraphPad Prism software (Version 9, GraphPad Software, San Diego, CA, USA). A p-value < 0.05 was considered to be significantly different. 3 Results 3.1 PCR optimization for SERS measurement Ethanol is an effective and safe solvent that extracts organic ingredients including essential oils from the plant. To determine which ethanol extraction was the most appropriate or effective for PCR age determination using SERS, the SERS spectra of 1-year old, the “newest” PCR, were compared with those of 40-year old, the “oldest” PCR, after extraction with different concentrations (50 %, 75 %, and 100 %) of ethanol. As shown in Fig. 1 , when the differences of the SERS peaks between 1-year old and 40-year old PCR samples were compared, they were marginal when they were extracted with 50 % ethanol (Fig. 1a) to the most noticeable with 100 % ethanol (Fig. 1c). More interestedly, the peak intensity in SERS spectra of 40-year old PCR samples was similar or remained the same among the extracts with 50 % to 100 % ethanol, whereas the intensity of all the SERS peaks of 1-year old PCR samples was increased as the ethanol concentration was increased in the extraction (Fig. 1). These data may suggest that the extraction with 100 % ethanol maximizes the difference of SERS peaks between PCR products with different ages (the newest versus the oldest). 3.2 Differences of SERS spectra between PCR products with different ages All the samples were extracted with 100 % ethanol. The intensity levels of these SERS peaks were not always consistent across the different age groups. Overall, the peaks of both 30- and 40-year old samples were at the lowest levels as compared with those of “younger” groups, and they both were overlapped in the most measurements. The peaks of 10-year old PCR remained the highest intensity except the peak at 1607 cm−1. All the PC scores between different age groups were compared, and PC1, PC2, and PC3 were most diagnostically significant for identifying the age (from 1-year old to over 30-years old) of PCR (P < 0.000). As shown in Fig. 4 , the PCA score plots of different age groups showed a significant separation between 1-, 10-, 20- and 30- or 40-years old PCR products, in which the samples between 30 and 40 years old were not clearly separated in the PCA score plots. These data may suggest that our method of using this LDA discrimination model could accurately identify the age of the PCR products that were not stored over 30 years. The PCR age identification using LDA discrimination model based on the SERS spectra was confirmed using LOO-CV method. As shown in Table 1, 15 out of 15 in 1-, 10- and 20-years old groups (100 % accuracy), 12 of 15 in 30-years old group (80 % accuracy, 20 % in 40-years old group) and 13 of 15 in 40-year old group (86.7 % accuracy, 13.3 % in 30-years old group) were classified correctly. In the cross-validated classification, 15 of 15 in both 1- and 10-years group (100 % accuracy), 14 of 15 in 20-years group (93.3 % accuracy, 6.7 % in 40-years group), and 12 of 15 in both 30-years and 40-years old groups (80 % accuracy, 20 % in 40-years or 30-years old group) were correctly identified (Table 1 ). Overall, the accuracy of prediction using SERS was 93.3 % in the original grouped cases and 90.7 % in the crossed-validated grouped cases. 4 Discussion Aged PCR is precious and has bee

However, whether the hesperidin content decreases following the increase in storage time just like the changes of the peak intensity at 1607 cm−1 remains further investigation. Bourget P. et al. have directly compared the performance of both Raman spectroscopy and high-performance liquid chromatography for analytical quality control of complex therapeutic products (Bourget, Amin, Vidal, Merlette, & Lagarce, 2014). They demonstrate that both methods provide excellent and similar results in the analytic validation key criteria. However, the Raman device offers several distinct advantages such as a fast analytical response of<2 min, reduction of the risk of errors because no intrusion or dilution are needed, negligible maintenance costs and the budget for technician training. This preliminary research for the first time demonstrates the feasibility of using a Raman spectrometer to determine the age or product quality of PCR in the market. However, further research and development of this technique for monitoring the quality of this natural product is required, including a more in-depth complementary study to identify the compound that are specifically associated with PCR aging and building a Raman device specifically for easy qualitative determination of PCR and other types of food additives without the need of sample preparation in the laboratory. 5 Conclusions The present study has demonstrated the success o

chunk_text: tive determination of PCR and other types of food additives without the need of sample preparation in the laboratory. 5 Conclusions The present study has demonstrated the success of using SERS spectra combined with statistical analysis to verify the PCR age from 1 year to 30 years PCR, but failed to discriminate the 40 years from 30 years PCR. Some specific Raman peaks such as at 1607 cm−1 may reflect the specific components such as hesperidin in PCR. Thus, SERS may represent an easy and convenient tool for further development to precisely distinguish the storage age of PCR in the market. The limitation for this technology to separate much old samples such as over 30 years may due to two possible reasons. Firstly, the contents of ethanol-extracted ingredients between 40 years and 30 years PCR were not significant different, and secondly our SERS technique needed further to be improved such as using other types of nanoparticles that can enhance the Raman signals of age-markers. title: Optimizing BP neural network algorithm for Pericarpium Citri Reticulatae (Chenpi) origin traceability based on computer vision and ultra-fast gas-phase electronic nose data fusion
chunk_text: This study utilized computer vision to extract color and texture features of Pericarpium Citri Reticulatae (PCR). The ultra-fast gas-phase electronic nose (UF-GC-E-nose) technique successfully identified 98 volatile components, including olefins, alcohols, and esters, which significantly contribute to the flavor profile of PCR. Multivariate statistical Analysis was applied to the appearance traits of PCR, identifying 57 potential marker-trait factors (VIP > 1 and P < 0.05) from the 118 trait factors that can distinguish PCR from different origins. These factors include color, texture, and odor traits. By integrating multivariate statistical Analysis with the BP neural network algorithm, a novel artificial intelligence algorithm was developed and optimized for traceability of PCR origin. This algorithm achieved a 100% discrimination rate in differentiating PCR samples from various origins. This study offers a valuable reference and data support for developing intelligent algorithms that utilize data fusion from multiple intelligent sensory technologies to achieve rapid traceability of food origins.

It holds significant importance in culinary practices and traditional medicinal applications within oriental nations such as China, Korea, and Japan. This method facilitates rapid classification and prediction of PCR samples originating from different regions. 2 Materials and methods 2.1 Sample collection Seventy batches of dried PCR samples (aged 3 years) were obtained from Ealing Pharmaceutical Company Limited located in Shijiazhuang, China. The samples were stored in a −20 °C refrigerator before use. Detailed information about the samples can be found in Table S1 . 70 batches of PCR were collected from each of the following five origins: Guangdong (GD), Sichuan (SC), Zhejiang (ZJ), Anhui (AH), and Jiangxi (JX). Each sample was assigned a unique geo-label, such as GD-PCR, SC-PCR, ZJ-PCR, AH-PCR, and JX-PCR. The latitude and longitude ranges for the samples were between 22.35°N to 34.20°N and 104.02°E to 121.12°E, respectively. For more details and photos of the sampling sites, see Fig. S1 . All samples were pulverized into powder, sieved through a 50-mesh sieve and stored in a dry, airtight environment prior to UF-GC-E-nose analysis. A mixture of series alkanes (nC6 ∼ nC16, Lot: A0142930) was purchased from RESTEK Co. chunk_text: uter vision 2.2.1 Sample color extraction by python algorithm An algorithm was developed in Python to extract the appearance color of PCR samples. Initially, images were obtained from the PCR samples, with auto white balance and auto exposure being employed during the experiment, and no color gain being utilized. The PCR samples were positioned directly beneath the camera on a platform. All images were saved in JPG format with dimensions of 860 × 480 pixels. For each batch of PCR samples, a total of 300 images were collected, consisting of 100 images for the outer epidermis, 100 images for the inner epidermis, and 100 images for the powder. Chromaticity values were then extracted from the collected images using the color extraction technique. This study employed the RGB value vector summation approach, incorporating additional metrics such as yellowness (Y) = R + G, purpurability (P) = R + B, cleanness (C) = G + B, and whiteness (W) = R + G + B. Finally, a total of 490 datasets were acquired through computer vision, encompassing 7 detections, 14 batches, and 5 categories. The detailed procedure for extracting chroma values using the Python algorithm is presented in Table S2 . 2.2.2 Sample texture extraction by python algorithm A Python algorithm was established to extract the texture features of PCR samples. All images were collected and saved in JPG format (860 × 480 pixels). A total of 200 images were collected for each batch of PCR samples (100 for the outer epidermis and 100 for the inner epidermis). In this study, texture features were extracted from the PCR samples using Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT). DWT can capture local features and detailed information about the signal by decomposing the signal into subbands of different frequencies. For texture feature extraction, the original samples are subjected to DWT decomposition to obtain subband images with different frequencies. For each sub-band image, texture features are computed, and the extracted texture features are combined or selected to obtain the final texture feature vector. DWT decomposes the original image into four sub-bands, including LL, LH, HL and HH. The LL component represents the general contour of the sub-image, and the LH, HL and HH represent the horizontal, vertical and diagonal details, respectively. In this way, DWT can efficiently extract texture features from samples for texture analysis and texture recognition tasks in the fields of image processing, pattern recognition and computer vision. A total of 280 datasets (4 detections × 14 batches × 5 categories) were obtained from computer texture. The sample stirring rate, incubation temperature and incubation time were determined. The odor components of the sample that evaporated during the incubation process were concentrated in the upper part of the closed gas phase vials, eventually reaching equilibrium. 1.0 g of sample was loaded into the gas phase vial (20.0 mL) and transported by a robotic arm to the incubator for incubation; the stirring speed selected was 500 rpm, the stirring time for each cycle was 7 s (5 s of stirring and 2 s of stopping), the temperature was set at 55 °C and the incubation time was 10 min. 2.3.2 Sample detection The specific parameters for sample detection were as follows: sample injection volume, 250 μL; injection rate, 125 μL/s; inlet temperature, 200 °C; and detector trap temperature, 40 °C. The injection time was 7 s. The initial temperature of the column temperature chamber was 48 °C, and the programmed temperature ramps were from 4 °C/s to 90 °C, 1 °C/s to 160 °C, 0.2 °C/s to 165 °C, 2 °C/s to 225 °C. The data acquisition time was 120 s, the acquisition period was 0.01 s, hydrogen was used as the carrier gas, and the flow rate was 1 mL/min. Each batch of PCR samples was measured three times, and the results were taken as the mean value. 2.3.3 Analysis of volatile compounds The volatile components in the samples were characterized according to the Kovats retention index of the sample pe

The Kovats retention indices of the peaks from two columns [DB-5 (10 m × 0.18 mm × 0.4 μm) and DB-1701 (10 m × 0.18 mm × 0.4 μm)] were to find the corresponding chemical compositions in the ArochemBase database. 2.4 Analysis of BP neural network algorithm The neural network model utilized in this study comprises an input layer, a hidden layer (which can be multiple), and an output layer. Neurons within the network are interconnected with neurons in the preceding and succeeding layers, possessing individual weights and biases. To construct this model, a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) was employed, utilizing the back-propagation (BP) algorithm. The extrinsic traits of PCR samples were quantitatively collected and optimized through multivariate statistical analysis, subsequently serving as input layers for the neural network model. If the output doesn't match the desired output, back-propagation occurs. The output is transmitted through hidden layers to the input layer, and error is distributed among all units. This helps adjust the weights of each unit. The BP network has interconnected layers: input, output, and hidden nodes. The results of this analysis are presented in Fig. 6 (B–G). 4 Conclusions This study utilized computer vision and ultra-fast gas phase electronic nose technology to examine the morphological, chromatic, and gustatory characteristics of PCR samples derived from diverse sources. Employing a multivariate statistical approach, appearance-related data were extracted, revealing 57 factors associated with outer epidermis color, powder color, outer epidermis texture, and odor out of a total of 118 trait factors. These factors exhibit potential as marker-trait factors that can be utilized to differentiate PCR samples from various sources. The integration of multivariate statistical analysis with the BP neural network algorithm was employed, resulting in a discrimination rate of 100% and enabling rapid differentiation of PCR samples from diverse sources. This study provides reference and data support for the construction of intelligent algorithms based on the data fusion of multiple intelligent sensory technologies base

title: Simultaneous recycling of flavonone and polymethoxyflavonoids from Chenpi processing residue based on their complementary action on glycolipid lowering activity: Innovative combination use of yeast and aqueous two-phase system
chunk_text: This study aimed at recycling flavonoids with glycolipid lowering activity from Chenpi processing residue produced by essential oil extraction. The crude Chenpi flavonoids obtained by ethanol reflux mainly contained flavonone (hesperidin) and polymethoxyflavonoids (nobiletin, tangeretin, sinensetin, and isosinensetin), which complementally exerted strong glycolipid lowering activity as revealed by digestive enzyme inhibitory activity, molecular docking and network pharmacology. The reducing sugar and water-soluble impurities were efficiently removed by yeast fermentation and aqueous two-phase system (ATPS) extraction, respectively. The optimal combination use of yeast (2 % w/v, CN36) and ATPS formed by 22 % (w/w) (NH4)2SO4 and 25 % (w/w) ethanol improved flavonoid purity to 60.25 %, enriched flavonone and polymethoxyflavonoids by 6.69-fold, and enhanced digestive enzyme inhibitory activity, which was superior to the use of individual yeast or ATPS, unoptimized combination, macroporous resin (XAD-16), and ethyl acetate. This study was the first to develop a recyclable biophysical method for simultaneous enrichment of flavonone and polymethoxyflavonoids.

title: Simultaneous recycling of flavonone and polymethoxyflavonoids from Chenpi processing residue based on their complementary action on glycolipid lowering activity: Innovative combination use of yeast and aqueous two-phase system
chunk_text: Guangzhou 510641 China This study aimed at recycling flavonoids with glycolipid lowering activity from Chenpi processing residue produced by essential oil extraction. The crude Chenpi flavonoids obtained by ethanol reflux mainly contained flavonone (hesperidin) and polymethoxyflavonoids (nobiletin, tangeretin, sinensetin, and isosinensetin), which complementally exerted strong glycolipid lowering activity as revealed by digestive enzyme inhibitory activity, molecular docking and network pharmacology. The reducing sugar and water-soluble impurities were efficiently removed by yeast fermentation and aqueous two-phase system (ATPS) extraction, respectively. The optimal combination use of yeast (2 % w/v, CN36) and ATPS formed by 22 % (w/w) (NH4)2SO4 and 25 % (w/w) ethanol improved flavonoid purity to 60.25 %, enriched flavonone and polymethoxyflavonoids by 6.69-fold, and enhanced digestive enzyme inhibitory activity, which was superior to the use of individual yeast or ATPS, unoptimized combination, macroporous resin (XAD-16), and ethyl acetate. This study was the first to develop a recyclable biophysical method for simultaneous enrichment of flavonone and polymethoxyflavonoids. Molecular docking was used to further verify the interaction between Chenpi characteristic flavonoids and glycolipid digestive enzymes. A lower binding energy in molecular docking demonstrated a stronger affinity to the enzyme, indicating a potentially greater inhibitory ability. As displayed in Table 1 , Chenpi characteristic flavonoids had binding energies ranging from −7.82 to −5.69 kcal/mol and interacted mainly with 14 residues when docking to pancreatic lipase. Additionally, the lowest binding energy was observed in hesperidin, indicating its potentially greater pancreatic lipase inhibitory activity, which supported the above results. As shown in Fig. 3A, hesperidin was promising to interact with pancreatic lipase at Val322, His224, Ser195, Cys286, and Val325 by hydrogen bonds, and Gln324 through hydrophobic interaction. Whereas the catalytic sites of pancreatic lipase consisted of Ser153, Asp177 and His264, indicating the pancreatic lipase inhibitory activity of hesperidin was possibly not through competitive inhibition. Huang et al. (2020) found that it belonged to non-competitive inhibition, which was consistent with our results. On the other side, when docked to α-glucosidase, the binding energies of Chenpi characteristic flavonoids varied from −8.23 to −5.93 kcal/mol and interacted with 10 residues of the enzyme (Table 1). Above all, flavanone (hesperidin) and PMFs showed complementary action on glycolipid lowering activity through multiple targets and pathways. In summary, the in vitro and in silico evaluation revealed that flavonone (hesperidin) and PMFs complemented each other in regulation of glycolipid digestion, absorption and metabolism. Therefore, it was of great importance to simultaneously enrich both flavonone and PMFs from crude Chenpi flavonoids. 3.3 Exploration of purification efficiency of yeast fermentation coupled with ATPS extraction 3.3.1 Exploration of feasibility of yeast fermentation and ATPS extraction As indicated in 3.1, C-E-55 had the highest content of Chenpi characteristic flavonoids among all crude Chenpi flavonoids but remained low to be applied as a functional ingredient for regulation of glycolipid digestion, absorption and metabolism. It was measured that C-E-55 consisted of 47.75 % total sugar, 39.10 % reducing sugar, 1.11 % total nitrogen, and 2.73 % ash. The lipid content was not detected due to the treatment of supercritical CO2 extraction. Therefore, the major impurity in C-E-55 was reducing sugar and other water-soluble impurities. The purification strategy should follow the principle of removing impurities without losing active flavonoids i.e. flavonone (hesperidin) and PMFs. As indicated in Fig. 5A, the yields of purified Chenpi flavonoids by yeast fermentation ranged from 52.22 % to 57.06 %, while the yields of those by ATPS extraction varied. The use of K2HPO4 had a significantly higher yield (61.00 ± 1.75 %) than those of (NH4)2SO4 and K2CO3 (p < 0.05), suggesting that (NH4)2SO4 and K2CO3 might be more effective in purification of Chenpi flavonoids. RSC values of all purified Chenpi flavonoids were significantly decreased, suggesting that the yeast fermentation and ATPS extraction strategies did remove reducing sugar. The use of K2CO3 in ATPS extraction performed the best effect on removing reducing sugar, followed by the use of K2HPO4 in ATPS extraction and yeast fermentation. As shown in Fig. 5B, all purified Chenpi flavonoids by yeast fermentation increased in TFC, with high recovery rates ranging from 84.64 % to 100.44 %. Therefore, yeast fermentation was able to utilize reducing sugar to increase the purity of Chenpi flavonoids in a highly conserved manner. In the perspective of ATPS extraction, only the use of (NH4)2SO4 performed purification efficiency on Chenpi flavonoids, with the highest TFC (23.45 % ± 0.16 %) in all purified Chenpi flavonoids with a recovery rate of 62.17 %, indicating that (NH4)2SO4 was the optimal salt in ATPS extraction. For a better understanding of the purification characteristics in flavonoids of all approaches, the contents of Chenpi characteristic flavonoids were measured. As displayed in Fig. 5C, 5 flavonoids were well preserved in Chenpi flavonoids purified by yeast fermentation, and the sample fermented by CN36 had the highest content among them. On the other hand, the total characteristic flavonoids content of Chenpi flavonoids purified by ATPS composed of (NH4)2SO4 was significantly higher than those in all other samples (p < 0.05), suggesting that (NH4)2SO4 was the most effective salt for forming ATPS to enrich Chenpi flavonoids. Meanwhile, the highest levels of PMFs were observed in Chenpi flavonoids purified by ATPS composed of K2CO3, possibly due to its greatest effect on removing reducing sugar (Fig. 5A). However, hesperidin was strongly lost when K2CO3 was used, probably being degraded by alkaline hydrolysis (Pyrzynska, 2022). It was consistent with the findings of Yazdabadi et al. (2019) that salts might alkalize the ATPS, possibly causing damage to the pH-sensitive biomolecules. Comprehensively considering RSCs, flavonoids contents and recovery rates, CN36 and (NH4)2SO4 were optimal for yeast fermentation and ATPS extraction, respectively. Overall, although purification by ATPS composed of (NH4)2SO4 achieved an excellent effect on flavonoids enrichment, RSC still remained considerable. Whereas, yeast fermentation by CN36 consumed reducing sugar rapidly and cyclically, thus preserving flavonoids to a great extent.

As indicated in Fig. 6A, the concentration of reducing sugar in the supernatant continuously decreased during the 6 h fermentation of CN36. Increasing the yeast concentration to 2 % (w/v) accelerated the consumption process of reducing sugar. The concentration of total flavonoids in the supernatant decreased, but increased when the fermentation extended, remaining above 84 % at the end of fermentation. The concentration of CN36 and fermentation time were optimized as 2 % (w/v) and 4 h, respectively. (2) Optimal ATPS extraction parameters. To ensure the continuity of the purification process and avoid repeated drying and dissolution, the aqueous solution of C-E-55 after the maximum removal of reducing sugar by yeast fermentation was concentrated and directly used as a part of water component of ATPS formed by (NH4)2SO4 and ethanol. The ATPS containing Chenpi flavonoids was intensely mixed and centrifuged to obtain the upper phase that was repeatedly extracted by the fresh bottom phase of ATPS composed of (NH4)2SO4, ethanol and deionized water for removing water-soluble impurities and enhancing the purity of Chenpi flavonoids (Fig. 1). The initial additive amount of C-E-55 used in the entitle ATPS extraction processes, (NH4)2SO4 concentration, ethanol concentration and extraction times were the key factors affecting the purification efficiency. As displayed in Fig. 6B1, the yield and RSC of purified Chenpi flavonoids decreased with the increased addition amount of C-E-55, while TFC and its recovery rate increased. The reducing sugar and flavonoids were not saturated at a low addition of C-E-55, which decreased the partition coefficient and weakened the purification efficiency. Meanwhile, the extraction efficiency and recovery rate were improved with a larger addition amount of C-E-55, which reduced the cost for purification of Chenpi flavonoids. Therefore, the optimum addition amount of C-E-55 was 5 % (w/w), with low RSC (12.64 ± 0.16 %) and high TFC (27.74 ± 0.80 %). Obviously, the purification efficiency of yeast fermentation coupled with ATPS extraction was significantly improved compared with individual yeast fermentation or ATPS extraction. The addition of salt led to the phase separation and formed ATPS because of the salting-out effect, which was influenced by the salt concentration (Shahriari et al., 2012). Nevertheless, more impurities could also be extracted in the upper phase with the increased volume, leading to an increase in yield but constant in TFC. The introduction of more ethanol would cause salt precipitation, therefore the optimal ethanol concentration was 25 % (w/w). Overall, the optimal ATPS for Chenpi flavonoids purification was composed of 22 % (w/w) (NH4)2SO4 and 25 % (w/w) ethanol, resulting in a decrease in RSC (9.50 ± 0.09 %) and an increase in TFC (30.33 ± 1.75 %). As displayed in Fig. 6B4, the yield of purified Chenpi flavonoids decreased with increasing extraction times, while RSC reached equilibrium at the second extraction. TFC increased significantly (p < 0.05) after 5 times extraction by ATPS and then remained stable, but the recovery rate decreased continuously because a few flavonoids were distributed in the bottom phase in each extraction, causing the loss. In addition, as seen in Fig. 6B5, the color of the upper phase in ATPS became lighter with multiple extractions, indicating that not only the reducing sugar but also the pigment was removed. Additionally, the other water-soluble impurities i.e. proteins and gum resin could also be removed by multiple extraction, ultimately improving the purity of Chenpi flavonoids. Overall, the optimal purification process for Chenpi flavonoids with glycolipid lowering activity by yeast fermentation coupled with ATPS extraction was as follows. In addition, YF-ATPS-5 had an increased Chenpi characteristic flavonoids content of 383.76 ± 4.70 mg/g (6.69-fold enrichment) through the simultaneous enrichment of hesperidin and PMFs, exhibiting ideal regulation effects on glycolipid digestion, absorption and metabolism. 4 Conclusion In this study, Chenpi flavonoids were optimally recycled by reflux extraction with 55 % (v/v) ethanol from Chenpi processing residue produced by essential oil extraction. On the basis of demonstration of the complementary glycolipid lowering activity of flavonone and PMFs, a recyclable biophysical method named yeast fermentation coupled with ATPS extraction for the simultaneous enrichment of flavonone and polymethoxyflavonoids was developed to achieve 5.38/6.69-fold total/characteristic flavonoids content and ideal glycolipid lowering activity for the first time. This study highlighted a feasible strategy for the simultaneous recovery and purification of Chenpi bioactive flavonoids, which realized the utilization of Chenpi functional ingredients and facilitated the development of glycolipid lowering function foods. Nevertheless, the large-scale extraction and purification processes and the in vivo glycolipid lowering activity of Chenpi flavonoids, which were not explored in the present study, still needed to be validated. Microbes: Drivers of Chenpi manufacturing, biotransformation, and physiological effects
chunk_text: Chenpi holds a rich history of both edible and medicinal applications worldwide, garnering increased attention from researchers in recent years due to its diverse physiological effects. While current research predominantly exploresed its chemical composition and physiological effects, there remains a notable gap in knowledge concerning its manufacturing, characteristic chemical substances, and the underlying mechanisms driving its physiological effects. In this review, the impacts of microbes on the manufacturing, biotransformation, and physiological effects of Chenpi were summarized, as well as the present status of product development. Furthermore, this review engaged in an in-depth discussion highlighting the challenges and shortcomings in recent research, while proposing potential directions and prospects. Additionally, the claim that “The longer the aging, the better the quality” of Chenpi was scientifically evaluated for the first time, providing a solid theoretical foundation for advancing the Chenpi industry.

Chenpi holds a rich history of both edible and medicinal applications worldwide, garnering increased attention from researchers in recent years due to its diverse physiological effects. While current research predominantly exploresed its chemical composition and physiological effects, there remains a notable gap in knowledge concerning its manufacturing, characteristic chemical substances, and the underlying mechanisms driving its physiological effects. In this review, the impacts of microbes on the manufacturing, biotransformation, and physiological effects of Chenpi were summarized, as well as the present status of product development. Furthermore, this review engaged in an in-depth discussion highlighting the challenges and shortcomings in recent research, while proposing potential directions and prospects. Additionally, the claim that “The longer the aging, the better the quality” of Chenpi was scientifically evaluated for the first time, providing a solid theoretical foundation for advancing the Chenpi industry. Graphical abstract Unlabelled Image Keywords Chenpi Manufacturing Biotransformation Physiological effects Microbiome Applications Data availability No data was used for the research described in the article. 1 Introduction Citrus fruits are globally significant economic crops, with the worldwide citrus cultivation area and production reaching 9.05 million hectares and 151.88 million tons, respectively, in 2022 (Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, 2022) (Fig. 1A and B). In regions such as China, Japan, South Korea, India, and Southeast Asia, dried citrus peels are commonly used in culinary practices and traditional medicine. Particularly in China, with its long history of use, mature processing techniques, and extensive scientific research, citrus peels aged for three years are also known as Chenpi (Fig. 1C). Chenpi is mainly produced in the provinces of Guangdong, Jiangxi, Sichuan, Fujian, and Zhejiang in China. Currently, the Chinese Pharmacopoeia recorded four varieties: Guang Chenpi (Citrus reticulata ‘Chachi’), Chuan Chenpi (Citrus reticulata ‘Dahongpao’), Zhe Chenpi (Citrus reticulata ‘Unshiu’), and Jian Chenpi (Citrus reticulata ‘Tangerina’) (Chinese Pharmacopoeia Commission, 2020). Among these, Guang Chenpi accounts for 70 % of the total Chenpi production, with Xinhui Chenpi being the most common, constituting 90 % (Fig. 1D). Chenpi has high medicinal and culinary value and is often used as a traditional spice and premium seasoning in East and Southeast Asia. Tracing back in history (Fig. 1E)

However, in recent years, most of the reviews on Chenpi were primarily focused on the main components, biological activities, pharmacological effects, and identification techniques of Chenpi. Conversely, a detailed description of the influence of microbes in their manufacturing, biotransformation, and physiological effects is lacking. Thus, this review focused on the processing of Chenpi, providing a comprehensive discussion of the changes in substance and quality during aging. Meanwhile, we explored the bi-directional effects of Chenpi and its active ingredients with the host gut microbiota, along with an assessment of the current status of its product development. This review aims to establish a clear “microbial-chemical characterization/bioactivity” axis, which will provide constructive suggestions for future scientific research and industrial development of Chenpi. Additionally, transforming citrus peels into Chenpi represents a strategy for the efficient and high-value utilization of citrus by-products, achieving a win-win scenario for sustainable and comprehensive resource utilization while contributing to climate change mitigation. This approach is expected to stimulate greater interest in leveraging additional biomass waste to support net-zero emissions goals. 2 The manufacturing process of Chenpi The ancient manufacturing process of Chenpi includes planting, harvesting, selecting, washing, cutting, drying, flipping, storing, and aging (Fig. 3A), forming the traditional concoction techniques of “Three years of seedling, three years of fruits, three bat

chunk_text: cting, washing, cutting, drying, flipping, storing, and aging (Fig. 3A), forming the traditional concoction techniques of “Three years of seedling, three years of fruits, three batches of harvesting, three varieties, three petals of peeling, three years of tanning, three levels of peeling, three years of aging, and long-term storage”. However, with the advancement of technology, the manufacturing of modern Chenpi is increasingly trending towards scientific, automated, and intelligent processes. In modern manufacturing process, the key steps include fresh fruits, micro-nano bubble cleaning, efficient decomposition, green and energy-saving drying, precise aging, and digital traceability (Fig. 3B). The raw material for Guang Chenpi, Pericarpium Citri Reticulatae (PCR), is typically harvested from the onset of Autumn (August–December) and is divided into three periods: from the beginning of Autumn to the Autumn Equinox (August–October), from the Autumn Equinox to the beginning of Winter (October–November), and from the beginning of Winter to the Winter Solstice (November–December). According to “Xinhui Chenpi Geographical Indication Products”, citrus peels harvested from the three different periods mentioned above have been classified as Citri Reticulatae Pericarpium Viride (CRPV), reddish PCR, and red PCR based on the harvesting period [Product of geographical indication-Xinhui Chenpi (DB4407/T 70–2021), Regional Standard)] (Fig. 3C). The perceived effectiveness of the three types of peels varies, with CRPV being regarded as more pungent and astringent, and commonly utilized f

The perceived effectiveness of the three types of peels varies, with CRPV being regarded as more pungent and astringent, and commonly utilized for medicinal purposes. Red PCR, with a mellower flavor, demands specific aging conditions, is more expensive, and is generally used as a tea or seasoning for high-class ingredients. The efficacy of reddish PCR falls between that of CRPV and red PCR, making it widely applicable (Li, Ren, et al., 2023). In general, active components in citrus peels vary depending on the harvesting period. A recent study using broadly targeted metabolomics techniques discovered higher levels of hesperidin in red PCR compared to CRPV and reddish PCR. Moreover, naringenin, hesperidin, and 3,3′,4′,5,6,7,8-heptamethoxyflavonoids exhibited higher CRPV than in PCR harvested at other times of the year (Zhang et al., 2020). Following harvesting, fresh PCR undergoes initial grading, washing, and screening. Subsequently, the even and three-valve connected peel is removed using the traditional positive three-knife or two-knife method. After skin removal, the peels are shade-dried for 4–5 h, allowing for natural water loss and wilting, which leads to a soft texture. The peels are then counter-peeled, ensuring that the inner layers face outward. Following this, the peels undergo natural sun-drying to regulate moisture levels and achieve dryness. Finally, the dried citrus peels are packed into ventilated containers such as sacks or straw bags and placed in a warehouse for natural aging. Warehouse ventilation is reduced when moistu

chunk_text: , the dried citrus peels are packed into ventilated containers such as sacks or straw bags and placed in a warehouse for natural aging. Warehouse ventilation is reduced when moisture returns from February to May annually, followed by tumble-drying from May to November. The traditional raw tanning process mainly relies on the heat from natural sunlight and airflow to evaporate water in Guang Chenpi, providing the advantages of simplicity and ultraviolet sterilization. However, the process has some limitations and is greatly affected by factors such as site conditions, pests, local climate, air temperature, humidity, and hygienic conditions, potentially leading to variations in the quality of Chenpi. With the advancement of industrial technology, various drying methods, including hot air drying, heat pump drying, solar drying, microwave drying, infrared radiation drying, vacuum freeze drying, and variable temperature differential pressure puffing drying, have emerged as alternatives to traditional solarization for Chenpi drying. A previous study compared the drying characteristics and quality attributes of PCR using four different drying technologies: hot air impingement drying (HAID), medium- and short-wave infrared drying (MSWID), temperature and humidity process control, and freeze drying (Sun, Li, et al., 2023). The findings revealed that HAID and MSWID exhibited higher drying rates, total flavonoid content, total volatile oil content, and levels of aldehydes and alkenes compared to the other drying methods, with HAID also demonstrating the lowest energy consumption. Therefore, HAID is identified as a CRP drying method with superior quality, shorter drying time, and lower energy consumption. 3 Aging process of Chenpi Natural fermentation of Chenpi, commonly known as aging, refers to the natural drying of fresh citrus peels after picking. In general, citrus peels can only be called Chenpi after a three-year aging process. Traditionally, fresh citrus peels are considered to possess a new, pungent, warm, and dispersing nature, making them prone to gas consumption and potential harm to the body's positive elements. Aging is undertaken to mitigate its potency and change its efficacy, thereby enhancing its medicinal and edible value. Sun Simiao of the Tang Dynasty asserted in the Thousand Gold Food Therapy that “The medicine is better if the citrus peels are pungent and spicy for a long time” (Sun, 1985). For Chenpi, the storage technology employed during aging is crucial in determining its medicinal and food value. The aging warehouse must be well-ventilated, dry, and positioned on an elevated terrain with a cool, dry environment with no direct sunlight. Environmental humidity is typically maintained below 60 %, and ambient temperature is kept at room temperature (Yan et al., 2021) (Fig. 3D). During the first three years of aging, Chenpi should be periodically turned to the sun, at least once a year, and stability is generally achieved after five years (Zhong et al., 2

The decrease in alkaloid content in Chenpi may be closely related to alleviating its drying properties before aging. 3.2.4 Phenolic acids and polysaccharides The content of polysaccharides and phenolic acids increases during the early storage period, followed by a subsequent decrease and stabilization over time. In addition to flavonoids, volatile oils, and alkaloids, water-soluble pectin polysaccharides are also important bioactive chemical substances in Chenpi. Recent research has focused on the changes in polysaccharide content during storage. From 5 to 10 years, there is a slight decrease in polysaccharide content with prolonged storage. However, between 10 and 20 years, the polysaccharide content remains stable. Furthermore, compared to fresh fruit peel stored for 1 year, aged pectin from 5 to 10 years of storage exhibit decreased methylation, an increase in soluble bound phenolic acid content, higher solubility, and a more complex monosaccharide composition (He, 2021). Interestingly, another study observed a decrease in the molecular weight of Chenpi polysaccharides with storage time, revealing relative molecular masses of 1175, 361, 213, and 185 kDa for 5, 10, 15, and 20 years of storage (Zhou, Jiang, et al., 2021), which suggested that the polysaccharides may undergo degradation during storage. 3.3 Microbial evolution during the aging process of Chenpi The accumulation of active ingredients during the storage process of Chenpi enhances its medicinal efficacy and increases its value. Micro

Through comprehensive microbial diversity sequencing technology, Chen et al. (2017) observed that the dominant bacterial phyla in Guang Chenpi at different aging stages were Firmicutes (63.41 %), Cyanobacteria (22.11 %), and Proteobacteria (12.30 %). The dominant bacterial genera were identified as Bacillus, Streptococcus, and Pseudomonas putida. Another study illustrated that Methylobacterium and Sphingomonas were dominant samples aged for 1 year. Bacillus was dominant in samples aged for 2 years, and Pseudomonas and Stenotrophomonas dominated samples aged for 4 years. Lactococcus became the dominant bacteria in samples aged for 5 years (Yang, He, Yang, Shen, Chen, & Liu, 2021). Interestingly, microbial community structure was similar, but dominant genera differed when the aging time was the same in different regions. Analyzing microbial community structure in Guang Chenpi samples aged naturally for a year in Beijing, Sichuan, Yunnan, and Guangdong, revealed that Methylocella and Bryobacter were dominant bacterial genera in Beijing, while Methylobacterium, Sphingomonas, Bacillus, Lactococcus Methylobacterium, Sphingomonas, Bacillus and Lactococcus dominated in Sichuan. In Guangdong, Rubellimicrobium and Lactobacillus were dominant, and in Yunnan, Glabridinium, Lactobacillus, Ralstonia, and Glutamicibacter dominated (Yang, He, Yang, Shen, Wang, et al., 2021). This suggests that the environment is an import

chunk_text: nt, and in Yunnan, Glabridinium, Lactobacillus, Ralstonia, and Glutamicibacter dominated (Yang, He, Yang, Shen, Wang, et al., 2021). This suggests that the environment is an important factor influencing the dominant bacterial genus in Chenpi. 3.3.2 Fungi evolution in Chenpi aging process The surface fungal composition of different Chenpi samples remains fundamentally consistent, with some variations in dominant genera. Correlation analysis revealed that the bacterial diversity of Chenpi exhibited no correlation with storage time, whereas fungal diversity displayed a significant correlation with storage time. Over prolonged storage, the abundance of Xeromyces and Xerochrysium increased, the abundance of Symmetrospora decreased, and the abundance of Mortierella increased and then decreased (Liu, 2019). Another study analyzed Guang Chenpi samples aged 1–5 years using high-throughput sequencing technology (Yang et al., 2021). They identified Zasmidium, Cladosporium, Symmetrospora, and Fusarium as dominant fungi in samples aged for a year. Samples aged for 3 years exhibited Cladosporium, Aureobasidium, Cladosporium, Aureobasidium, and Aspergillus as dominant fungi, while Xeromyces dominated in samples aged 4 years. Similarly, when aging times were consistent across different regions, variations in abundance and diversity were not significant, but the dominant fungal genera differed. In Sichuan, Symmetrospora and Aspergillus dominated, Pseudocercospora and Chaetomium dominated in Guangdong, while Zasmidium and Phaeosphaeriopsis dominated in Yunnan (Yang, He, Yang, Shen, Wang, et al., 2021). These results also reflect the differences in the dominant fungal genera of Chenpi from different varieties, storage years, and production regions. 3.4 Methods of accelerated aging process The manufacturing process of Chenpi still follows the traditional method of natural aging, which requires several years or even decades. It should be noted that under the storage conditions of natural aging, it is also conducive to the growth of Aspergillus mold. Therefore, there is an urgent need for effective accelerated aging methods. Considering the time-intensive of the natural aging process, especially during the warm and humid spring and summer seasons, which are crucial periods for aging, historical manufacturing practices have involved accelerating the aging of Chenpi by humidification and heating (Fu et al., 2018). Researchers have established an accelerated aging warehouse, replacing natural ventilation with a non-laminar air system and introducing constant temperature and humidity equipment. This maintains the warehouse environment at a stable temperature of 30 °C and humidity of 75 % throughout the aging process, resulting in a 55-day acceleration of the

This maintains the warehouse environment at a stable temperature of 30 °C and humidity of 75 % throughout the aging process, resulting in a 55-day acceleration of the peel aging process (Zhong et al., 2019) (Fig. 3I). This discovery provides a new approach for rapid aging of Chenpi and holds significant implications for practical manufacturing. On the other hand, Lei Gong's Explanation of Herbal Properties points out that Chenpi is “More than the plum summer and the strong gas all eliminated”, which may be attributed to the suitable temperature and humidity for microbial growth during the rainy season of plum and summer, leading toenzymatic metabolism and the production of substances that influence the accumulation of active ingredients in Chenpi. The higher the surface water activity in Chenpi, the higher the total flavonoid content and fungal abundance. Certain molds can also enhance the medicinal properties of Chenpi during the aging process. Microbial fermentation is a green and friendly modern bioprocessing technology widely applied in the deep processing of food and natural products, including Chinese herbal medicines (CHM). During the fermentation process, microbes produce hydrolytic enzymes that facilitate the release and transformation of active ingredients, alter the structure of toxic components in CHM, and reduce their side effects, thereby enhancing their pharmacological efficacy. Furthermore, microbial fermentation is an excellent strategy for improving the sensory flavor of food or CHM. Microbes can hydrolyze nutrients in fermented substrates, ge

chunk_text: ent of Chenpi with Aspergillus niger may involve the transformation of naringin and improvement of internal chemical reactions (Zhang, Tong, et al., 2023). Similarly, another study found that co-fermentation with Monascus purpureus and Saccharomyces cerevisiae increased the content of free flavonoids in the fermented product by 48.12 % compared to unfermented samples, while the content of flavonoid glycosides (hesperidin and naringin) decreased (Shen et al., 2024). Conversely, the content of flavanone glycosides (hesperidin and naringenin) increased, and the antioxidant capacity was enhanced. The composition and content of plant flavonoids are closely related to their antioxidant activity. When the 3-hydroxy structure of flavanone glycoside is substituted by glycoside, its antioxidant activity decreases. The higher the degree of glycosylation of flavonoid glycosides, the weaker the antioxidant capacity. This may be due to co-fermentation promoting the release of intracellular and insoluble active components such as flavonoids and the accumulation of flavonoid glycosides, thereby generating stronger antioxidant activity. On the other hand, the action of microbial enzymes can disrupt plant tissue structure, promote the release of volatile compounds, and increase their content. The study by Shen et al. (2024) also demonstrated that co-fermentation with Monascus purpureus and Saccharomyces cerevisiae can reduce the pungent odor of Chenpi. There is increasing scientific evidence that a delicate balance of microbes in the gut and other tissues is disrupted in various disease states, such as neurological diseases, cardiovascular diseases, gastrointestinal diseases, and even cancer (Li, Zou, et al., 2023). The reason why Chenpi is so precious is that it has multiple potential health benefits, including antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, reducing liver damage, regulating the gastrointestinal tract, modulating the gut microbiota, and hypolipidemic activities (Fig. 5A). Fig. 5B and Table 1 demonstrated the physiological effects of Chenpi through the modulation of gut microbiota. The following will summarize and discuss these findings in detail. 4.2.1 Anti-obesity Obesity constitutes a significant global public health challenge, characterized by excessive body weight and the accumulation of adipose tissue resulting from an imbalance in energy intake (Blüher, 2019). The World Health Organization has incorporated obesity management into the prevention strategies for non-communicable diseases. Projections indicate that by 2025, global obesity prevalence is expected to reach 18 % in men and surpass 21 % in women (Tantengco, 2022). Obesity is recognized as a risk factor for various metabolic disorders, including type 2 diabetes, insulin resistance, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), cardiovascular disease, and hypertension (James, 2008). Several active ingredients in Chenpi exhibit anti-obesity effects by regulating gut microbiota. For instance, rutin supplementation was found to effectively reduce weight gain and

title: Microbes: Drivers of Chenpi manufacturing, biotransformation, and physiological effects
chunk_text: the vessel walls (Wang et al., 2022). Chenpi has been manufactured and consumed in China, and has been reported to have the advantages containing bioactive components, sensory quality, and health effects, with a wide range of applications in food, health food, and medicine (Fig. 6A). According to the official website of the State Administration for Market regulation of China (https://www.samr.gov.cn/), 174 types of registered health food products contain Chenpi as raw material, and the most extensively confirmed effect is its ability to improve gastrointestinal function (Fig. 6B), mostly administered as capsules (Fig. 6C). In summary, as the demand increases, the processing industry of Chenpi is expected to produce more products. In addition to traditional food products, Chenpi extracts can be employed to prepare cosmetic and personal care products, as well as to develop functional food products owing to its antioxidant and other properties. 5 Conclusion This review provideed a macroscopic perspective on the role of microbes on the manufacturing, biotransformation, and physiological effects of Chenpi, revealing their inherent connections. Additionally, a systematic analysis of the substance transformation during the aging process of Chenpi was conducted, and the claim that “The longer the aging, the better the quality” was dialectically discussed from a scientific perspective. Considering that traditional Chenpi manufacturing processes can take several years or even decades to complete, therefore, it is necessary to utilize probiotics to accelerate the fermentation of Chenp

title: Microbes: Drivers of Chenpi manufacturing, biotransformation, and physiological effects
chunk_text: ditional Chenpi manufacturing processes can take several years or even decades to complete, therefore, it is necessary to utilize probiotics to accelerate the fermentation of Chenpi in the future to meet the diverse needs of consumers. Currently, our understanding of the changes in substance content during the aging process of Chenpi is still insufficient. Future research should employ modern omics technologies for a deeper analysis to examine the variations in the content and composition of major bioactive substances in Chenpi during the aging process. This will further elucidate the significance of microbes in mediating the effects of Chenpi during aging. Furthermore, although several bioactivities of Chenpi have been reported, most existing studies have only established associations between Chenpi and its active components, gut microbiota, and disease phenotypes, with causality yet to be determined. Future research should aim to obtain more accurate information on the composition of gut microbiota, active components of Chenpi, and their metabolites through the use of modern genomics, metabolomics, and proteomics approaches. This will provide a better understanding of how they interact within the host and exert their physiological effects, ultimately facilitating the translation of experimental research into clinical applications. title: Dynamics of chemical profile and microbial community in 3 consecutive years reveal Rhodococcus and Apiotrichum are potential microbes contributing to quality formation of Guang Chenpi
chunk_text: Currently, there remains a debate regarding the functional microorganisms responsible for the quality formation of Guang Chenpi (GCP). Thus, the metabolite profiles and microbial diversity of GCP samples subjected to natural treatment versus those sterilized via electron beam irradiation were investigated over a three-year period. It was found the main constituents of GCP were influenced both by spontaneous changes and microbial activity. In naturally treated GCP, we revealed a decrease in volatile components like terpenoids, alongside variations in flavonoid content. After 36 months of storage, there was a significant increase in hesperitin content (0.084–0.103 mg/g), while nobiletin content exhibited a marked decrease (7.294–2.825 mg/g). Microbial community succession can be categorized into four distinct stages based on storage duration, with Rhodococcus and Apiotrichum emerging as the predominant microbial genera (>35 %) at the 36-month mark. These two taxon were thought to be potential microbial organisms contributing to the chemical transformations in GCP.

chunk_text: g the functional microorganisms responsible for the quality formation of Guang Chenpi (GCP). Thus, the metabolite profiles and microbial diversity of GCP samples subjected to natural treatment versus those sterilized via electron beam irradiation were investigated over a three-year period. It was found the main constituents of GCP were influenced both by spontaneous changes and microbial activity. In naturally treated GCP, we revealed a decrease in volatile components like terpenoids, alongside variations in flavonoid content. After 36 months of storage, there was a significant increase in hesperitin content (0.084–0.103 mg/g), while nobiletin content exhibited a marked decrease (7.294–2.825 mg/g). Microbial community succession can be categorized into four distinct stages based on storage duration, with Rhodococcus and Apiotrichum emerging as the predominant microbial genera (>35 %) at the 36-month mark. These two taxon were thought to be potential microbial organisms contributing to the chemical transformations in GCP. Consequently, these samples may not accurately represent the dynamic changes in microbial communities and chemical components during the storage process of tangerine peels (Yang, He, et al., 2022). In recent years, a series of studies conducted by Wang et al. (2015), Zhang et al. (2017), and Yang, Xu, et al. (2021) investigated the effects of artificially accelerated the aging of dried tangerine peels. This acceleration was achieved through exposure to elevated temperatures (30 °C) and high humidity levels (95 % relative humidity). Under these conditions, the peels experienced mold growth, which was associated with an increase in flavonoid content, including total flavonoids, hesperidin, and tangerine. Notably, this increase in flavonoid components exhibited a positive correlation with the proliferation of Aspergillus niger. However, it is important to note that in the conventional production process of GCP, the peels are typically sun-dried to inhibit mold growth. Additionally, polymethoxyflavones present in the peels have been shown to suppress the growth of A. niger (Wu et al., 2014), thereby rendering the artificial mold promotion methods employed in these studies somewhat contentious. In the present study, we collected freshly produced dried peels of C. reticulata ‘Chachiensis’ and examined the alterations in their chemical composition over 3 consecutive years, both in the presence and absence of microbial influence. The objective of this research was to determine the extent to which microorganisms contribute to the quality formation of GCP and to identify the specific microorganisms that play a predominant role in this process. 2 Materials and methods 2.1 Experimental materials Freshly produced GCP was obtained from three locations within the Xinhui District, i.e. Chakeng Village (CK), situated in the primary production area (22°27′17″N; 113°4′14″E), Nantan Town (NT) located in the secondary core production area (22°29′46″N; 113°0′30″E), and Huicheng Qunsheng Village (KQ), found in non-core production areas (22°29′58″N; 112°59′59″E). The fruits were harvested in December 2018 and underwent the following processing steps: the mature fruits were cleaned, the peels were removed, and the peels were allowed to naturally dehydrate and shrink. Subsequently, the peels were positioned with the white side of the inner capsule facing upwards and dried on-site at the collection location. The samples were identified by the corresponding author and subsequently deposited in the herbarium of Southern Medical University. Following collection, the samples were divided into two groups after being packaged in Tyvek materials: the natural placement group, which received no treatment (NT, CK, KQ), and the sterilization group, which underwent sterilization via electron beam irradiation (MNT, MCK, MKQ) To investigate potential changes in the chemical components of the sterilization group changes

Prior to the experiment, certain samples were sterilized using electron beam irradiation, and it was confirmed that the irradiation dose applied did not significantly alter the composition of GCP. The sterilized samples were evaluated in accordance with the sterility testing methods outlined in the Chinese Pharmacopoeia (2020). Throughout the 36-month storage period, the collected samples were maintained in a dry, well-ventilated environment with a humidity level not exceeding 70 % and temperatures not surpassing 35 °C (Jiangmen Administration for Market Regulation, 2021). The electronic beam irradiation process was conducted by Shenzhen Gerui Radiation Technology Co., Ltd., with an irradiation dose set at 14 kGy. 2.2 Detection of volatile components To investigate the dynamic alterations in the volatile components of GCP, samples stored for varying durations of 0, 6, 12, 18, 24, and 36 months were analyzed. The volatile components were assessed utilizing solid phase microextraction gas chromatography-liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (SPME-GC–MS). A sample of 0.50 g of powdered GCP was placed in a sampling bottle, and subjected to a water bath at 90 °C. The volatiles were adsorbed for a duration of 30 min using a coating fiber (model 51,082, Supelco, Inc., Bellefonte, PA, USA), followed by desorption at 200 °C for 5 min. Data acquisition for GC–MS was conducted using a 7890 A gas chromatograph equipped with a thermal conductivity detector (TCD) (Agilent Technologies, Inc., CA, USA). Separation of the components was achieved with a TG-5MS capillary column (30.0 m × 250 μm × 0.25 μm, Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc., MA, USA). The initial temperature of the oven was set at 40 °C, which was subsequently increased at a rate of 3 °C/min to 100 °C, and then ramped at 7 °C/min to 220 °C for an additional 3 min, employing a split ratio of 50:1. The temperature of the GC injector was maintained at 200 °C, and electron impact mode (EI) ion sources were utilized for mass spectral analysis across a scan range of 30–550 m/z. The measurement data were presented as the mean values accompanied by standard deviation (SD). Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version 21.0 (SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA), with a significance threshold set at P < 0.05. Data that met the criteria for normal distribution and homogeneity of variance were analyzed using One-Way analysis of variance (ANOVA).
