At the initial time point (0 months), d-limonene was the predominant component across all samples, comprising between 57.04 % and 60.12 %. This was followed by gamma-terpinene, which ranged from 16.92 % to 18.69 %, and methyl 2-(methylamino) benzoate, with a concentration of 4.93 % to 7.06 %. Additionally, alpha-farnesene was present at levels between 1.44 % and 2.55 %, while p-cymene ranged from 1.49 % to 2.01 %. After 36 months of storage, d-limonene and gamma-terpinene remained the major constituents, with concentrations of 69.77 % to 75.33 % and 12.39 % to 13.51 %, respectively. However, the third, fourth, and fifth most abundant components shifted to beta-myrcene (1.66 % to 2.01 %), alpha-pinene (1.33 % to 1.62 %), and beta-pinene (0.96 % to 1.13 %). Over the course of storage, there was a general decline in the volatile components detected in each sample group, with certain components, such as 2-methoxy-4-vinylphenol, alpha-copaene, and alpha-copaene, becoming undetectable primarily in the latter half of the observation period. After 36 months, the sterilization group exhibited a greater number of volatile components compared to the natural placement group (30 versus 26), although these differential components were present in minimal quantities, below 0.05 % (see Table S1). Notably, when comparing the concentrations at zero months, only hesperitin and nobiletin exhibited significant changes after thirty-six months of storage in GCP (P < 0.001). The trends observed in the concentrations of the other four flavonoids during the 0–36 month period in the sterilization group were consistent with those in the natural placement group.

The richness of the surface microorganism community, assessed using the ACE and Chao indices, demonstrated a decline during the initial storage period (0–24 months), followed by a significant increase at 24 months, and a subsequent decrease in the later stages of storage (P < 0.01). A Venn diagram constructed from OTU data revealed the presence of 63 shared bacterial OTUs and 81 shared fungal OTUs across all samples, with unique bacterial and fungal OTUs being more prevalent in samples stored for 24 months (Fig. 2 ). Specifically, 154, 39, 130, and 99 bacterial OTUs were identified as unique to the 0, 12, 24, and 36-month samples, respectively, while 57, 58, 79, and 51 unique fungal OTUs were observed for the same time points. These newly identified OTUs may emerge during the aging process, potentially influencing the quality formation of GCP. To assess the overall differences in microbial communities of GCP at varying storage durations, principal coordinates analysis (PCoA) was conducted. The clustering results from the PCoA analysis for both bacteria and fungi were analogous, revealing that microbial community succession could be categorized into four distinct stages based on storage duration (Fig. 2B, Fig. 2E). The clear separation of samples from 0, 12, 24, and 36 months indicated that the microbial community underwent significant changes throughout the storage period from 0 to 36 months.

The succession of fungal communities during the storage of GCP exhibited patterns analogous to those observed in bacterial communities. As the duration of storage increased, certain microbial genera emerged as the predominant taxa. Initially, genera such as Penicillium (24.94 %), Zasmidium (17.57 %), Symmetrospora (9.19 %), and Aschersonia (4.82 %) were prevalent; however, their relative abundances diminished over time (see Fig. 2F). Conversely, Cladosporium still maintained a relatively stable abundance throughout the storage period, ranging from 5.62 % to 11.03 %. Over time, Apiotrichum supplanted Penicillium and Fusarium as the dominant microorganism, achieving a relative abundance of 37.57 %. Notably, Aspergillus was also identified, with its relative abundance increasing from 1.20 % to 2.96 % between 0 and 12 months, peaking at 9.79 % at 24 months, before declining to 4.51 % at 36 months. Throughout the storage period, the identified species of Aspergillus included A. penicillioides, A. gracilis, A. minisclerotigenes, A. fumigatus, and A. aculeatus, while A. niger was not detected. To assess the microbial variations across different storage durations, the Mann–Whitney U test was employed. The phenomena observed in our study exhibit both congruencies and discrepancies with prior research findings. However, our findings do not corroborate this study. Our results indicate that the five flavonoids analyzed exhibited spontaneous changes over the course of storage. In our study, the biotransformation of nobiletin within GCP may be mediated by enzymes from functional microorganisms, which remove a methoxy group to yield tangeretin (Fig. S6). 5 Conclusion Through the analysis of the metabolite profile and microbial diversity of GCP over a 3-year natural storage period, we observed a decline in volatile components with high molecular weight, particularly in the types of terpenoids and long-chain fatty hydrocarbons within the natural placement group. The most significant alterations in volatile components were noted at the 24-month mark, indicating that this two-year period is a critical juncture for changes in the volatile constituents of GCP. During the 36-month storage period, fluctuations were observed in the levels of five flavonoids within the natural placement group; however, when compared to the initial 0-month storage, there were no significant changes in the final concentrations of hesperidin, tangeretin, and naringin, while hesperitin significantly increased and nobiletin significantly decreased. The composition of microbial genera constantly changed over storage time. The relative percentage of Aspergillus in GCP remained consistently low, with no identification of A. niger. Consistent with the trends observed in volatile components, microbial diversity was significantly higher at the 24-month storage interval. By the 36-month mark, Rhodococcus and Apiotrichum emerged as the predominant genera among the surface

chunk_text: microbial diversity was significantly higher at the 24-month storage interval. By the 36-month mark, Rhodococcus and Apiotrichum emerged as the predominant genera among the surface microorganisms of GCP. A comparative analysis of the metabolic profiles between the natural placement group and the sterilization group led to the conclusion that both volatile and flavonoid components of GCP are influenced by surface microorganisms, although they can also develop spontaneously in the absence of microbial presence. Following a conditional screening process, Rhodococcus and Apiotrichum were identified as functional microorganisms that significantly impact the quality changes of GCP during storage. These findings establish a foundational basis for further research and provide a theoretical framework for the scientific storage and quality enhancement of GCP. title: Integrated analysis of dynamic changes in volatile and non-volatile compounds in Chuan Chenpi (Citrus reticulata ‘Dahongpao’) during aging by GC-IMS and UPLC-MS/MS
chunk_text: Chuan Chenpi (CCP), the peel of the ancient Chinese citrus variety Citrus reticulata ‘Dahongpao’, enhances its edible and medicinal value through aging. This study focuses on CCP samples aged 1–8 years, aiming to explore the dynamic changes during aging. Although aging induced noticeable changes in color, Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) analysis revealed no significant alterations in functional groups. Volatile and non-volatile metabolomic analyses indicated that aging primarily affects metabolite content rather than types, and both composition and antioxidant activity reached relatively high levels in the fourth year. The experimental results illustrate that the improvement in CCP quality induced by aging does not follow a linear pattern but exhibits fluctuations. The findings verify that the fourth year serves as a critical turning point for CCP's quality. This study clarifies the dynamic variation of chemical components in CCP during aging, thereby providing a scientific basis for the selection of its aging duration.

chunk_text: though aging induced noticeable changes in color, Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) analysis revealed no significant alterations in functional groups. Volatile and non-volatile metabolomic analyses indicated that aging primarily affects metabolite content rather than types, and both composition and antioxidant activity reached relatively high levels in the fourth year. The experimental results illustrate that the improvement in CCP quality induced by aging does not follow a linear pattern but exhibits fluctuations. The findings verify that the fourth year serves as a critical turning point for CCP's quality. This study clarifies the dynamic variation of chemical components in CCP during aging, thereby providing a scientific basis for the selection of its aging duration. It has been utilized as an herbal medicine for thousands of years, demonstrating excellent efficacy in treating digestive and respiratory disorders (Cai et al., 2025). Owing to its rich content of various bioactive compounds such as flavonoids, alkaloids, and essential oils, CRP also possesses considerable edible value, serving as a valuable source of health food

chunk_text: ng multiple analytical instruments, it is possible to accurately identify changes during the aging process of CCP and achieve precise differentiation of its aging duration. In this study, a combination of analytical techniques including E-eye, E-nose, GC-IMS, and UPLC-MS/MS was employed to comprehensively and systematically characterize the dynamic changes in color, odor, and chemical composition during the aging process of CCP aged 1–8 years (CCPY1–8). The research elucidated the transformation patterns during CCP aging, identified the optimal aging duration, and provided a scientific basis for standardizing the aging procedure. These findings hold significant implications for the comprehensive utilization and development of C.reticulata ‘Dahongpao’ peel and its application in health food products. 2 Materials and methods 2.1 Materials and reagents All samples of Chuan Chenpi (CCP) used in our research, with aging periods ranging from one to eight years (designated as CCPY1 to CCPY8), were provided by Sichuan Wanwu Bencao Health Technology Co., Ltd. The raw materials were collected from Chaoyang Town, Shizhong District, Neijiang City. Citrus samples were collected from the same cultivar, C. reticulata ‘Dahongpao’, grown in a single planting base. Fruits were uniformly harvested annually from late December to early January of the following year during 2017–2024. After washing, the fruits were manually peeled, and the peels were naturally sun-dried to obtain fresh CCP. Subsequently, the fresh CCP was packed into cloth bags, placed in wooden boxes, and aged on the second floo

Subsequently, the fresh CCP was packed into cloth bags, placed in wooden boxes, and aged on the second floor of a cool, dry, and well-ventilated warehouse (to prevent moisture damage). The aging temperature and humidity varied with seasons (annual average temperature: 15–24 °C; annual average humidity: 72%–80%) without any artificial intervention. The CCP samples were turned over and sun-dried annually in August. All samples were subjected to three biological replicates. Methanol, acetonitrile, and formic acid were purchased from Merck Drugs & Biotechnology, USA, and were chromatographically pure. Methanol, potassium bromide (KBr) and potassium persulfate (K2S2O8) were purchased from Chengdu Kelon Chemicals Co. 2-Butanone, 2-Pentanone, 2-Hexanone, 2-Heptanone, 2-Octanone, and 2-Nonanone were all supplied by Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China). 1,1-diphenyl-2-trinitrophenylhydrazine (DPPH) and 2,2′-azino-bis-3-ethylbenzothiazoline-6-sulfonic acid (ABTS) were purchased from Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Technology Co (Shanghai, China). Total antioxidant capacity (T-AOC) assay kit (ferric ion reducing antioxidant capacity, FRAP) was purchased from Nanjing Jiancheng Bioengineering Institute (Nanjing, Jiangsu Province, China). All reagents were of analytical grade, with the exception of KBr which was of spectral grade. 2.2 Analysis of the physicochemical properties of CCP from different aging years 2.2.1 Total aerobic plate counting and Escherichia coli counting The total aero

(Shandong, China), which holds China Metrology Accreditation (CMA), International Laboratory Accreditation Cooperation - Mutual Recognition Arrangement (ILAC-MRA), and China National Accreditation Service for Conformity Assessment (CNAS) qualifications. The determination of total aerobic plate count was carried out in accordance with the national standard GB 4789.2–2022. Precisely weigh 25 g of sample powder and add it to 225 mL of sterile normal saline, homogenize at 8000 r/min for 2 min to prepare a 1:10 dilution. After serial gradient dilution (from 10−1 to 10−6), select 3 appropriate dilutions, aspirate 0.1 mL of each and evenly spread it on nutrient agar medium plates (3 parallel samples for each dilution). Incubate at a constant temperature of 36 °C ± 1 °C for 48 h ± 2 h before counting, and express the results as colony-forming units per gram (CFU/g). The determination of Escherichia coli was performed with reference to the industry standard SN/T 0169–2010. Take the aforementioned 1:10 dilution and inoculate it into lactose bile salt fermentation tubes using the Most Probable Number (MPN) method, incubate at 36 °C ± 1 °C for 24 h ± 2 h for primary fermentation. Pick the gas-producing bacterial liquid and inoculate it on Eosin Methylene Blue agar medium for isolation and culture. Sel

chunk_text: at 36 °C ± 1 °C for 24 h ± 2 h for primary fermentation. Pick the gas-producing bacterial liquid and inoculate it on Eosin Methylene Blue agar medium for isolation and culture. Select typical colonies for Gram staining and biochemical identification, then refer to the MPN index table based on the number of positive tubes, and express the results as MPN/g. 2.2.2 Determination of flavonoid content The quantification of hesperidin, nobiletin, and tangeretin was performed according to the method specified in the ChP (2020 Edition, Volume I) (Chinese Pharmacopoeia Commission, 2020) for the determination of CRP. Specifically, approximately 0.2 g of the powdered sample was accurately weighed into a stoppered conical flask. Then, 25 mL of methanol was precisely added, the flask was sealed and weighed. The mixture was subjected to ultrasonication (300 W, 40 kHz) for 45 min. After cooling, the flask was weighed again, and the weight loss was compensated by adding methanol. The solution was mixed well, filtered through a 0.22 μm microporous membrane, and stored in an injection vial for HPLC analysis. The HPLC analysis was conducted using an Agilent 1260 system (Agilent Technologies Inc., California, USA) equipped with an Agilent SB-C18 column (250 mm × 4.6 mm, 5 μm). The mobile phase consisted of acetonitrile (A) and water (B). The elution program was set as follows: initially 78% B, maintained for 10 min, then linearly changed to 52% B over 10 min, and held for another 10 min. The flow rate was 1.0 mL/min, the column temperature was maintained at 30 °C, and the injection volume was 5

Detection wavelengths were set at 283 nm for hesperidin and 330 nm for nobiletin and tangeretin, using a UV detector. In addition, the CCP extract was also utilized for the determination of total flavonoid content. The results indicated that the total aerobic plate count remained relatively high within the first five years of aging, while from the sixth year onward, it stabilized at a low level. Despite the relatively higher counts observed in the early aging stage, they were still far below the general limit for food products (typically ≤105 CFU/g). Regarding Escherichia coli detection, this indicator was undetectable in all CCP samples (<3.0 MPN/g). Collectively, these findings demonstrate that CCP maintains high edible safety throughout the entire aging period. The variation in microbial counts during aging may be attributed to the annual sun-drying process conducted in August. However, the specific microbial taxa undergoing succession and the underlying succession patterns during CCP aging require further investigation using microbiome sequencing technologies. In this study, we quantified the changes in total flavonoids and three specific flavonoid monomers during the aging process of CCP. During aging, the total flavonoid content increased continuously over the first four years, peaking at 9.73% in the fourth year, after which it declined but remained stable and ultimately higher than the initial level (Fig. 1A). Unexpectedly, the hesperidin content exhibited continuous fluctuations throughout the aging process (Fig. D), which may be associated with metabolic activities of microorganisms on the peel surface. However, antioxidant activity among different samples exhibited a fluctuating pattern. Specifically, antioxidant activity declined slightly in the initial aging stage, though not significantly, and subsequently increased to levels exceeding the initial values (Fig. 7A-C). While previous studies have generally reported a continuous enhancement of antioxidant activity with prolonged aging, our results did not show a monotonic increase. Instead, we observed alternating periods of enhancement and reduction. We therefore propose that the antioxidant activity of CRP increases within a limited aging window, while exhibiting an overall increasing or fluctuating trend over a broader time scale. According to Bian et al. (2022), the antioxidant activity of GCP increased over a long-term aging period of 1–11 years, with the most pronounced increase occurring during the first five years, followed by a more gradual rise. This finding aligns to some extent with our observations, though we were unable to validate it further due to the lack of CCP samples with longer aging times. Moreover, existing literature lacks comprehensive studies on continuous temporal changes in the bioactivity of aged CRP. It is also worth noting that the variation in antioxidant activity was consistent with the trend of flavonoids. This suggests that the health-promoting

The results showed that the flavonoid content in CCP initially increased and then decreased during the aging process, reaching a relatively high level in the fourth year. With prolonged aging time, the surface color of CCP gradually darkened, and the response intensity of the electronic nose sensors to CCP decreased. The FTIR results indicated that the aging process did not alter the types of compounds present in CCP, nor did it lead to the formation of any new functional groups. A total of 55 VOCs were identified in all samples by GC-IMS, most of which decreased in content during aging. As for non-volatile components, 1343 secondary metabolites were identified using non-targeted metabolomics. Although the composition of metabolites did not change significantly during aging, their contents exhibited dynamic fluctuations. Through OPLS-DA analysis, 76 shared DAMs were screened across all comparison groups, which can serve as key biomarkers for determining the aging duration of CCP. In terms of bioactivity, the antioxidant activity first increased and then decreased. In conclusion, our study demonstrates that significant changes occur in the color, metabolite contents, and biological activities of CCP during the aging

In conclusion, our study demonstrates that significant changes occur in the color, metabolite contents, and biological activities of CCP during the aging process. The most prominent changes take place within the first four years, indicating that the fourth year serves as a critical turning point for CCP quality evolution. Meanwhile, this study also reveals that within a limited timeframe, the quality improvement of CCP induced by aging may not follow a linear trend but rather exhibits a fluctuating pattern. This study provides a scientific basis for determining the aging period of CCP, facilitating the establishment of a tiered storage system. This system not only helps reduce long-term storage costs but also improves the utilization efficiency of raw material resources. Furthermore, the research transforms the traditional experience-based approach for assessing the aging year into an objective evaluation method based on chemical composition content, offering valuable references for market supervision and management. However, our research still lacks in vitro or in vivo validation of these activities, which will be the focus of our subsequent work. In addition, microorganisms also play a crucial role in the aging process. Our current study has not yet elucidated the effects of microorganisms on CCP aging, and subsequent research will be conducted from a microbial perspective to further unravel the aging mechanism of CCP. title: Exploration of optimal preparation strategy of Chenpi (pericarps of Citrus reticulata Blanco) flavouring essence with great application potential in sugar and salt-reduced foods
chunk_text: To obtain flavouring essence with application potential in sugar and salt-reduced foods, the optimal strategy for extraction and microencapsulation of essential oil (EO) from Chenpi was investigated. UPLC-QTOF-MS/MS and liquid–liquid-extraction-GC–MS confirmed the selectivity for volatiles ranked in hydrodistillation > supercritical fluid extraction > solvent extraction. The aroma characteristic of Chenpi EO was distinguished by 33 key volatiles (screened out via headspace-SPME-GC–MS) and quantitative descriptive analysis. EO extracted by supercritical fluid extraction was preferred for preserving the original aroma of Chenpi and displaying more fruity, honey and floral. Chenpi flavouring essence with superior encapsulation efficiency, particle size, water dispersibility, and thermostability was obtained through optimally microencapsulating EO with gum arabic and maltodextrin (1:1) by high-pressure homogenization coupled with spray drying. Chenpi flavouring essence was able to reduce the usage of sugar and salt by 20 % via enhancing flavour perception of sweetness and saltiness. This study first developed a flavouring essence promisingly effective in both sugar and salt-reduced foods.

A rapid weight loss of Chenpi EO occurred at around 107℃, due to its thermal instability. Then Chenpi EO was completely decomposed at around 450℃. The weight loss of S4-H and S4-H-wall could be divided into 3 stages. It started with a slight weight loss at around 100℃ for the evaporation of moisture, then sustained until 220℃ with a plateau. Both S4-H and S4-H-wall had rapid weight loss in the second stage roughly ranging from 220℃ to 360℃, and eventually in a plateau for the last stage. It was similar to the observation from Bajac et al. (2022). The wall material remained intact before 220℃ and prevented Chenpi EO inside from evaporation. As the temperature continued to rise, wall material started evaporating, causing weight loss in S4-H-wall and S4-H. Meanwhile, with the wall collapsed, Chenpi EO encapsulated inside S4-H was exposed and rapidly evaporated, resulting in greater weight loss in S4-H. This was also reflected on the DTG curve that the weight loss rate of S4-H in the second stage was higher than that of S4-H-wall. In summary, the thermal stability of Chenpi flavouring essence was greatly improved after being optimally encapsulated, expanding the range

title: Exploration of optimal preparation strategy of Chenpi (pericarps of Citrus reticulata Blanco) flavouring essence with great application potential in sugar and salt-reduced foods
chunk_text: stage was higher than that of S4-H-wall. In summary, the thermal stability of Chenpi flavouring essence was greatly improved after being optimally encapsulated, expanding the range of applications in food industry. 3.7 The ability of Chenpi flavouring essence in enhancing flavour perception of sweetness and saltiness 3.7.1 Confirmation of the ability of Chenpi flavouring essence in enhancing flavour perception of sweetness and saltiness Odor not only affected our choices of foods before eating but also made a difference in the formation of flavour when eating foods (Shepherd, 2006). Guichard et al. (2020) revealed that odors with the potential for sweetness enhancement usually possessed the descriptions of fruity, sweet, and floral, while herbs were commonly identified as saltiness enhancers (Barnett et al., 2019). The unique aromatic characteristics of Chenpi EO made Chenpi flavouring essence a candidate for the enhancement of both sweetness and saltiness. Therefore, the effects of Chenpi flavouring essence on sweetness and saltiness in simple aqueous system were investigated. The aqueous dispersion of S4-H (0.1 %, w/w) was tested by panelists via QDA, and evaluated to be Chenpi-like aroma and tasteless. Almost no sweetness or saltiness was aware, while bitterness was detected in the aftertaste, in accordance with the taste of Chenpi described by Chinese Pharmacopoeia (version 2020). As indicated in Fig. 6 A, when S4-H was added, the sucrose solution tasted significantly sweeter (p < 0.05). It was the citrus feel that might enhance the sweetness, which was held in the mout

title: Exploration of optimal preparation strategy of Chenpi (pericarps of Citrus reticulata Blanco) flavouring essence with great application potential in sugar and salt-reduced foods
chunk_text: eractions, and eventually forming the complex flavour (Shepherd, 2006). To further verify whether the aroma of Chenpi flavouring essence contributed to the enhancements of sweetness and saltiness, the panellists were asked to taste again with a nose clip. The samples with 0.1 % S4-H tasted dull as references with a nose clip, and the Chenpi aroma was unable to be detected. It was because the nose clip blocked retronasal stimulation. As a result, the enhancement effect on sweetness and saltiness almost disappeared with a nose clip (Fig. 6A), which was significantly different from that without one (p < 0.05). It demonstrated that it was the unique Chenpi aroma of S4-H affected the taste via retronasal stimulation, and eventually enhanced sweetness and saltiness. A similar conclusion was observed by Greis et al. (2022) reporting that the nose clip blocked the sensory of lemon and vanilla aroma and invalidated the sweetness enhancement on yogurts. Briefly, Chenpi flavouring essence was a dual enhancer for sweetness and saltiness by the special Chenpi-like (with both citrus and herbs contributing) aroma. 3.7.2 Exploration of the ability of Chenpi flavouring essence in reducing sugar and salt usage Additionally, the ability of Chenpi flavouring essence in reducing sugar and salt usage was explored via the method of relative to the reference. A series of solutions with 0.1 % S4-H and different concentrations of sucrose/salt (0 %∼50 % reduction) were prepared and scored relative to the reference that 5.0 % sucrose or 1.0 % salt solution. Fig. 6B demonstrated that the addition of 0.

title: Exploration of optimal preparation strategy of Chenpi (pericarps of Citrus reticulata Blanco) flavouring essence with great application potential in sugar and salt-reduced foods
chunk_text: ions of sucrose/salt (0 %∼50 % reduction) were prepared and scored relative to the reference that 5.0 % sucrose or 1.0 % salt solution. Fig. 6B demonstrated that the addition of 0.1 % S4-H in solution with reduced sucrose or salt concentration by 20 % reached the same sweetness or saltiness as reference. Thus, the usage of sucrose and salt could be reduced by 20 % in the presence of 0.1 % S4-H. Moreover, some panellists even couldn’t tell the difference in saltiness between the reference and solution with reduced salt concentration by 30 % in the presence of 0.1 % S4-H. Oliveira et al. (2021) succeeded in reducing 25 % sugar in yogurt with 0.2 % vanilla flavour while not affecting the sweetness, and as well accepted as samples in ideal concentration of sugar with 0.2 % strawberry flavour. Meanwhile, Bertelsen et al. (2020) found that vanilla aroma performed a stronger effect on apple nectar compared with water matrix, which implied that the taste enhancement could be more significant in complex food systems. In short, Chenpi flavouring essence with the characteristic Chenpi aroma was an outstanding dual enhancer for flavour perception of sweetness and saltiness, functioning via cross-modal interactions. The addition of only 0.1 % Chenpi flavouring essence could effectively reduce the usage of sugar or salt by 20 % in a simple water system while bringing the attractive Chenpi aroma. Therefore, Chenpi flavouring essence had a significant range of applications in foods, because of its dual effects on both sweet and salty perspectives and attractive aroma. 4 Conclusion In this

title: Exploration of optimal preparation strategy of Chenpi (pericarps of Citrus reticulata Blanco) flavouring essence with great application potential in sugar and salt-reduced foods
chunk_text: pi flavouring essence had a significant range of applications in foods, because of its dual effects on both sweet and salty perspectives and attractive aroma. 4 Conclusion In this study, for the first time, a flavouring essence with dual effects on sweetness and saltiness enhancement was developed through gradual investigation of the optimal and industrializable strategy for the extraction and microencapsulation of high-quality Chenpi EO. Supercritical fluid extraction exhibiting high selectivity for volatiles and preserving the original aroma of Chenpi was the optimal strategy for the extraction of high-quality EO. High-pressure homogenization coupled with spray drying using gum arabic and maltodextrin (1:1) as wall material was the optimal strategy for the microencapsulation of high-quality EO. Chenpi flavouring essence, with superior encapsulation efficiency, particle size, water dispersibility, and thermostability, reduced the usage of sugar and salt by 20 % while bringing the satisfactory aroma, which verified its great application potential in sugar and salt-reduced foods. title: Metabolite profiling and ‘dryness’-like effect analysis of ‘Chenpi’ plant tea (Citri Reticulatae Pericarpium peel) with and without steaming peocessing
chunk_text: Citri Reticulatae Pericarpium peel (‘Chenpi’ tea) is a popular food-medicine functional tea, which mainly existing unsteamed (CRP) and steamed (SCRP) products. In this study, a combination of electronic nose and GC–MS analysis showed that aged SCRP had a more intense aroma, which was attributed to the significant reduction or disappearance of components representing refreshing aroma, such as β-Myrcene and d-Limonene, while some components with thick odors like Valencene were newly formed. For the ‘dryness’-like effect, the weaker effect of SCRP relative to CRP was initially confirmed in rats, as characterized by water intake, submandibular gland index, and hemorheology, consistenting with the expression trend of aquaporin (AQP) 2, 3 and 5 mRNA. Molecular docking further revealed that the key differential components responsible for the different ‘dryness’-like effects of SCR and SCRP by affecting AQPs were Narirutin, Rutin, Calceolarioside C, Hesperidin, Melitidin and Limonin. Taken together, our findings enhance the understanding of steaming processing-induced aroma and ‘dryness’-like effect changes in ‘Chenpi’ tea and their impact on consumer experience, offering a novel perspective for optimizing ‘Chenpi’ tea products.

Department of Traditional Chinese Medicine Guangdong Pharmaceutical University Guangzhou 510006 China ⁎⁎ Corresponding authors. 1 These authors contributed equally to this work Citri Reticulatae Pericarpium peel (‘Chenpi’ tea) is a popular food-medicine functional tea, which mainly existing unsteamed (CRP) and steamed (SCRP) products. In this study, a combination of electronic nose and GC–MS analysis showed that aged SCRP had a more intense aroma, which was attributed to the significant reduction or disappearance of components representing refreshing aroma, such as β-Myrcene and d-Limonene, while some components with thick odors like Valencene were newly formed. chunk_text: tudy initially validated in rats that SCRP can effectively reduces the “dryness” side effect of CRP. The aroma changes between CRP and steamed CRP were then analyzed using an electronic nose technique. Subsequently, by using UPLC-Q-Exactive Orbitrap/MS, HS-GC–MS and chemometrics techniques, a comprehensive analysis of the chemical composition differences between the two types of CRP tea was conducted, revealing the key components responsible for the changes in aroma and primary functional constituents. Finally, the differential effects of CRP and steamed CRP on alleviating “dryness” through the regulation of aquaporins were confirmed by molecular docking. This study lays the foundation for further exploration of the chemical migration mechanisms and their potential role in modulating dryness in CRP and SCRP. 2 Materials and methods 2.1 Samples and chemicals Ten batches each of CRP and SCRP were collected and purchased from various companies and markets, with details provided in Table S1. These samples were identified by Associate Professor Liu Jizhu from the College of Traditional Chinese Medicine at Guangdong Pharmaceutical University as the dried and mature peel of Citrus reticulata Blanco and its cultivated varieties, belonging to the Rutaceae family. Voucher specimens are stored in the herbarium of the College of Traditional Chinese Medicine at Guangdong Pharmaceutical University, Guangzhou, Guangdong Province, China. The calibration curves were constructed by plotting the IS-normalized peak areas versus concentrations. The limit of detection (LOD) and LOQ were determined by concentrations of samples that generated peaks above 3 and 10 times the signal-to-noise (S/N) values, respectively. The precision was evaluated by RSD value after 6 consecutive injections; One sample was used to prepare 6 test solutions in parallel, and the repeatability was evaluated by investigating the peak area RSD value of the index components; The samples were injected at 0, 2, 4, 6, 12, and 24 h, respectively, and the peak area RSD values of the index components were calculated at 6 time points to evaluate the stability within 24 h. 2.5 Data processing LC-MS Data acquisition was achieved by Xcalibur software (version 4.0, Thermo Fisher, Waltham, MA, USA). The conversion of some components between CRP and SCRP is traceable. Prunin is formed by losing a glucose unit from Narirutin, and the decrease of its content could be explained by heat during steaming process to its aglycone Naringin (Fig. 4A). This study provided a comprehensive evaluation of the effects of steaming on Citri Reticulatae Pericarpium peel, called ‘Chenpi’ tea, emphasizing the changes in its aroma profile and the modulation of its “dryness”-like effects. For the aroma, the results revealed that steaming processing significantly altered the volatile metabolites of CRP, changing its aromatic profile by generating a unique blend of volatile metabolites while reducing certain freshness-associated components. Despite the expected loss of some volatile metabolites due to heat, the steaming processed CRP (SCRP) was found to have a more intense aroma, which could be attributed to the formation of new generated aromatic metabolites during the steaming processing. This suggested that the “dryness”-inducing properties of ‘Chenpi’ tea are closely linked to its impact on AQPs, which could be moderated by steaming. Molecular docking simulations provided further insights. Some non-volatile metabolites that contribute greatly to the distinction between CRP and SCRP, high in content, and content increased with steaming processing, such as Narirutin and Rutin, showed strong binding affinities for AQP2 and AQP5; Similarly, some non-volatile metabolites, such as Hesperidin and Melitidin, were significantly decreased after steaming and showed strong binding ability to AQP3. In summary, this research underscored the importance of existing popular processing methods for ‘Chenpi’ tea, steaming, in modifying the sensory and “dryness”-like effect. title: Elucidation of the diverse molecular signatures and transformation pathways of flavor metabolites in age-stratified citri reticulatae pericarpium (ChenPi) and their enzymatic hydrolysates: A perspective from the flavor space
chunk_text: The aging duration associated with pectin present in Citri Reticulatae Pericarpium (CP) is crucial to its flavor profile. Herein, flavor features including sensory evaluation, odor and taste compounds of differently aged CP and its enzymatic hydrolysis production (CPEH) were characterized, followed by identifying the precursor substances, thereby outlining the transformation pathway. Finally, flavor space based on 1444 molecular descriptors and their concentration were established. For the sensory evaluation, enzymatic hydrolysis promoted both odor and taste attributes. In light of the identified compounds, enzymatic hydrolysis facilitated the production of various key aroma compounds and taste compounds of interest. The transformation of fatty acids, amino acids, terpenes, glycolysis, and the TCA cycle were identified as the primary pathways for generating the flavor compounds. Finally, flavor space of 10-year aging CPEH demonstrated the significant differences compared with that of 10-year aging CP. These results provide a novel flavor space to visually reflect the flavor characteristic and indicated that enzymatic hydrolysis promoted the flavor profile of CP.

To profoundly figure out the formation and transformation mechanism of flavor compounds in CP during aging time and enzymatic process, precursor compounds including fatty acids and free amino acids are investigated to construct mechanistic maps. Furthermore, molecular descriptors are employed to establish the flavor space of differently aged CP and CPEH. Ultimately, we aim to evaluate whether controlled enzymatic hydrolysis can serve as a scalable post-aging step to bridge the flavor gap of younger CP, thereby alleviating reliance on prolonged storage. 2 Materials and methods 2.1 Samples and reagents CP samples were collected from companies in Guangdong Province. Four batches, aged 1, 3, 7, and 10 years, were analyzed for flavor compounds. The detailed aging process are as followed. The CP samples were dried in the temperature-controlled warehouse maintained between 25 and 28 °C with adequate ventilation. In addition to temperature control (25–28 °C) and ventilation, the storage humidity was maintained at approximately 50–60 %. The peels were sun-exposed for 6–8 h per session, with biannual turning to ensure homogeneous oxidation. The aging period was calculated from the completion of the drying process. Once the specified aging periods (1, 3, 7, and 10 years) were reached, the CP were harvested between October and November, sealed in storage bags, and kept in a warehouse designed to minimize the loss of VOCs. In the following, the samples were transported to the laboratory and stored at 4 °C before analysis. Chemical reagent

Chemical reagent information is in Table S1. 2.2 Experimental design CP aged for 1,3,7, or 10 years were each split into two parallel treatments. (a) water extraction (aging-only control) and (b) enzymatic hydrolysis. Notably, to isolate the effect of enzymes, the water extraction sample underwent the identical protocol but without adding enzymes. Consequently, the sole difference between (a) and (b) was the presence/absence of pectinase and papain. The enzymatic method, patented in China (patent No. CN 116420863), was slightly modified in this study. It enhances the release of flavor and bioactive compounds using pectinase and papain to degrade pectin. The CP was ground into a fine powder, measured to 10 ± 0.1 g, and mixed with deionized water at a 1:8 ratio. Pectinase (0.5 %) and papain (0.2 %) were added based on the sample's dry weight. Enzymatic hydrolysis occurred at 55 °C for 4 h with an oscillation speed of 150 rpm. The mixture was heated to 90 °C for 15 min to inactivate the enzymes, where the sealing film was utilized to cover the conical flask to minimize the volatilization of VOCs. Subsequently, the heated mixture was filtered for further analysis. A control group was prepared without enzymes. All the following experiments are conducted using the treated filtrate. As shown in Fig. 1 (a) and Table S4, the dominant aroma descriptors included citrus, woody, sweet, floral, fatty, herbal, and mint. For CPEH samples, citrus aroma scores showed a consistent decline from 3.3 (1-year) to 1.8 (10-year), indicating that prolonged aging may reduce citrus aroma intensity. This decrease is likely due to the degradation or transformation of monoterpenes such as limonene and linalool over time, as previously reported (Jiang et al., 2023). In contrast, woody, sweet, floral, fatty, herbal, and mint notes increased significantly with aging (p < 0.05). Interestingly, despite the sensory decrease in citrus aroma, a greater number of monoterpenes, terpenes, and aldehydes were tentatively identified in older samples using HS-SPME-GC × GC-qTOF-MS. This may be attributed to oxidative, hydrolytic, or enzymatic reactions that increase VOC complexity, contributing to a shift in aroma balance rather than simple intensification of citrus notes. Additionally, Duncan's test revealed that between CP and CPEH samples, floral, woody, sweet, fatty, herbal, and mint attributes were significantly different (p < 0.05), while citrus and woody notes did not differ significantly (p > 0.05). title: Metabolomics combined with extraction optimization and biochemical assays revealed flavonoids and in vitro and in vivo antioxidant activity of Ponkan Chenpi
chunk_text: Ponkan Chenpi (PC), derived from the dried and aged peel of ripe Ponkan citrus, is a traditional product with both medicinal and edible value. In this study, an untargeted metabolomics approach utilizing UPLC-QTOF-MS/MS was employed to characterize the metabolite profiles of PCs aged for 1, 3, 5, and 8 years (PC1, PC3, PC5, and PC8). A total of 1455 metabolites were characterized, with flavonoids exhibiting relatively high quantity and abundance. Clear differences in both metabolite profiles and metabolic pathways were observed among PCs of different aging periods. Furthermore, flavonoid extracts were prepared from the PCs, with the content of flavonoid compounds determined by HPLC as the response value. The optimal extraction parameters, determined by single-factor analysis and response surface methodology, were 65 % ethanol concentration, 50 min ultrasonic time, 65 °C ultrasonic temperature, and a 1:65 solid-liquid ratio. Subsequent free radical scavenging assays demonstrated that the PC5 extract exhibited superior antioxidant activity. Correlation analysis indicated that flavonoid monomers—hesperidin, nobiletin, tangeretin, and 5-demethylnobiletin were significantly correlated with antioxidant activity. Network pharmacology and molecular docking analyses revealed that proteins such as PPARγ, COX-2, and ALB were the core targets through which these flavonoids exert antioxidant effects. Finally, the in vivo efficacy of PC5was verified in a D-gal-induced oxidative damage mouse model, which demonstrated that PC5 extract significantly improve the hepatic oxidative stress state and alleviate tissue damage in mice. This work provides a theoretical foundation for the quality evaluation and high-value utilization of PC.

chunk_text: ted equally to this paper Ponkan Chenpi (PC), derived from the dried and aged peel of ripe Ponkan citrus, is a traditional product with both medicinal and edible value. In this study, an untargeted metabolomics approach utilizing UPLC-QTOF-MS/MS was employed to characterize the metabolite profiles of PCs aged for 1, 3, 5, and 8 years (PC1, PC3, PC5, and PC8). A total of 1455 metabolites were characterized, with flavonoids exhibiting relatively high quantity and abundance. Clear differences in both metabolite profiles and metabolic pathways were observed among PCs of different aging periods. Furthermore, flavonoid extracts were prepared from the PCs, with the content of flavonoid compounds determined by HPLC as the response value. The optimal extraction parameters, determined by single-factor analysis and response surface methodology, were 65 % ethanol concentration, 50 min ultrasonic time, 65 °C ultrasonic temperature, and a 1:65 solid-liquid ratio. Subsequent free radical scavenging assays demonstrated that the PC5 extract exhibited superior antioxidant activity. Correlation analysis indicated that flavonoid monomers—hesperidin, nobiletin, tangeretin, and 5-demethylnobiletin were significantly correlated with antioxidant activity. Network pharmacology and molecular docking analyses revealed that proteins such as PPARγ, COX-2, and ALB were the core targets through which these flavonoids exert antioxidant effects. Finally, the in vivo efficacy of PC5was verified in a D-gal-induced oxidative damage mouse model, which demonstrated that PC5 extract significantly improve the hep

The extract solution was filtered to obtain the flavonoid extract of PCs, which was subsequently lyophilized. Prior to HPLC analysis, a 5 mg portion of the lyophilized sample was dissolved in HPLC-grade methanol, followed by filtration through a 0.22 μm organic membrane. Briefly, 50 μL of sample solution (1 mg/mL) was reacted with the respective assay working solutions (150 μL for DPPH, 200 μL for ABTS, and 1.2 mL for FRAP) under dark conditions. As shown in Fig. 7A, before the formal experiment, the male KM mice (6 weeks old) were acclimatized for 7 days in a specific environment (24 ± 2 °C, and 60 ± 5 % relative humidity) with ad libitum access to food. Subsequently, the mice were divided into 6 groups: the control group, the D-gal model group, PC5 treatment groups at concentrations of 150, 300, and 600 mg/kg (PC5-L, PC5-M, PC5-H), and the Vc treatment group. Vc, a well-established and potent antioxidant, was selected as the positive control to provide a benchmark for evaluating the in vivo antioxidant efficacy of the PC5 extract. Each group (excluding the control group) received a daily subcutaneous injection of 300 mg/kg D-gal at the nape of the neck in the morning, while the control group received an equivalent volume of normal saline. In the afternoon, each group was administered purified water or the sample solution by gavage. The entire process lasted for 56 days. On the final day, the open field test was conducted on the mice. The D-galactose-induced oxidative damage model is accompanied by central nervous system dysfunction, characterized by anxiety-like behaviors and reduced exploratory desire (Parameshwaran, Irwin, Steliou, & Pinkert, 2010). The open field test can indirectly reflect neurobehavioral changes caused by

The open field test can indirectly reflect neurobehavioral changes caused by oxidative stress by evaluating the spontaneous exploratory behavior and tension of mice in an unfamiliar environment. In an open-top square box, each mouse was gently placed in the center. A camera positioned directly above captured the movement trajectory, which was then analyzed using the animal behavior software ToxTrac (version v2.61) (Rodriguez et al., 2017). At the end of the experiment, the mice were euthanized under anesthesia, and their livers were collected. The organ index was calculated based on the mouse's body weight and liver weight. The livers were homogenized in PBS at a 1:9 volume ratio under low temperature and high speed. The expression level of MDA and the activities of various antioxidant enzymes (T-SOD, CAT, and GSH-Px) were measured according to the instructions of their respective detection kits. In addition, liver samples were fixed with 4 % paraformaldehyde, then dehydrated in alcohol, and embedded in paraffin. Tissue sections were stained with hematoxylin-eosin, and images were captured using an ECLIPSE Ts2-FL optical microscope (Nikon, Japan) to evaluate histopathological changes. 2.9 Statistical analysis Statistical analyses were conducted with SPSS 20.0. Graphical illustrations were generated using Origin 2025. 3 Results and discussion 3.1 Metabolomics analysis Metabolomics analysis included a total of 24 PC samples, covering four age groups (PC1, PC3, PC5, and PC8), with six biological replicates per group, and multivariate statistical analysis was performed. To obtain a more comprehensive understanding of the chemical composition of PCs with different aging years, a UPLC-QTOF-MS/MS method was established. The raw ion peak data acquired from the instrument were subjected to peak identification and alignment, thereby yielding the raw abundance information of metabolic ions in the samples. The total ion chromatograms of PCs in both positive and negative ion modes are shown in Fig. 1A–B. In addition, to ensure reliable and high-quality metabolomic data, QC samples were employed during detection to evaluate the intra-group reproducibility and inter-group variation of metabolite profiling across different PC groups. A total of 24 PC samples representing four aging years (analyzed in both positive and negative ion modes) were subjected to multivariate statistical analysis using the partial least squares-discriminant analysis (PLS-DA) method implemented in the R package stats. As shown in Fig. 1C, the six replicates from the same aging year were clustered into a unified region, while samples from different years were clearly separated, indicating that chemical compositions were relatively similar and stable within the same aging year but exhibited substantial differences across different aging years.

chunk_text: separated, indicating that chemical compositions were relatively similar and stable within the same aging year but exhibited substantial differences across different aging years. Furthermore, QC samples were densely clustered in the PLS-DA score plot, demonstrating minimal intra-group variation, which confirms the high stability of the non-targeted metabolomic approach and the reliability of the acquired data. Using Agilent MassHunter Workstation for data analysis, we identified a total of 1455 metabolites in all PCs under both positive and negative ion modes. Within Class A, the major categories included lipids and lipid-like molecules (31.61 %), phenylpropanoids and polyketides (13.47 %), organoheterocyclic compounds (12.57 %), not available (12.43 %), and benzenoids (10.99 %), as shown in Fig. 1D. Evidently, in terms of metabolite numbers across all samples, lipids and lipid-like molecules constituted the largest category, followed by phenylpropanoids and polyketides as another abundant class. However, when considering the relative abundance of metabolites across different aging years of PCs, the proportion of phenylpropanoids and polyketides consistently exceeded 50 %, far surpassing all other superclasses. By contrast, flavonoids are widely recognized as potent natural antioxidants owing to the presence of multiple phenolic hydroxyl groups in their molecular structures. Their antioxidant efficacy is mediated through diverse mechanisms, including direct free radical scavenging, metal ion chelation, and upregulation of endogenous antioxidant enzyme activities (Hassanpour & Doroudi, 2023). Nevertheless, the possibility of synergistic antioxidant effects among lipids and lipid-like molecules, phenylpropanoids and polyketides, and other metabolites cannot be excluded. For instance, hydrophobic constituents in volatile oils may enhance cell membrane permeability and thereby facilitate the absorption and utilization of phenylpropanoids and polyketides (Angane, Swift, Huang, Butts, & Quek, 2022). Pathway enrichment analysis was subsequently performed to elucidate the functional significance of these metabolites. As illustrated in Fig. 1F, G, and H, these correspond to the early aging stage (PC3 vs. PC1), the intermediate stage (PC5 vs. PC3), and the late stage (PC8 vs. PC5), respectively. Across all stages, multiple pathways were consistently enriched, including gap junctions, regulation of actin cytoskeleton, autophagy-other, autophagy-yeast, phospholipase D signaling, cAMP signaling, ABC transporters, aminoacyl-tRNA biosynthesis, biosynthesis of secondary metabolites, glycerophospholipid metabolism, and more. These findings highlight fundamental changes in cell communication, lipid metabolism, and the accumulation of secondary metabolites. The disparity in antioxidant capacity among different flavonoid extracts can be explained by differences in the composition or concentration of individual flavonoid monomers. While PC5 exhibited the highest total content of the quantified flavonoids (Table 1), its superior antioxidant activity is likely attributable to more than just quantity. Integrating the metabolomics results (Fig. 2), the five-year aging point appears to represent an “optimal window period”. At this stage, the transformation of glycosides has led to a significant accumulation of potent antioxidant agents such as aglycones and polymethoxyflavones (e.g., nobiletin, tangeretin), which are known for their high radical scavenging efficiency. This specific profile, representing an optimal combination and ratio of different flavonoid subclasses, likely results in a synergistic antioxidant effect that surpasses that of other aging periods. Pearson correlation coefficients were used to assess the relationship between antioxidant activity and flavonoid content. Previous studies have also demonstrated a significant correlation between flavonoids and the antioxidant activity of plant extracts (Muflihah, Gollavelli, & Ling, 2021; Xiong et al., 2022). In accordance with Fig. 5D, the contents of the flavonoid monomers (hesperidin, nobiletin, tangeretin, and 5-demethylnobiletin) were significantly correlated with the antioxidant indicators (DPPH, ABTS, and FRAP), with positive correlation coefficients all exceeding 0.6, which sugg

Among these, hesperidin exhibited the largest number of potential targets, a total of 206, whereas nobiletin had the fewest, with only 94. The predicted targets of tangeretin and 5-demethylnobiletin were 167 and 129, respectively. In addition, according to the criterion of a relevance score greater than 1 in the GeneCards database, 1314 targets related to oxidative damage-associated diseases were successfully retrieved. As shown in Fig. 6A, a comparison of flavonoid-related targets with oxidative damage-related targets revealed 195 overlapping targets. To further explore the potential protein–protein interactions among these 195 targets, a PPI network was constructed, from which 28 core targets were subsequently identified (Fig. 6B). These core targets are considered to represent the key proteins through which flavonoids may exert their antioxidant activity. As a preliminary exploration of the potential binding sites of flavonoid compounds, this study identifies PPARγ, COX-2, and ALB as core targets for hesperidin, nobiletin, tangeretin, and 5-demethylnobiletin, thereby offering valuable insights into the potential therapeutic targeting of flavonoids. The biological relevance of these targets in oxidative stress is well-documented. PPARγ is a nuclear receptor that plays a crucial role in regulating inflammation and metabolism, and its activation has been shown to suppress oxidative stress by upregulating antioxidant enzymes. COX-2 is a key pro-inflammatory enzyme whose expression is elevated during oxidative stress, and its inhibition is a known strategy to mitigate oxidative damage. ALB, the most abundant plasma protein, acts as a major sacrificial antioxidant by scavenging free radicals and binding metal ions that catalyze oxidation (Lee & Alexander, 2017; Renna, Diez, Lembo, & Miatello, 2013). The strong binding affinity of these flavonoids to these key targets provides a plausible mechanistic framework for their antioxidant effects. 3.5 In vivo antioxidant activity analysis The PC5 sample with the best in vitro activity was selected for animal experiments to further test its in vivo activity using a D-gal-induced oxidative damage model. chunk_text: The PC5 sample with the best in vitro activity was selected for animal experiments to further test its in vivo activity using a D-gal-induced oxidative damage model. The trajectories of mice in each group in the open field test are shown in Fig. 7B. It can be seen that the mice in the model group exhibited more wall-following behavior and less entry into the central area. This behavioral pattern is considered to be indicative of increased anxiety and decreased exploratory desire in animals, both of which are typical behavioral changes associated with oxidative damage and, in severe cases, senescence (Parameshwaran et al., 2010). After oral administration of PC5 extract and Vc, the mice became more active and entered the central area significantly more often. Furthermore, D-gal is mainly metabolized in the liver, and excessive D-gal can increase the metabolic burden on the liver, leading to structural and histological damage to the liver in mice(Azman & Zakaria, 2019). The liver index of each group is shown in Fig. 7C. Compared with the normal control group, the decreased index in the model group reflects a decline in the body's metabolic capacity and damage to the liver metabolic tissues. In contrast, compared with the model group, the indices of the low, medium, and high dose groups of PC5 and the positive control group were increased. Fig. 7D–E show the effects of PC5 on the expression level of MDA and the expression activities of various antioxidant enzymes in the liver. Compared with normal mice, the MDA content in D-gal-induced mice was significantly increased, and the antioxidant enzyme activities were significantly decreased. Compared with the D-gal-induced damage group, the MDA content was significantly reduced and the antioxidant enzyme activities were significantly increased after intervention with different concentrations of PC5, and a dose-effect relationship was observed within the tested concentration range. Among them, MDA is one of the final products of the lipid peroxidation reaction, and its content is a recognized indicator for measuring the degree of lipid peroxidation. When oxidative damage occurs in the body, the lipid peroxidation of biological membranes will be aggravated, leading to an increase in MDA content, which indirectly reflects the degree of oxidative damage to the body's tissues (Ayala, Muñoz, & Argüelles, 2014). T-SOD, CAT, and GSH-Px are important antioxidant enzymes in the body and constitute a key defense system against oxidative stress. They work synergistically to effectively inhibit the process of lipid peroxidation and are crucial for maintaining the body's redox balance and enhancing overall antioxidant capacity (Jomova et al., 2024). Therefore, these results all suggest that PC5 has a protective effect on oxidative stress in D-gal-induced mice. Although the direct expression levels of core targets such as PPARγ and COX-2 were not quantified in this study, the observed changes in downstream biomarkers provide functional va

chunk_text: ical conditions, truly demonstrating their regulatory role. Taken together, PC5 possesses strong antioxidant potential from the chemical to the biological level. PC5 is characterized by its high levels of hesperidin, nobiletin, tangeretin, and 5-demethylnobiletin. The bioavailability of these compounds is essential for their in vivo efficacy. Hesperidin, as a flavonoid glycoside, can be hydrolyzed by gut microbiota into its more readily absorbable aglycone, hesperetin (Sivaslioglu & Goktas, 2024). The other polymethoxyflavones, owing to their relatively strong lipophilicity, have been shown to possess favorable oral bioavailability and the capacity to permeate various biological membranes, including the blood–brain barrier (An, Liu, Kim, Madden, & Wang, 2025). Therefore, the significant hepatoprotective effects observed in the D-gal–induced mouse model treated with PC5 extract are likely attributable, at least in part, to these characteristic flavonoids with high bioavailability, which also represent the primary contributors to its potent in vitro antioxidant activity. 4 Conclusion This study integrated metabolomics and chemical indicators to systematically investigate the differences in metabolite composition, flavonoid accumulation, and antioxidant activity of PCs across different aging periods. The results of untargeted metabolomics revealed that flavonoids occupy a central role in the chemical composition of PCs and exhibit distinct variation patterns with prolonged aging. chunk_text: composition of PCs and exhibit distinct variation patterns with prolonged aging. The optimized ultrasound-assisted extraction process significantly enhanced the extraction efficiency of flavonoids, while in vitro antioxidant assays confirmed that PC5 exhibited the strongest radical scavenging capacity. Correlation analysis and molecular docking indicated that hesperidin, nobiletin, tangeretin, and 5-demethylnobiletin are likely the key flavonoid monomers driving the antioxidant effects, primarily through their interactions with proteins such as PPARγ, COX-2, and ALB. In a D-gal-induced oxidative damage mouse model, it was further verified that PC5 extract can significantly improve the hepatic oxidative stress state in mice. Our findings suggest that the 5-year aging stage represents a critical period for flavonoid accumulation and antioxidant potential. Given that PC5 demonstrated superior in vitro activity and exerted in vivo protective effects comparable to the positive control Vc, it can be considered a high-value candidate for the development of functional foods and pharmaceutical ingredients. Overall, this work not only offers valuable insights for the quality evaluation and scientific utilization of PCs at different aging stages but also establishes a theoretical foundation for developing high value-added products in the functional food and pharmaceutical industries. title: Dried tangerine peel polysaccharide accelerates wound healing by recruiting anti-inflammatory macrophages
chunk_text: Macrophage polarization is a key process involved in wound healing. The continuous release of proinflammatory cytokines by macrophages inhibits the healing process of chronic wounds, such as diabetic wounds. To promote wound healing, it is important to change the phenotype of resident macrophages to prevent inflammation. We previously reported that dried tangerine peel polysaccharide (DTPP) binds to and inhibits the TLR4/MD-2 complex, which is crucial for the inflammatory activation of macrophages, suggesting the potential of DTPP in wound healing applications. Both zebrafish and mouse models were used to evaluate the therapeutic efficacy of DTPP. Moreover, we found that DTPP recruited macrophages to the wound area and promoted their M2 repolarization. Using hyperglycaemic zebrafish and db/db mouse models, we discovered that DTPP accelerated wound healing in vivo in metabolic disorders. Our results suggest that DTPP promotes the recruitment of macrophages, shifts macrophages towards the anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype, and ultimately accelerates the wound healing process.

Editor: Hajo Haase Macrophage polarization is a key process involved in wound healing. The continuous release of proinflammatory cytokines by macrophages inhibits the healing process of chronic wounds, such as diabetic wounds. To promote wound healing, it is important to change the phenotype of resident macrophages to prevent inflammation. We previously reported that dried tangerine peel polysaccharide (DTPP) binds to and inhibits the TLR4/MD-2 complex, which is crucial for the inflammatory activation of macrophages, suggesting the potential of DTPP in wound healing applications. Both zebrafish and mouse models were used to evaluate the therapeutic efficacy of DTPP. Moreover, we found that DTPP recruited macrophages to the wound area and promoted their M2 repolarization. Using hyperglycaemic zebrafish and db/db mouse models, we discovered that DTPP accelerated wound healing in vivo in metabolic disorders. Our results suggest that DTPP promotes the recruitment o

chunk_text: ycaemic zebrafish and db/db mouse models, we discovered that DTPP accelerated wound healing in vivo in metabolic disorders. Our results suggest that DTPP promotes the recruitment of macrophages, shifts macrophages towards the anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype, and ultimately accelerates the wound healing process. Keywords Wound healing Macrophage polarization Dried tangerine peel polysaccharide (DTPP) Inflammation Data availability Data will be made available on request. 1 Introduction Wound healing is a complex process involving various cells and tissues [1]. Macrophages, which are immune cells known for their plasticity and ability to adopt different phenotypes, are important in this process [2,3]. The differentiation of macrophages, especially during classical activation of the proinflammatory state (M1) or alternative activation of the anti-inflammatory state (M2), is important in regulating the progress of wound healing [4–6]. M1 macrophages express tumour necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) and interleukins and produce nitric oxide (NO) and reactive oxygen species (ROS), which suppress microbiota growth but damage tissue [7,8]. M2 macrophages exert anti-inflammatory effects by upregulating vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), haem oxygenase 1 (HMOX-1), and CD206, which facilitate wound healing [9]. In chronic wounds, such as those in patients with diabetes, the inflammatory response is often dysregulated, leading to increased secretion of proinflammatory cytokines by macrophages [6,10]. A persistent anti-inflammatory environment can interfere with normal healing processes, r

title: Dried tangerine peel polysaccharide accelerates wound healing by recruiting anti-inflammatory macrophages
chunk_text: ulated, leading to increased secretion of proinflammatory cytokines by macrophages [6,10]. A persistent anti-inflammatory environment can interfere with normal healing processes, resulting in delayed wound closure and an increased risk of infection [11,12]. Decreased numbers of M2 macrophages and increased M1:M2 macrophage ratios in wounds reduce the levels of anti-inflammatory cytokines, inhibiting the wound healing process [13]. Local tissue infiltration of wounds and the conversion of resident macrophages to the M2 phenotype can be directed to facilitate the normal healing process of wounds. Therefore, changing the phenotype of macrophages residing in the wound microenvironment becomes important under proinflammatory conditions to improve their efficiency [14,15]. It has been widely reported that M2 polarization of macrophages using hydrogels, scaffolds, and micro/nanoparticles facilitates diabetic wound healing [16–19]; however, most of these materials are either complicated or expensive. Polysaccharides have demonstrated clinical potential for chronic wounds due to their beneficial properties, including low cost, ease of manufacture, biodegradability, and ability to form hydrogels [20]. Polysaccharides extracted from several traditional Chinese herbs have been demonstrated to possess anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and immunological activities [21]. We focused on investigating the therapeutic potential of tangerine peel polysaccharide (DTPP), which is derived from dried tangerine peel and is a traditional Chinese medicine. Our previous study revealed that DTPP has anti

title: Dried tangerine peel polysaccharide accelerates wound healing by recruiting anti-inflammatory macrophages
chunk_text: potential of tangerine peel polysaccharide (DTPP), which is derived from dried tangerine peel and is a traditional Chinese medicine. Our previous study revealed that DTPP has anti-inflammatory effects on macrophages by directly binding to Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4)/myeloid differentiation factor 2 (MD-2). The binding of DTPP to the TLR4/MD2 complex activates TLR4 signalling in the microenvironment [22]. However, the anti-inflammatory activity of DTPP during chronic wound healing has yet to be clarified. Given that diabetic ulcers are often in a proinflammatory state, DTPP may be a promising candidate for accelerating the healing of diabetic ulcers due to its anti-inflammatory properties. To investigate whether DTPP accelerates wound healing, both zebrafish and mouse models were used in the present study. Our results showed that DTPP treatment improved wound healing in zebrafish and mice by recruiting macrophages and inducing repolarization. In addition, the efficacy of DTPP for diabetic wound healing was evaluated in hyperglycaemic zebrafish and db/db mouse models. Our results provide valuable insight into the mechanism responsible for the beneficial effects of DTPP on wound healing and emphasize the importance of targeting macrophage polarization to improve outcomes in chronic wound healing. 2 Materials and methods 2.1 Polysaccharide extraction and purification Dried tangerine peel was purchased from Xinbaotang (Guangdong, China). Dried tangerine peel (DTP) powder was obtained by drying and cutting the peel into small pieces, followed by grinding into powder using a high-speed mechanical blender. Extraction was performed at room temperature. An appropriate amount of DTP powder was placed in a round-bottom flask, petroleum ether was added, and the mixture was refluxed at 40 °C for 2 h. The residue was washed three times with 95 % ethanol and dried in an oven to obtain DTP residue. The concentration of the extract yielded a crude polysaccharide solution. Chloroform-n-butanol was added to form a white gelatinous material, which was removed after three repetitions. Subsequently, 95 % ethanol was added at three times the liquid volume, and the mixture was left to stand for 24 h. After centrifugation for 20 min, the purified DTPP was obtained through multiple washes with absolute ethanol. The polysaccharide was stored in a vacuum desiccator to prevent moisture from being present in the air. 2.2 Animals and animal maintenance Six- to eight-week-old BALB/c mice (male, weight = 20–25 g) and db/db (male, weight = 30–35 g) mice were purchased from Weitong Lihua (Guangzhou, China), and the experiments were performed under SPF grade standards. The animal experiments were conducted following the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and were approved by the Animal Experiment Ethics Committee of Jinan University, Guangzhou, China. The zebrafish were maintained in a water circulation system, the water temperature was maintained at 28 °C, the conductivity was adjusted to 500–550, and the pH of the culture water was adjusted to 7.5–8.0. All the experiments conducted in this study were approved by the Research Ethics Committee of Jinan University (20230310–0021). 2.3 Establishment of the zebrafish tail fin regeneration model The zebrafish tail fin regeneration model was generated as we previously described. Briefly, the fish were divided into four groups after tail amputation. A vertical incision was made in the middle of the tail along the longitudinal axis of the fish, and the tail was bisected and cut in a direction parallel to the longitudinal axis of the fish, forming an approximately right-angled incision. Solutions of DTPP at concentrations of 2.5, 10, and 40 μg/ml were prepared, and the treated zebrafish were placed in different concentrations of DDTP culture medium. Each incision was photographed and recorded under a camera. The growth and healing of the fish tails were observed and recorded every 2 days during the experimental period. 2.4 Establishment of a mouse wound healing model The mouse skin was cleaned with sterile water and then cleansed with 70 % alcohol swabs. Using a sterile punch, a circular full-thickness skin wound with a diameter of 6 mm was created on the back of each mouse. Specifically, DTPP was dissolved in the culture water of zebrafish with amputated tail fins, and the length of the regenerated tail fin was measured under a stereoscopic microscope. The recovery rate of the tail fin was calculated as shown in Fig. 1 A and 1B. As shown in Fig. 1C-D, DTPP significantly enhanced the regeneration of excised tail fins in zebrafish at concentrations of 10 and 40 μg/mL after 8 days of treatment. The increase in the regeneration rate became significant on the tenth day following exposure to 2.5 μg/mL DTPP. These findings suggest that DTPP effectively accelerates wound healing in zebrafish in a time- and dose-dependent

These findings suggest that DTPP effectively accelerates wound healing in zebrafish in a time- and dose-dependent manner. 3.2 DTPP promotes wound healing in mice To confirm the ability of DTPP to promote wound healing in mammals, a skin wound model was established in mice as previously described [17]. As depicted in Fig. 2 A and 2B, DTPP significantly enhanced wound healing in mice at concentrations of 10 and 40 μg/mL after 3 days of treatment. By the fifth day after DTPP exposure, further improvement in wound healing was observed, with a significant difference noted in the 2.5 μg/mL group. Mice treated with 40 μg/mL DTPP almost fully recovered from the wounds, whereas those in the control group only exhibited partial recovery. These results indicate that the time- and dose-dependent acceleration of wound healing is conserved in mice. To delve deeper into the mechanisms of wound healing in mice, skin samples were subjected to paraffin sectioning. Haematoxylin and eosin (HE) staining of the sections revealed that DTPP facilitated epidermal growth within the wound area in mice at concentrations ranging from 2.5–40 μg/mL. In the control mice, the skin wounds had not yet closed, whereas the skin of the DTPP-treated mice presented a coalescent histology. In the low-dose treatment group, the epithelial tissues were still not connected with the stromal tissue. The epidermis recovered well after treatment with 10 and 40 μg/mL DTTP. Additionally, the newly formed epidermis in the DTPP-treated groups increased in thick

Additionally, the newly formed epidermis in the DTPP-treated groups increased in thickness with increasing dose. Furthermore, DTPP treatment increased the intensity of sebaceous glands and other accessory organs around the wound areas in mice (Fig. 2C). These findings suggest that DTPP effectively promotes wound healing in vivo. 3.3 DTPP enhances macrophage infiltration within the wound area in zebrafish Various cell types, including epidermal cells, fibroblasts, leukocytes, and vascular endothelial cells, participate in the wound healing process [5,20–22]. Among these factors, macrophages play crucial roles in wound healing. Thus, a transgenic zebrafish line, tg(mpeg: EGFP), was utilized to monitor macrophage migration in live individuals. The results indicated that DTPP treatment increased macrophage aggregation within the wound area, as evidenced by the accumulation of green fluorescence (Fig. 3 A-B). These findings suggest that DTPP facilitates wound healing via macrophages. 3.4 DTPP induces alternative activation of mouse macrophages in vitro and in vivo To investigate the effects of DTPP on the polarization of macrophages, mouse bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs) were used. As shown in Fig. 4 A, DTPP did not induce classical activation (M1 polarization) of BMDMs but inhibited the activation induced by lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and interferon γ (IFNγ), as indicated by reduced nitric oxide (NO) production. Therefore, alternative activation of BMDMs was further evaluated. Fi

Fig. 4B and 4C demonstrate that DTPP induced alternative activation (M2 polarization) of BMDMs, as indicated by increased CD206 expression and decreased iNOS expression. These results suggest that DTPP induces M2 polarization of macrophages in vitro. To confirm the role of DTPP in the polarization of macrophages in vivo, immunohistochemistry (IHC) was performed to assess alternative activation within the skin wound area. As shown in Fig. 4C, the number of CD206-positive macrophages increased, whereas the number of F4/80-positive macrophages decreased with DTPP treatment, indicating infiltration of alternatively activated macrophages induced by DTPP in vivo in mice. The activation of TLR4 signalling is crucial for M1 macrophages, whereas the activity of TLR4 is suppressed in M2 macrophages. To validate the importance of alternatively activated macrophages during wound healing, both TLR4 agonists and antagonists were used. The results demonstrated that DTPP significantly promoted tail fin recovery without the use of TLR4 agonists or antagonists, whereas the activation of TLR4 by LPS suppressed the recovery efficiency and abolished the promoting effect of DTPP. Interestingly, blockade of TLR4 by IAXO-102 did not further improve the healing efficiency but did affect DTPP, suggesting that DTPP stimulates tail fin regeneration by driving the M2 polarization of macrophages in a TLR4-dependent manner. Different doses of DTPP were then dissolved in the water, and the tail fin-truncated hyperglycaemic zebrafish were then placed in the water with DTPP. As shown in Fig. 6 , the wounds in db/db mice remained almost unchanged within 9 days after surgery, whereas DTPP significantly promoted the healing of wounds in db/db mice without affecting their motility, suggesting the potential of DTPP for wound healing in diabetic mice.Fig. 7. . 4 Discussion The current study investigated the impact of DTPP on wound healing, particularly focusing on the alternative activation of macrophages. Our results demonstrated the beneficial effects of DTPP on tissue regeneration, including enhanced wound closure, regenerative repair of the epithelium, proliferation of sebaceous glands and other skin appendages, and infiltration of M2-type macrophages at the wound site. These findings collectively indicate an increase in the wound-healing process. Throughout the different stages of wound healing, distinct phenotypic alterations in macrophages accompany the process [23,24]. During the inflammatory phase, tissue-resident macrophages release proinflammatory mediators such as chemokines, cytokines (including interferon-γ (IFN-γ)), and growth factors to attract immune cells such as neutrophils for the clearance of foreign and damaged cells [25–28]. Following the resolution of cellular debris, neutrophils can trigger a shift towards anti-inflammatory macrop
