chunk_text: as neutrophils for the clearance of foreign and damaged cells [25–28]. Following the resolution of cellular debris, neutrophils can trigger a shift towards anti-inflammatory macrophage polarization [29–31]. Studies have shown that M1 polarization, which results in the failure of the M1 to M2 transition of macrophages, impedes diabetic wound healing [32–35]. In our study, DTPP facilitated wound healing via M2 macrophage recruitment, which is also consistent with previous studies. Previous research has highlighted the ability of polysaccharides from J. scopolorum to induce iNOS protein expression and NO production, thereby modulating macrophage function [36]. Interestingly, our findings revealed a significant reduction in NO production in the experimental group treated with high concentrations of DTPP, suggesting an inhibitory effect on the polarization of M1-type macrophages induced by LPS and IFN-γ. Conversely, the substantial infiltration of M2-type macrophages in the early stages of wound healing indicated that DTPP facilitated the transition from the inflammatory phase to the proliferative phase, promoting overall wound healing. DTPP may competitively bind to sites where LPS or IFN-γ typically interact with macrophage receptors, impeding the activation of M1-type macrophages and fostering alternative activation with the involvement of TLRs [37]. Notably, polysaccharides extracted from specific citrus peels can upregulate iNOS expression and NO production. The polysaccharides utilized in our study were derived from five-year-old tangerine peel and exhibited diverse therapeutic effects, implying that different citrus peel varieties may confer distinct efficacies, thereby holding promise for future applications in various contexts. 5 Conclusion In this study, we demonstrated that DTPP enhances both healthy and diabetic wound healing in zebrafish and mice. Our results revealed that DTPP significantly promoted the regeneration of excised tail fins in zebrafish and accelerated wound healing in mice in a time- and dose-dependent manner. Histological analysis in mice revealed that DTPP facilitates epidermal growth, leading to a thicker newly formed epidermis and increased intensity of sebaceous glands and accessory organs around the wound area. Furthermore, our findings suggest that DTPP promotes wound healing by increasing macrophage infiltration and inducing alternative activation of macrophages, particularly M2 polarization. Overall, DTPP has promising potential as a wound-healing accelerator for both nonmammalian vertebrates and mammals. 6 Consent for publication All the authors approved the publication of this manuscript. 7 Ethics approval and consent to participate All experiments conducted in this study were approved by the Research Ethics Committee of Jinan University. title: A simple method to discriminate Guangchenpi and Chenpi by high-performance thin-layer chromatography and high-performance liquid chromatography based on analysis of dimethyl anthranilate
chunk_text: Citri Reticulatae Pericarpium (CRP), the dried pericarp of Citrus reticulata Blanco, can be divided into “Guangchenpi” (GCP, the dried pericarps derived from Citrus reticulata ‘Chachi’) and “Chenpi” (CP, the dried pericarps derived from other cultivars of Citrus reticulata Blanco). To discriminate between GCP and CP, a simple and reliable high-performance thin-layer chromatography (HPTLC) method was firstly developed to analyze the volatile compound dimethyl anthranilate, and a high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) method was established to simultaneously quantify dimethyl anthranilate and three predominant flavonoids (hesperidin, nobiletin and tangeretin) in CRP samples. Both the HPTLC analysis and HPLC-orthogonal partial least squares discrimination analysis (OPLS-DA) indicated that GCP can be effectively distinguished from CP based on analysis of dimethyl anthranilate. Our results indicated that dimethyl anthranilate can be used as a marker compound for discrimination of GCP and CP. This work provided a convenient approach which might be applied for quality evaluation of CRP.

Citri Reticulatae Pericarpium (CRP), the dried pericarp of Citrus reticulata Blanco, can be divided into “Guangchenpi” (GCP, the dried pericarps derived from Citrus reticulata ‘Chachi’) and “Chenpi” (CP, the dried pericarps derived from other cultivars of Citrus reticulata Blanco). To discriminate between GCP and CP, a simple and reliable high-performance thin-layer chromatography (HPTLC) method was firstly developed to analyze the volatile compound dimethyl anthranilate, and a high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) method was established to simultaneously quantify dimethyl anthranilate and three predominant flavonoids (hesperidin, nobiletin and tangeretin) in CRP samples. Both the HPTLC analysis and HPLC-orthogonal partial least squares discrimination analysis (OPLS-DA) indicated that GCP can be effectively distinguished from CP based on analysis of dimethyl anthranilate. Our results indicated that dimethyl anthranilate can be used as a marker compound for discrimination of GCP and CP. This work provided a convenient approach which might be applied for quality evaluation of CRP. Generally, the pericarps from Citrus reticulata ‘Chachi’ (“Guangchenpi” in Chinese, GCP), particularly planted and harvested in Xinhui County (Guangdong province, China), is considered to have superior quality compared with CRP derived from other cultivars (collectively called “Chenpi” in Chinese, CP) [3,4]. In the current Chinese Pharmacopoeia (2015 edition), the only marker compound for quality control of CRP was hesperidin. However, GCP and CP share close behavior in morphology and the content of hesperidin, GCP could not be discriminated from CP based on the analysis of hesperidin [5]. Phytochemical studies demonstrated that various components are present in CRP, such as flavonoids, alkaloids and volatile oils, among which flavonoids and volatile oils are considered as the effective substances of CRP [6–9]. The volatile compounds in CRP exhibited extensive bioactivity, such as anticancer and antimicrobial activity [8]. Despite many reports describing the discrimination of GCP and CP by qualitative and quantitative analysis of flavonoids contained, we accidentally found that the profile and con

Despite many reports describing the discrimination of GCP and CP by qualitative and quantitative analysis of flavonoids contained, we accidentally found that the profile and content of flavonoids in certain CP samples (e.g., CP from Sichuan province) were almost the same as that of GCP. Thus, it was impossible to distinguish GCP and CP by analysis of flavonoids. Recently, Duan et al. [10] established a GC–MS metabolomics method to qualitatively compare the volatile constituents in GCP and CP, and fifteen metabolites including dimethyl anthranilate were finally identified as chemical markers. Dimethyl anthranilate, an aromatic compound originating from fruits and wines, might be involved in the difference of aroma in dried tangerine peel [11,12]. To the best of our knowledge, no previous study has been reported to distinguish GCP and CP by simultaneous analysis of volatile compounds and flavonoids. To establish a simple method to discriminate GCP and CP, we developed a high-performance thin-layer chromatography (HPTLC) method for identification of dimethyl anthranilate in CRP samples for the first time. Also, a high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) method was established to simultaneously analyze dimethyl anthranilate and three predominant flavonoids (hesperidin, nobiletin and tangeretin). Orthogonal partial least-squares discriminate analysis (OPLS-DA) was further utilized to discriminate between GCP and CP samples collected from different origins. This study might provide a feasible and simple method for discrimination of CRP. 2 Materials and methods 2.1 Plant m

(Chengdu, China). Dimethyl anthranilate (C4) was purchased from Aladdin Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China). The structures of 4 reference compounds are shown in Fig. 1A. The purity of all these four compounds was higher than 98%. The extraction solvent methanol was purchased from Nanjing Chemical Reagent Factory, China. HPLC-grade acetonitrile and formic acid were obtained from Merck (Darmstadt, Germany). Deionized water was prepared through a Milli-Q system (Millipore, Bedford, MA, USA). Each sample powder (0.2 g) was accurately weighed and extracted by 10 mL methanol using an ultrasonic bath for 60 min. After cooling, methanol was added to the extracted solution to reach the original weight. The CRP extracts were centrifuged at 16,200g at 4 °C for 10 min subsequently. Once the supernatants were prepared, they were used individually. For HPTLC analysis, a 700 μL sample of the supernatant was evaporated to dryness under reduced pressure at 45 °C using EZ2 Plus Solvent Evaporation Station. The residue was dissolved by addition of 100 μL methanol as the sample solution. For HPLC analysis, an aliquot of 2 μL of the supernatant was injected. For HPTLC analysis, dimethyl anthranilate was accurately weighed and then dissolved in methanol. The stock solution was then diluted to 0.25 mg/mL as working standard solution. For HPLC analysis, the four reference standards were weighed accurately and then diluted in methanol. The standard working solution was mixed immediately before analysis by diluting the stock solutions to the required concentrations. The solutions were stored at 4 °C to prevent sample degradation. 2.4 HPTLC analysis For the HPTLC analysis (General Rules 0502 of 2015 Chinese Pharmacopoeia), 3 μL of different sample solutions and 1 μL of dimethyl anthranilate working standard solution were transferred to a GF254 silica gel pl

The different developing solvent compositions were optimized for separation of the CRP samples. The CRP samples and standard solution were applied as bands 10 mm long at 5-mm distances on HPTLC plates using the automated sampler. Plates were then developed in a pre-saturated twin-through chamber, and the developing distance was 6 cm. After development, the plates were taken from the chamber, and allowed to air-dry. Visualization of HPTLC plates was performed under UV at 365 nm. 2.5 HPLC methods The HPLC-DAD analysis was performed on an Agilent 1290 high performance liquid chromatography (Agilent Technologies, Palo Alto CA, USA). Separation of CRP extracts was performed on an Agilent ZORBAX Extend-C18 column (4.6 mm × 50 mm, 1.8 μm, Agilent Technologies, MD, USA). The mobile phase consisted of 0.1% formic-water (A) and acetonitrile (B), with a gradient program as follows: 0–8 min, 15–19% B; 8–10 min, 19–19% B; 10–12 min, 19–40% B; 12–19 min, 40–40% B; 19–23 min, 40–47% B. The sample injection was 2 μL and the flow rate was set at 0.7 mL/min. Different mobile phase systems including chloroform, petroleum ether and petroleum ether/ethyl acetate (10:1, v/v) were tested, and petroleum ether/ethyl acetate (10:1, v/v) gave good separation of the compound of interest. The retention factor (Rf) and color of the bands were compared between the standard and samples from different regions to confirm the presence of the marker in samples [13,14]. The convenient HPTLC method established showed good repeatability and durability. The band of dimethyl anthranilate on the HPTLC plate was clearly visible under 365 nm UV light, and dimethyl anthranilate gave characteristic blue colored band at Rf of 0.42. The validated method was successfully applied to analyze GCP and CP samples. As shown in Fig. 2 , dimethyl anthranilate was present in all GCP samples, while it was not detected in CP samples, indicating that the characteristic band of dimethyl anthranilate was exclusive due to GCP. 3.2 Quantification of dimethyl anthranilate and three predominant flavonoids of CRP from different origins by HPLC-DAD 3.2.1 Optimization of extraction conditions Dimethyl anthranilate and three predominant flavonoids (hesperidin, nobiletin and tangeretin) were further quantified by HPLC method. According to our previous study [15], ultrasonic extraction by methanol was the most efficient approach for the flavonoids in CRP samples. To get a better extraction efficiency of dimethyl anthranilate, extraction time (30, 60, and 90 min) and extraction volume (1:50, 1:125, 1:250) were optimized using univariate test. The results showed that extraction with 10 mL of methanol for 1 h was the most efficient condition for extraction of dimethyl anthranilate and flavonoids. 3.2.2 Method validation The linear range, regression equation, correlation coefficient of each analyte, and LOD and LOQ values are summarized in Table 2 . Each calibration curve was plotted with a series of concentrations of reference solutions. All calibration curves were of acceptable linearity with R2 > 0.9993. The LOD and LOQ values were <0.781 μg/mL and 0.254 μg/mL, respectively. title: Citri Reticulatae Pericarpium (Chenpi): Botany, ethnopharmacology, phytochemistry, and pharmacology of a frequently used traditional Chinese medicine
chunk_text: Ethnopharmacological relevance Citri Reticulatae Pericarpium (Rutaceae, CRP), commonly called as Chenpi (陈皮) in Chinese, is most frequently used as a qi-regulating drug in thousands of Chinese medicine prescriptions. CRP is found mainly in major citrus-producing areas such as the Guangdong, Guangxi, Sichuan, Fujian, and Zhejiang Provinces of China. Since thousands of years in China, CRP has been used widely in clinical practice to treat nausea, vomiting, indigestion, anepithymia, diarrhea, cough, expectoration, and so on. Currently, CRP is listed in the Pharmacopoeia of the People's Republic of China. The present paper reviews the botany, ethnopharmacology, phytochemistry, pharmacology, quality control, and toxicology of CRP. Materials and methods Information on CRP was gathered from various sources including the books on traditional Chinese herbal medicine; scientific databases including Elsevier, PubMed, and ScienceDirect; Baidu Scholar; CNKI; and others and from different professional websites. Results Approximately 140 chemical compounds have been isolated and identified from CRP. Among them, volatile oils and flavonoids are generally considered as the main bioactive and characteristic ingredients. CRP possesses wide pharmacological effects such as having a beneficial effect on the cardiovascular, digestive, and respiratory systems, antitumor, antioxidant, and anti-inflammatory properties; and a protective effect on the liver and nerve. Moreover, hesperidin is chosen as an indicator in the quantitative determination of CRP, and the quantity of aflatoxin in CRP must not exceed the standard limit mentioned in the pharmacopoeia. Conclusions In brief, CRP has a warming nature, and hence, it can be used in harmony with a lot of medicines. CRP not only exhibits its effects individually but also aids other medicines exhibit a better effect. CRP can be consumed with tea, food, alcohol, and medicine. Irrespective of the form it is being consumed, CRP not only shows a synergistic effect but also has strengths on its own. Modern pharmacological studies have demonstrated that CRP has marked bioactivities, especially on the diseases of the digestive and respiratory systems. The bioactivities of CRP are useful for its clinical application and provide prospects for the development of drugs as well as food and health products for people. Although CRP is a commonly used drug in the traditional Chinese herbal prescription, there is an urgent need for further research on its synergistic effect with other herbs based on the compatibility theory of TCM, which would further increase our understanding on the compatibility theory of TCM.

Ethnopharmacological relevance Citri Reticulatae Pericarpium (Rutaceae, CRP), commonly called as Chenpi (陈皮) in Chinese, is most frequently used as a qi-regulating drug in thousands of Chinese medicine prescriptions. CRP is found mainly in major citrus-producing areas such as the Guangdong, Guangxi, Sichuan, Fujian, and Zhejiang Provinces of China. Since thousands of years in China, CRP has been used widely in clinical practice to treat nausea, vomiting, indigestion, anepithymia, diarrhea, cough, expectoration, and so on. Currently, CRP is listed in the Pharmacopoeia of the People's Republic of China. The present paper reviews the botany, ethnopharmacology, phytochemistry, pharmacology, quality control, and toxicology of CRP. Materials and methods Information on CRP was gathered from various sources including the books on traditional Chinese herbal medicine; scientific databases including Elsevier, PubMed, and ScienceDirect; Baidu Scholar; CNKI; and others and from different professional websites. Results Approximately 140 chemical compounds have been isolated and identified from CRP. Among them, volatile oils and flavonoids are generally considered as the main bioactive and characteristic ingredients. CRP possesses wide pharmacological effects such as having a beneficial effect on the cardiovas

CRP possesses wide pharmacological effects such as having a beneficial effect on the cardiovascular, digestive, and respiratory systems, antitumor, antioxidant, and anti-inflammatory properties; and a protective effect on the liver and nerve. Moreover, hesperidin is chosen as an indicator in the quantitative determination of CRP, and the quantity of aflatoxin in CRP must not exceed the standard limit mentioned in the pharmacopoeia. Conclusions In brief, CRP has a warming nature, and hence, it can be used in harmony with a lot of medicines. CRP not only exhibits its effects individually but also aids other medicines exhibit a better effect. CRP can be consumed with tea, food, alcohol, and medicine. Irrespective of the form it is being consumed, CRP not only shows a synergistic effect but also has strengths on its own. Modern pharmacological studies have demonstrated that CRP has marked bioactivities, especially on the diseases of the digestive and respiratory systems. The bioactivities of CRP are useful for its clinical application and provide prospects for the development of drugs as well as food and health products for people. Although CRP is a commonly used drug in the traditional Chinese herbal prescription, there is an urgent need for further research on its synergistic effect with other herbs based on the compatibility theory of TCM, which would further increase our understanding on the compatibility theory of TCM. The “Xing qi” (行气) effect of CRP, which ranges from internal to external effects, not only promotes the circulation of qi (energy) throughout the body, thereby soothing our emotions including anger, irritability, and frustration, but also is widely used in a variety of “stagnation” characteristics of qi, such as food stagnation, with pain and distention symptoms. CRP is mainly used for the auxiliary treatment of external contraction, indigestion, abdominal fullness and distention, cough with expectoration of phlegm, weakened state of the body, and other diseases. In addition, CRP strengthens the spleen, relieves inappetence, lubricates the intestine, strengthens the bones, and enriches the kidney. CRP was registered in the first edition of the Chinese Pharmacopoeia (1953 version), and the latest edition (2015 version) contains more than 10% of Chinese patent medicines. Modern pharmacology studies indicate that CRP possesses wide pharmacological actions such as effects on the gastrointestinal and respiratory systems; antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and anticancer activities; and protective effects on the liver and nerves. Because of extensive pharmacological effects and universal folk use, researchers began focusing attention on CRP, gradually studying its chemical components. The main components are volatile oils, flavonoids, and alkaloids. In addition, it also contains a small quantity of microelements, vitamins, pectin, polysaccharide, etc. Among them, volatile oils and flavonoids have been the most studied and possess the best bioactivity. C. reticulata Blanco has been cultivated since more than 3000 years and is mainly distributed in the Guangdong, Guangxi, Sichuan, Fujian, and Zhejiang Provinces of China. The cultivars of C. reticulata Blanco mainly include C. reticulata “Chachi” (茶枝柑), C. reticulata “Dahongpao” (大红袍), C. reticulata “Unshiu” (温州蜜柑), and C. reticulata “Tangerina” (福橘). Among the main CRP cultivars, the pericarp of C. reticulata “Chachi” (茶枝柑) is the best national product. Owing to the main production in the Xinhui or Sihui District of Guangdong Province in China, it is also known as Guang Citri Reticulatae Pericarpium (GCRP) (Xiong and Yan, 2012). In recent years, the phenomenon of fake and shoddy goods has become very common; hence, chemical composition and quality control of CRP of different origin has attracted increased attention of researchers and needs further relevant study. Unlike the common orange, this kind of fruit has characteristics of slightly concave, obvious column marks. Sometimes it has a small navel, and sometimes there is a radiation ditch around the pedicle. Moreover, it has a horizontal diameter of 4.6–5.9 cm × 6.3–7.1 cm, weight of 100–138 g, and thickness of 2.7–3.3 mm; 15–25 seeds; and multiple embryos. CRP is cultivated only to obtain its peels as a TCM, and not as a food, because this orange tastes bitter, while their pericarps are thick and tough. The ripe fruit is picked usually in late autumn and early winter, then its pericarps are shelled, and the pericarps are dried under ventilation or low temperatures. To prepare the CRP into a processed medicine, impurities must be removed, water must be sprayed, shredded, and desiccated. This product appears as irregular strips or as filaments. (Fig. 1B). The Chinese medicine theory believes that the longer the storage time, the better the quality. Hence, its storage period ranges from 1 year, 2 years, and 3 years to more than 10 years (Wang et al., 2015). The reason for this is the change in the amount of flavonoids and volatile oils. CRP, as shown in Fig. 1C, is stored for decades. The inner surface is light yellowish white, and the outer surface is orange-red or reddish-brown (Chen, 2015). 2.2 Ethnopharmacology With an extensive scope for physiological and pharmacological effects, CRP has been traditionally used in China for centuries. It was initially recorded in the Variorum of Shennong's Classic of Materia Medica (Shennong Bencao Jing) written during the period of the Eastern Han Dynasty. In this monograph, CRP was classified as a “top grade” drug because it is mainly used to dispel heat and cure oppression in the chest and it can nourish the stomach by consuming it for a long time; thus, the patient can get rid of halitosis, dispel gas from his body, and excrete feces. CRP is also recorded in many other TCM classics including the Main Points for Materia Medical Usage (Ben cao bei yao) and the Materia Medical of Decoction (Tang ye ben cao). In other words, CRP can be used alone in the treatment of diseases, as well as be combined with other herbal medicines to enhance the therapy results. In accordance with the authoritative textbook of Chinese pharmacy, CRP has a bitter and acrid flavor, a neutral nature, and is attributive to the spleen and liver channels. CRP is described as possessing the power to regulate qi, to strengthen the spleen, to dry dampness, and to resolve phlegm. In clinical practice, CRP is primarily applied for digestive and respiratory diseases such as treatment of indigestion, stomach ache, abdominal distension, and cough by combining with other herbs based on the TCM theory (Chen, 2015). Considering its extensive clinical effects, a large amount of prescriptions containing CRP were inherited from generation to generation. The frequency of CRP use is the highest when combined with other compounds that can regulate qi and activate blood circulation, such as with fructus aurantii (枳壳), fingered citron (佛手), Cyperus rotundus (香附), fructus amomi (砂仁), white peony root (白芍), Salvia miltiorrhiza (丹参), and so on (Wu et al., 2014). In addition, CRP also provides broad development prospects for the medical science of sports, nutrition, geriatrics, beauty, and other fields. Compound compatibility of Chinese medicine is a commonly used clinical treatment approach. However, the mechanisms of compatibility and synergistic effect of CRP in compounds are not clear enough until now. First, compound compatibility is not necessarily a simple superposition of the biological effects of multiple pharmacological substances. Chinese herbal compounds consumed orally primarily require a good absorption capacity in the gastrointestinal tract to play a systemic role and achieve the acting site, which exactly is the property of CRP thus improving gastrointestinal absorption function. Therefore, as a TCM with an effect of regulating qi and eliminating phlegm in clinic, the frequent use of CRP in Chinese herbal prescription is not accidental. Second, Chinese medicinal compounds must overcome the drug water solubility, stability, permeability, and other factors that affect the absorption process to achieve improvement in the oral bioavailability, to control the sustained and stable release of drug in the blood, and to show good pharmacological effects. CRP in compounds promotes the absorption of other TCM compounds, and this view is reflected in the classic compounds such as Liujunzi Decoction and Buzhong Yiqi Decoction. CRP is a rare and edible medicine obtained from abundant sources and at a low price. There has been increasing concern from the society on the use of CRP as a commonly used TCM in motherland medicine and in a majority of formulas. We hope that this review will highlight the importance of CRP and serve as a new reference for researchers in the future. Nevertheless, the synergistic mechanism and cooperative effect between CRP and the compound are not yet clear enough. Further research should be focus on the mechanism of action of the pharmacological effects and pharmacokinetics of CRP. In addition, there is an urgent need to inherit the theory of TCM by clarifying the connotation, mechanism, and synergistic effect of CRP with the compounds. It is believed that it can promote the understanding of the compatibility theory of TCM through further studies on CRP in Chinese herbal compound prescription. More importantly, we should deepen the international cooperation and exchanges, expand research ideas, inherit the tradition, and make innovations. We believe that CRP will have not only an extraordinary status in China but also a broader application prospect in the market worldwide. title: Study on the mechanism of the Chinese herbal pair Banxia-Chenpi in ameliorating polycystic ovary syndrome based on the CYP17A1 gene
chunk_text: Ethnopharmacological relevance As a typical Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) couplet medicine, Arum Ternatum Thunb. (Pinellia ternata (Thunb.) Makino, known as Banxia in Chinese) and Citrus Reticulata (pericarps of Citrus reticulata Blanco, known as Chenpi in Chinese) has been widely used in clinical practice for their properties of drying dampness, resolving phlegm, relieving oppression and masses. According to the TCM theories, the imbalance in fluid metabolism could lead to the accumulation of the excess dampness and phlegm, resulting in the pathological phenotype as ‘damp-phlegm syndrome’. It can further lead to polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) when this accumulation of the excess fluid presents in uterus, affecting women's fertility and endocrine function. Recent studies have indicated that Banxia-Chenpi herbal pair (BXCP) exhibits significant therapeutic effects on damp-phlegm syndrome, yet the precise mechanisms underlying its anti-PCOS actions remain to be fully elucidated. Aim of the study The objective was to investigate the signaling pathway involved in steroid biosynthesis, particularly the cytochrome P450 family 17, subfamily A, member 1 (CYP17A1), and to evaluate the effects and mechanisms of BXCP in ameliorating PCOS through both in vivo and in vitro experiments. Materials and methods A systematic evaluation was conducted to assess BXCP's effects on serum biochemical indicators and ovarian tissue pathology in a PCOS rat model (induced by high-fat diet + letrozole) and a DHT-induced human granulosa cells (KGN) model. Core targets were screened using absorbed components analysis, bioinformatics, metabolomics, and network analysis. RT-qPCR and Western blot techniques were employed to confirm the expression of CYP17A1 and related signaling molecule expression during BXCP's amelioration of PCOS, both in vivo and in vitro. Results BXCP significantly ameliorated PCOS in vivo by mitigating weight gain, regulating estrus cycles, and normalizing sex hormone levels in rats. It upregulated metabolites related to steroid biosynthesis, including cortolone and progesterone, with CYP19A1, AKR1C3, and HSD17B1 as key regulators of CYP17A1. The main BXCP components, Naringenin and Nobiletin, increased CYP17A1 and CYP19A1 protein expression while decreased AKR1C3 and HSD17B1. Conclusion In conclusion, BXCP ameliorates PCOS by activating the CYP17A1-centered steroid biosynthesis pathway. These findings provide new insights into BXCP's clinical potentials in the management of patients with PCOS, highlighting the importance of TCM in modern medicine.

Ethnopharmacological relevance As a typical Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) couplet medicine, Arum Ternatum Thunb. (Pinellia ternata (Thunb.) Makino, known as Banxia in Chinese) and Citrus Reticulata (pericarps of Citrus reticulata Blanco, known as Chenpi in Chinese) has been widely used in clinical practice for their properties of drying dampness, resolving phlegm, relieving oppression and masses. According to the TCM theories, the imbalance in fluid metabolism could lead to the accumulation of the excess dampness and phlegm, resulting in the pathological phenotype as ‘damp-phlegm syndrome’. It can further lead to polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) when this accumulation of the excess fluid presents in uterus, affecting women's fertility and endocrine function. Recent studies have indicated that Banxia-Chenpi herbal pair (BXCP) exhibits significant therapeutic effects on damp-phlegm syndrome, yet the precise mechanisms underlying its anti-PCOS actions remain to be fully elucidated. Aim of the study The objective was to investigate the signaling pathway involved in steroid biosynthesis, particularly the cytochrome P450 family 17, subfamily A, member 1 (CYP17A1), and to evaluate the effects and mechanisms of BXCP in ameliorating PCOS through both in vivo and in vitro experiments. Materials and methods A systematic evaluation was conducted to assess BXCP's effects on serum biochemical indicators and ovarian tissue pathology in a PCOS rat model (induced by high-fat diet + letrozole) and a DHT-induced human granulosa cells (KGN) model. Core targets were screened using absorbed components analysis, bioinformatics, metabolomics, and network analysis. RT-qPCR and Western blot techniques were employed to confirm the expression of CYP17A1 and related signaling molecule expression during BXCP's amelioration of PCOS, both in vivo and in vitro. Results BXCP significantly ameliorated PCOS in vivo by mitigating weight gain, regulating estrus cycles, and normalizing sex hormone levels in rats. It upregulated metabolites related to steroid biosynthesis, including cortolone and progesterone, with CYP19A1, AKR1C3, and HSD17B1 as key regulators of CYP17A1. The main BXCP components, Naringenin and Nobiletin, increased CYP17A1 and CYP19A1 protein expression while decreased AKR1C3 and HSD17B1. Conclusion In conclusion, BXCP ameliorates PCOS by activating the CYP17A1-centered steroid biosynthesis pathway. Therefore, this study proposes a strategy based on analysis of blood-absorbed components, metabolomics, bioinformatics, and integrated network analysis for identifying effective components of BXCP in treating PCOS and investigating the molecular mechanisms underlying its effectiveness. A “core drug components-core targets” network diagram was constructed, and this mechanism was validated in rat PCOS models induced by letrozole and HFD, as well as in DHT-induced KGN cell PCOS models. Steroids play a crucial role in mammalian biology, helping maintain homeostasis, regulate metabolism, and control reproduction by influencing numerous processes. Normal ovarian function, including follicular growth, oocyte maturation, and ovulation, largely depends on local steroid production and subsequent steroid-mediated signaling. Gonadotropins including FSH and LH regulate most ovarian steroid synthesis, acting on granulosa cells and theca cells within developing and mature follicles (Clement, 1987). In this experiment, six metabolites—Cortolone, Progesterone, Tetrahydrodeoxycorticosterone, 5-alpha-pregnane-3,20-dione, 11-Deoxycortisol, and Tetrahydrocortisol—were detected by comparing serum metabolites of rats in the CON group, MOD group, and BXCP group. According to the analysis, these six metabolites fall into the category of related metabolites in the steroid biosynthesis pathway. This result confirms the involvement of this metabolic pathway in the pathogenesis and treatment mechanism of PCOS in rats. Furthermo

Specifically, the regulation of CYP17A1 profoundly modulates the equilibrium of crucial hormones such as AMH, LH, E2, T, and FSH, which is vital for the restoration of ovarian function and the reconstruction of endocrine homeostasis. Furthermore, this study identified changes in various metabolites, and CYP17A1, as the central regulatory factor, manifests its core regulatory role through alterations in the levels of these metabolites, further reinforcing its central position within the steroid metabolic network. In summary, this study highlights the central role of CYP17A1 in the treatment of PCOS with the BXCP, constructing a clear mechanistic framework centered on CYP17A1 that directly regulates key hormone levels, thereby improving the pathophysiological state of PCOS. Moreover, there are limitations to this study due to the lack of human clinical trials for validation. CYP17A1 serves as a central regulatory factor in the steroid hormone synthesis pathway, and its expression and activity have significant impacts on hormone homeostasis in rats with PCOS. In vivo experimental results demonstrate that the combined application of Banxia and Chenpi can significantly regulate the expression of CYP17A1 and its downstream genes, including AKR1C3, CYP19A1, and HSD17B1. This regulatory effect contributes to the modulation of the homeostasis of crucial reproductive hormones such as E2 and T. Additionally, through analysis of components absorbed into the blood and combined analysis, the core components of BXCP were identified as Naringenin and Nobiletin. In vitro experimental results confirm that these components can regulate the homeostasis of key reproductive hormones such as E2 and T in KGN cells through the same mechanism. Our results not only provide scientific evidence for the potential medicinal value of BXCP in regulating steroid metabolism but also expand its application prospects for treating PCOS, laying a solid foundation for the development of new therapeutic drugs. Furthermore, these findings reveal the translational potential of BXCP in clinical settings, indicating that it may be an effective treatment option for PCOS with a high feasibility for translating from laboratory research to clinical application. title: Effects of storage period and heat treatment on phenolic compound composition in dried Citrus peels (Chenpi) and discrimination of Chenpi with different storage periods through targeted metabolomic study using HPLC-DAD analysis
source: Journal of Pharmaceutical and Biomedical Analysis
chunk_text: Dried Citrus peels, known as Chenpi in Chinese medicine, are a traditional medicine for the treatment of indigestion and inflammatory syndromes. In this study, we evaluated the effect of storage periods (1-year vs. 3-year) and heat treatment (90min vs. 3h at 120°C) on the total phenolic content (TPC) and bioactivity (anti-oxidant activity) of Chenpi. It was found that the long-term stored Chenpi had a higher TPC and superior 1,1-diphenyl-2-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH) radical-scavenging activity levels compared to the regular stored Chenpi, and that heat treatment increased both TPC and bioactivity. Subsequently, we developed and validated a high performance liquid chromatography with diode-array detection (HPLC-DAD) method to determine individual phenolic acids. Eleven phenolic compounds were determined in different Chenpi samples. Concentrations of total phenolic compounds were higher in long-term stored Chenpi and heat treatment raised the levels of those in regular stored Chenpi. In further study, a targeted metabolomic approach was applied to discriminate Chenpi with different storage periods. Two different phenolic acid fractions (free and ester) from the regular and long-term stored Chenpi were analyzed using the developed HPLC-DAD and the data were used in principal component analysis (PCA) on the HPLC-DAD peak areas of the 11 phenolic acids. Two principal components (PC1 and PC2) accounted for 87.1% of the variation between the regular and long-term stored Chenpi. In a two-dimensional plot of PC1 and PC2, the samples divided into four groups: two storage periods and two fractions.

Tel.: +82 31 290 7784/2 880 7844; fax: +82 2 886 7844. Dried Citrus peels, known as Chenpi in Chinese medicine, are a traditional medicine for the treatment of indigestion and inflammatory syndromes. In this study, we evaluated the effect of storage periods (1-year vs. 3-year) and heat treatment (90min vs. 3h at 120°C) on the total phenolic content (TPC) and bioactivity (anti-oxidant activity) of Chenpi. It was found that the long-term stored Chenpi had a higher TPC and superior 1,1-diphenyl-2-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH) radical-scavenging activity levels compared to the regular stored Chenpi, and that heat treatment increased both TPC and bioactivity. Subsequently, we developed and validated a high performance liquid chromatography with diode-array detection (HPLC-DAD) method to determine individual phenolic acids. Eleven phenolic compounds were determined in different Chenpi samples. Concentrations of total phenolic compounds were higher in long-term stored Chenpi and heat treatment raised the levels of those in regular stored Chenpi. In further study, a targeted metabolomic approach was applied to discriminate Chenpi with different storage periods. Keywords Storage period Heat treatment Phenolic acids Antioxidant activity PCA 1 Introduction Dried fruit peels of Citrus unshiu Markovich, C. reticulate Blanco, and C. tachibana Makino Tanaka, which are collectively known as Chenpi, have been widely used as a traditional medicine in Korea, China, and Japan. Chenpi extracts are used to treat indigestion and inflammatory syndromes of the respiratory tract such as bronchitis and asthma [1]. It is known that Chenpi contains more bioactive compounds, such as flavonoids, phenolic acids, and limonoids, than the citrus juice [2,3]. Like flavonoids, which are probably the major anti-oxidants in Chenpi, phenolic compounds are regarded as significant bioactive compounds and have been reported as anti-oxidative agents in various plants [4–6]. The total phenolic content of Chenpi has been correlated with the anti-oxidizing activity of Chenpi [7–9]. In biological systems, highly reactive free radicals and oxygen species modify nucleic acids, proteins, lipids, and DNA through oxidation, modifications that may initiate degenerative diseases [10–17]. Thus, Chenpi has potential as a health-promoting s

Thus, Chenpi has potential as a health-promoting substance. Phenolic compounds naturally exist in a phenolic acid form as hydroxybenzoic acid or hydroxycinnamic acid derivatives (Fig. 1 ), and are usually covalently bound to insoluble polymers. This limits the activity of bound phenolic compounds as natural anti-oxidative agents and there have been attempts to liberate bound phenolic acids. For example, bound low molecular weight phenolic compounds in citrus peels have been transformed into free phenolic acids through heat treatment; thereby increasing the anti-oxidant activity of the citrus peel extract [9]. In the current study, Chenpi samples with different storage periods (1 year vs. 3 years) and different heat treatments (90min vs. 3h at 120°C) were assessed for total phenolic content. Eleven individual phenolic acid compounds were determined using an optimized high performance liquid chromatography with diode-array detection (HPLC-DAD) method, which is the first simultaneous analysis of such a large number of phenolic compounds. This study allowed us to explain correlation between antioxidant activity and phenolic content of individual Chenpi samples. Metabolomic research methods offer high-throughput qualitative and quantitative measurement that can be used to monitor sample quality. Before powdering, portions of the Chenpi samples were held at 120°C for either 90min or 3h to evaluate the effect of heat treatment on the composition of phenolic compounds. Free phenolic acids (fraction A), soluble phenolic acid esters (fraction B), and insoluble-bound phenolic acids (fraction C) were prepared according to the Krygier et al.’s method [18] as described below and as schematically shown in (Fig. 2 ). Briefly, 30g of powdered sample was extracted in 20mL of a 70% methanol/70% acetone (1:1, v/v) mixture at room temperature. The supernatant was concentrated under reduced pressure, acidified to pH 2 with 6N HCl, and then extracted in hexane. The aqueous phase was extracted in the diethyl ether/ethyl acetate mixture (DE/EA, 1:1, v/v). The organic layer was dehydrated with sodium sulfate, followed by evaporation, to yield fraction A. The aqueous phase extract in DE/EA was alkali hydrolyzed in 4N NaOH, acidified, and then extracted with hexane. The resulting aqueous layer underwent extractions with hexane and DE/EA (as described for fraction A) resulting in fraction B. Fraction C was obtained from the 70% methanol/70% acetone extraction residue which was then treated with alkali hydrolysis followed by extraction with hexane and DE/EA as described for fraction B. 2.3 HPLC analysis and method validation A Waters-510 HPLC system (Milford, MA, USA) equipped with a DAD detect

HPLC-DAD was established to determine the 11 phenolic acids. For method validation, a gradient elution consisting of 50mM phosphoric acid in water and acetonitrile was applied and chlorogenic acid was the internal standard. A chromatogram of the standards is shown in Fig. 3 . Linearity, accuracy, precision, and the limit of quantification (LOQ) were examined for the method validation. The calibration curves showed good linearity (correlation coefficient (r 2)≥0.9941) within a range of 1–200μg/mL. The inter- and intra-day precisions, expressed as relative standard deviations (RSD), were determined at a concentration of 60μg/mL three times a day for 3 days. The intra-day precisions were ≤8.0% and the inter-day precisions were ≤9.6%. LOD ranged from 0.08 to 1.72μg/mL and LOQ was between 0.25 and 5.22μg/mL. Accuracy measured at 60μg/mL ranged from 96 to 118%. Gallic, protocatechuic, and β-hydroxybenzoic acids, not detected in regular stored Chenpi, were present in long-term stored Chenpi. Protocatechuic acid and protocatechuic aldehyde, which are usually bound to polysaccharidic material of cell wall in covalent form, are degraded by extracellular enzymatic activities (cellulases, laccases, peroxidases) [25,26]. Thus, it is possible that the reactions above occurred naturally during 2 years of extended storage. We also examined the effect of heat treatment and found that heat treatment increases the amount of phenolic acids in fraction A of regular stored Chenpi. In particular, 3h of heating was more effective than 90min of heating in increasing the amount of all phenolic acids, except for gallic and syringic acids, in fraction A. In fraction A of long-term stored Chenpi, the amount of protocatechuic, β-hydroxybenzoic, caffeic, and p-coumaric acids increased after heat treatment, with a greater increase following the 3h treatment compared to the 90min treatment. These different results might have been caused by the conversion of insoluble-bound phenolic compounds into free or soluble ester forms following degradation of esters to free forms during heat treatment and prolonged storage. 3.4 Discrimination of Chenpi with different storage periods using targeted metabolomic analysis The aim of metabolomics is to classify samples and understand the basic principles that contribute to the differences among them. Metabolomics has been applied to the classification of plants with principal component analysis often used as its main statistical approach [27]. PCA, with its general objectives of data reduction and interpretation [28], combines various experimental data and explains the variance–covariance structure of a set of variables through linear combinations of the variables. In this study, a targeted metabolomics approach was employed to discriminate Chenpi with different storage periods for the first time. Eleven phenolic acids were the target compounds used as variables. Initially, a PCA correlation matrix was calculated. chunk_text: s. Initially, a PCA correlation matrix was calculated. The matrix values were the degrees of association among the 11 variables derived from the peak areas of 11 phenolic acids in the HPLC-DAD analysis. Next, eigenvectors were extracted from the matrix to obtain the principal components (PCs), i.e., components that contain the majority of the available information in the dataset and can provide linear summaries of experimental outcomes [29]. The extracted eigenvectors are presented in Table 5 . Based on a scree plot of cumulative eigenvalues, we chose 2 PCs that explained 87.10% of the variations between the regular and long-term stored Chenpi. The two PCs (PC1 and PC2) explained 55.54% and 31.36% of the sample diversity, respectively. In PC1, phenolic acids with double bonds, such as caffeic, ferulic, and trans-cinnamic acids, produced negative eigenvectors. On the other hand, in PC2, variables containing a p-hydroxybenzoic acid structure, including gallic, protocatechuic, and β-hydroxybenzoic acids, exhibited positive eigenvectors while those with a double bond or a methoxy group, such as vanillic, caffeic, syringic, and p-coumaric acids, showed negative vectors. Lastly, PC scores were used to distinguish Chenpi samples of different storage periods. The calculated PC scores showed that fraction A from long-term stored Chenpi had positive PC1 and PC2 values while fraction A from regular stored Chenpi had positive PC1 and negative PC2 values. title: PCN-224/β-Cyclodextrin dual-modified magnetic nanocomposite for efficient extraction and determination of nobiletin and tangeretin in Chenpi-based beverages
source: Journal of Pharmaceutical and Biomedical Analysis
chunk_text: Polymethoxylated flavonoids such as nobiletin and tangeretin are the primary bioactive constituents of Chenpi. However, their accurate quantification in complex beverage matrices remains challenging. In this study, a novel dual-modified magnetic composite, Fe3O4@PCN-224@β-CD, was synthesized for the efficient extraction of these target analytes. The material integrated the high magnetization of Fe3O4 for rapid separation, the porous and π-electron-rich framework of PCN-224 for strong π–π interactions, and a β-cyclodextrin shell for enhanced hydrophobic inclusion and aqueous dispersibility. Coupled with UPLC–UV detection, a magnetic solid-phase extraction method based on this composite was established and optimized through single-factor experiments and response surface methodology. The developed method exhibited excellent linearity (R² ≥ 0.998), low detection limits (0.01–0.02 μg/mL), satisfactory precision and good recoveries (92.59–101.73%). Furthermore, the adsorbent demonstrated outstanding reusability over seven cycles. The high adsorption efficiency was attributed to the synergistic effect of π–π stacking and hydrophobic interactions within the composite. This study provided a robust and environmentally friendly strategy for the selective enrichment and accurate quantification of nobiletin and tangeretin in Chenpi-based beverages, highlighting the potential of PCN-224 and β-CD dual-functionalized magnetic composites for high-efficiency sample pretreatment in complex matrices.

However, their relatively low abundance, structural susceptibility, and the complexity of beverage matrices—which typically contain sugars, organic acids, pigments, and flavoring compounds—make their accurate quantification highly challenging. Therefore, establishing efficient and selective preconcentration methods to isolate target PMF from complex beverage matrices prior to instrumental analysis is of paramount importance. Among the available sample preparation technologies, magnetic solid-phase extraction (MSPE) has emerged as a highly efficient, rapid, and environmentally friendly sample pretreatment technique [6,7]. By combining solid-phase extraction with magnetic separation, MSPE facilitates the fast isolation and enrichment of analytes without the need for filtration or centrifugation, greatly simplifying operations and reducing solvent consumption [8]. Moreover, their large surface area and ease of surface modification make magnetic materials ideal for the selective adsorption of specific target compounds [9]. However, despite possessing excellent magnetization and ease of synthesis, pristine Fe3O4 nanoparticles are prone to oxidation and aggregation in aqueous environments due to strong magnetic dipole–dipole interactions [10]. chunk_text: To overcome these drawbacks, surface functionalization with porous or polymeric coatings has been widely adopted to provide additional adsorption sites and enhance stability [11,12]. Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs), characterized by their exceptionally high surface area, tunable pore structures, and versatile chemical functionality, are ideal candidates for constructing high-performance magnetic sorbents [13]. Among them, zirconium-based MOFs (Zr-MOFs), such as the Porous Coordination Network (PCN) series, exhibit remarkable chemical and thermal stability across a wide pH range due to the strong coordination between Zr⁴⁺ clusters and carboxylate oxygen atoms [14]. Specifically, PCN-224, composed of Zr⁴⁺ nodes and tetrakis (4-carboxyphenyl) porphyrin (TCPP) linkers, not only maintains structural integrity under acidic or alkaline conditions but also provides a highly conjugated aromatic skeleton rich in π-electron domains, facilitating strong π–π stacking interactions with planar aromatic molecules [15–17]. Recent studies have highlighted the high porosity and satisfactory performance of PCN-224–modified MOF composites in preconcentrating trace metal ions from water and organophosphorus pesticides from tea [18,19]. Nevertheless, pristine MOF structures sometimes exhibit limited hydrophobic affinity and poor dispersion stability in aqueous environments or complex food matrices, restricting their practical applications. Consequently, the rational design of hybrid magnetic sorbents with tailored surface functionalities remains essential to enhance extraction selectivity, and reusability under real-sample conditions. β-Cyclodextrin (β-CD), a cyclic oligosaccharide composed of seven α-(1,4)-linked D-glucopyranose units, has been widely employed to modify magnetic and porous sorbents due to its unique structural and physicochemical features [20,21]. Its hydrophobic inner cavity and hydrophilic outer surface enable host–guest inclusion with various organic molecules through hydrophobic interactions, hydrogen bonding, and π–π stacking, thereby enhancing molecular recognition and adsorption selectivity [20,22]. In addition, the abundant hydroxyl groups on β-CD improve the hydrophilicity and dispersion stability of composite materials in aqueous media and offer reactive sites for covalent linkage with other functional components [23]. Owing to its nontoxicity, biocompatibility and biodegradability, β-CD is highly regarded as an environmentally friendly modifier, making it ideal for sample pretreatment in food and environmental analyses [24,25]. Dirven by these considerations, a novel magnetic composite material, Fe3O4@PCN-224@β-CD, was rationally designed and synthesized in this study. In this composite, Fe3O4 nanoparticles served as the magnetic core to enable rapid magnetic separation, while the PCN-224 layer provided a porous coordination network with an abundant π-electron-rich aromatic framework to facilitate strong π–π interactions. The outer β-CD coating endowed the material with hydrophobic inclusion capability and enhanced aqueous dispersibility. The synthesized composite was comprehensively characterized, and its adsorption behavior toward five natural products with distinct structural features was systematically investigated to elucidate the structure–adsorption relationship. Moreover, the material was utilized for the enrichment and quantitative determination of nobiletin and tangeretin, with extraction parameters optimized to maximum efficiency. To determine the variables that significantly influenced extraction performance, a single-factor investigation was initially conducted. The examined parameters included adsorbent dosage (1.0–5.0 mg), extraction time (1.0–7.0 min), type of desorption solvent (methanol, acetonitrile, ethyl acetate, and isopropanol), elution time (0.5–7.0 min), elution volume (100–500 μL), ionic strength (NaCl concentration: 0–100 mM), and pH (3–11). Based on the results of the single-factor experiments, four key variables—adsorbent dosage (A), adsorption time (B), elution volume (C), and pH (D)—were further optimized using response surface methodology (RSM) with Design-Expert software. The final MSPE procedure consisted of two main steps: adsorption and desorption ( Fig. 1). Prior to extraction, the pH of all samples was adjusted to 6.0 using 0.1 mol/L HCl or NaOH. Spiked samples were prepared by adding a standard mixture to ultrapure water. Under the optimized conditions, 4 mg of the adsorbent was added to 5 mL of the spiked sample and dispersed by ultrasonication. As illustrated in Fig. 2e), similar to naked Fe3O4 particles, the Fe3O4@PCN-224@β-CD composite exhibited distinct hysteresis loops without remanence or coercivity, a hallmark of superparamagnetic behavior. According to the magnetization (M) versus magnetic field (H) curves, the saturation magnetization (Mₛ) of naked Fe3O4 particles was 72.82 emu/g, whereas that of synthesized composite decreased to 11.89 emu/g. As presented in Fig. S3, the synthesized material exhibited the lowest adsorption capacity for berberine, while the highest adsorption efficiency was observed for nobiletin. Nobiletin possessed a planar, rigid polycyclic aromatic structure with abundant π-electrons, allowing for strong π–π stacking interactions with PCN-224 [19]. In addition, the molecular size of nobiletin matched well with the pore dimensions of PCN-224, favoring its diffusion and retention within the framework channels. The presence of multiple methoxy substituents also enhanced molecular hydrophobicity, promoting its inclusion into the hydrophobic cavities of β-CD on the material’s surface, thereby achieving highly efficient adsorption [22]. In contrast, the other tested molecules failed to simultaneously activate these synergistic adsorption mechanisms due to their intrinsic structural characteristics: chlorogenic acid and geniposide were overly hydrophilic, berberine carried a positive charge, and emodin was affected by its polar functional groups. These features hindered π–π stacking or host–guest inclusion, resulting in markedly lower adsorption capacities compared to nobiletin. Additionally, the extraction performance toward nobiletin was investigated for Fe3O4, Fe3O4@PCN-224 and Fe3O4@PCN-224@β-CD

To investigate the underlying adsorption process, FT-IR and XPS spectra of the adsorbent were recorded before and after the adsorption of nobiletin and tangeretin. As shown in Fig. 6 , the peak at 3423 cm⁻¹ , corresponding to hydrogen-bonded O–H groups, broadened following adsorption. Furthermore, a new signal emerged at 1006 cm⁻¹ post-adsorption, corresponding to the C–O stretching vibration of polymethoxy groups, likely resulting from the retention of nobiletin and tangeretin on the adsorbent surface. These spectral changes evidence that β-CD provided a dominant contribution via host–guest inclusion and hydrophobic interactions; the strong hydrophobicity of the polymethoxy flavones enabled their effective incorporation into the hydrophobic cavity of β-CD [31]. Meanwhile, the characteristic aromatic CC stretching vibrations at 1603 cm⁻¹ and 1551 cm⁻¹ also broadened. This indicated that the TCPP ligands in the PCN-224 framework play another dominant role. Because nobiletin and tangeretin possess rigid, planar, and highly π-conjugated flavonoid skeletons, the TCPP ligands readily facilitate strong π–π stacking interactions with the aromatic rings of the analytes. This synergistic mechanism was further supported by the XPS survey spectra. After adsorption, the appearance of O KLL Auger indicated a significant increase in the number of surface oxygen atoms, confirming the successful capture of the analyte [32]. The C 1 s spectra (Fig. 6 c) displayed peaks at 284.26 eV, 286.18 eV, and 288.08 eV, corresponding to C-C/CC, C-O/C-N, and CO/CN bonds, respectively. Post-adsorption, these peaks shifted to 284.23 eV, 285.85 eV, and 288.25 eV. Such shifts suggested the presence of π–π interactions and hydrogen bonding at the interface [33]. Moreover, the O 1 s spectra showed a peak at 531.93 eV, corresponding to metal-oxide (M-O) bonds, which shifted to 531.72 eV post-adsorption, further supporting the interaction between the oxidized metal states and the analytes [34]. Regarding the metal nodes, subtle positive shifts in the binding energies of the Fe 2p and Zr 3d peaks (approximately 0.03–0.06 eV) were observed after adsorption. In contrast to the dominant roles of the organic ligands and β-CD, the Zr nodes (alongside the Fe sites) played an auxiliary role. The absence of free hydroxyl or carboxyl groups in nobiletin and tangeretin suggested that direct strong coordination with these metal nodes was unlikely. Thus, their contribution was more plausibly attributed to weak electronic interactions or dipole–dipole forces. Among various tested bioactive compounds, the composite exhibited outstanding adsorption efficiency toward PMF. Following the systematic optimization of MSPE parameters through single-factor experiments and RSM, an efficient method coupled with UPLC-UV detection was developed and validated for the determination of nobiletin and tangeretin. The proposed strategy demonstrated excellent linearity, low limits of detection, high precision, and satisfactory accuracy (92.59%–101.73%). Moreover, the adsorbent exhibited remarkable reusability, retaining over 90% of its initial adsorption capacity after seven consecutive cycles. The successful application of this method to commercial Chenpi-based beverages confirmed its suitability for the enrichment and accurate quantification of trace flavonoids in complex food matrices. Mechanistic investigations suggested that the adsorption process was primarily driven by π–π interactions and hydrogen bonding. title: Analysis of pesticide residues in commercially available chenpi using a modified QuEChERS method and GC-MS/MS determination
chunk_text: To ensure the safety of the commercially available chenpi, a convenient and fast analytical method was developed for the determination of 133 pesticide residues in chenpi using gas chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (GC-MS/MS). In this study, different extraction solvents, redissolution solvents and adsorbents were tested according to the recovery and purification effect to obtain a modified QuEChERS method. The samples were extracted with acetonitrile. During the clean-up step, octadecyl-modified silica (C18) and graphitized carbon black (GCB) were selected, and aminopropyl (NH2) was used instead of primary secondary amine (PSA) because of its weaker ion exchange capacity which had little effect on the recovery of ditalimfos. Samples were quantified by matrix-matched calibration with internal standards. All pesticides showed good linearity in the respective range, both with values of r 2 > 0.99. The average recoveries of the pesticides spiked samples ranged from 70.0% to 112.2% with the RSDs of 0.2%–14.4%. The modified QuEChERS method was validated and applied to twenty real samples. Five pesticides were found in eight batches, but no pesticide exceeded the maximum residue limits (MRL, MRL reference to European commission).

The samples were extracted with acetonitrile. During the clean-up step, octadecyl-modified silica (C18) and graphitized carbon black (GCB) were selected, and aminopropyl (NH2) was used instead of primary secondary amine (PSA) because of its weaker ion exchange capacity which had little effect on the recovery of ditalimfos. chunk_text: detected frequently in commercially available chenpi. Relevant literature shows that pesticides pollution in chenpi is serious [3]. Pesticides are very toxic to humans and research has shown that some pesticides have teratogenic, carcinogenic and mutagenic effects [4,5]. In 2016, Peng et al. [6] used gas chromatography to determine organophosphorus pesticides in chenpi and only 11 kinds of organophosphorus pesticides were determined by this method. Therefore, it is extremely important to establish a set of convenient and fast detection techniques for the determination of multiple pesticide residues in chenpi. Sample preparation is a crucial step in all analytical methods and an appropriate clean-up method was developed for the extraction of pesticide residues with high selectivity, and low co-extraction. The most common sample preparation methods include solid-phase extraction (SPE) [7,8], QuEChERS [9], solid-phase micro extraction (SPME) [10,11] and gel permeation chromatography (GPC) [12–14]. The QuEChERS (Quick, Easy, Cheap, Effective, Rugged, Safe) method was developed by Anastassiades et al. in 2003 [15] and it has become one of the most commonly used methods for the determination of pesticides. A typical QuEChERS method involves an extraction with acetonitrile (and water in dry commodities), followed by a phase partitioning assisted by salting out and further clean up by d-SPE. [16–19]. The method can be used to analyze many compounds, including highly polar pesticides and highly acidic compounds. It is suitable for the detection of samples with a low fat content and

title: Analysis of pesticide residues in commercially available chenpi using a modified QuEChERS method and GC-MS/MS determination
chunk_text: method can be used to analyze many compounds, including highly polar pesticides and highly acidic compounds. It is suitable for the detection of samples with a low fat content and a high water content. Furthermore, the method has been applied to pesticide determination of many different matrices like vegetables, fruits and tea [20–22]. In the clean-up step, sorbent C18 and primary secondary amine (PSA) are used in most published methods, and florisil is used in some, but NH2 is seldom used. NH2 has a similar adsorption performance to PSA, while PSA contains two amino groups giving it a higher ion exchange capacity than NH2. However, PSA sorbents result in the pH value of the final extract solutions being more than 8, which affects the stability of base-sensitive pesticides [23] and NH2 can be used when PSA affects the determination of analytes. In order to ensure food safety, in this study, a method was developed for multi-residue determination of pesticides in chenpi by GC-MS/MS and NH2 sorbent was used in a modified QuEChERS method because of the pesticides influenced by PSA. 2 Experimental 2.1 Chemicals and other materials Pesticide standards and the internal standard (IS), chlorpyrifos-d10 with a purity >98%, were provided by Dr. Ehrenstorfer (Augsburg, Germany). Pesticide residues can be easily extracted from small particle samples, so before use, all samples were ground to a powder mechanically, and passed through a no. 24 mesh sieve. (The particles retained in the sieve are not included for the analysis.) 2 g samples and 100 μL internal standard (2 μg/mL) were added to 50 mL polypropylene (PP) centrifuge tubes and then 10 mL acetonitrile was used for extraction. The ultrasonic extraction was carried out for 5 min and 0.8 g anhydrous MgSO4 and 0.2 g NaCl were added. Each mixture was shaken by hand for 1 min and centrifuged at 11,180 g (rcf) for 5 min. The solution was subjected to vortex mixing for 1 min, and then centrifuged at 7155 g (rcf) for 5 min, and 5 mL of the upper layer was transferred to a 50 mL round-bottom flask and evaporated to near dryness on a rotary vacuum evaporator at 40 °C. Compared with n-hexane and ethyl acetate, acetonitrile had the strong dissolving capability for the analytes, meeting the recovery requirement. Therefore, in this study acetonitrile was used as the extraction solvent. 3.2 Selection of solvent for redissolution Acetonitrile possesses many advantages for extraction, but the polarity of acetonitrile is high, which can damage the gas chromatography column. For the protection of chromatographic columns, before analysis, acetonitrile should be replaced. In this study, n-hexane and acetone were selected as solvents for redissolution. The recoveries of pesticides obtained with these two solvents are shown in Fig. 2. Compared with that of acetone, the recoveries of some pesticides were lower when redissolved with n-hexane, and approximately 42% of pesticides were outside the range of 60%–120%. Dimethoate and cis-chlordane were close to zero. When dissolved with acetone, most of analytical pesticides satisfied the recovery requirement. So acetone was chosen as the solvent for redissolution. 3.3 Optimization of adsorbents The use of co-extraction leads to an unsatisfactory peak shape, and an increased or inhibited response, which adversely affects the quantification. The adsorbents PSA, C18, Florisil, GCB and NH2 were investigated to choose the most appropriate purification method. If the extraction solution was injected into the GC-MS/MS without adding adsorbents, there was clear interference of the matrix for the pesticides bitertanol, cypermethrin, flucythrinate, and difenoconazole. The addition of Florisil for purification seemed to have no effect. C18 can be used for the reduction of lipids and non-polar interference. Because of the addition of C18, the matrices that interfered with the determination of pesticides, such as bitertanol, flucythrinate and difenoconazole, were removed. PSA can adsorb fatty acids and pigments extracted from chenpi to improve the chromatographic peak shape of cypermethrin ( Fig. 3). When the amount of PSA was 200 mg, the chromatographic peaks of cypermethrin isomers was free of interference from impurities. However, PSA clearly had an effect on the recovery of ditalimfos. This study compared the effect of the addition of 50, 100, 150, 200 mg PSA on the recovery of ditalimfos, and the results obtained are shown in Fig. 4. When the adsorbent amount was 50 mg, the recovery of ditalimfos was about 73.1%, while the recovery of ditalimfos decreased to 23.9% when the amount of PSA reached 200 mg. The main reason for this may be that PSA may increase the pH value of the final extract solutions to more than 8. According to the structure of ditalimfos ( Fig. 5), ditalimfos is unstable and decomposes easily in an alkaline environment, so as the amount of adsorbent is increased, the recovery of ditalimfos is reduced. Also, the extraction was improved when 30 mg GCB was added. In summary, 30 mg GCB was used as the adsorbent. 3.4 Validation study Under the modified QuEChERS method conditions, a validation study was carried out to evaluate the performance characteristics of the method for multiple pesticides in chenpi by estimating the linearity, limit of quantification (LOQ), accuracy (expressed by recovery), precision and matrix effects. Validation was performed following the European Union SANTE/11945/ 2015 guideline [28]. 3.4.1 Linearity The linearity for each pesticide was assessed in matrix-matched standard solution. The calibration curves of the compounds were obtained by plotting the pesticide/IS peak area ratios against the concentration of the corresponding calibration standards at eight different levels (1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 ng/mL). The linearity results are shown in Table 2. The linearity of the method for all the pesticides was satisfactory, with correlation coefficients (r 2) higher than 0.99. 3.4.2 LOQ The LOQ for each pesticide was defined as the lowest validated spiked level satisfying the requirement of recovery ranging from 70% to 120% and a relative standard deviation (RSD) less than 20%. Samples were spiked at two different concentrations: 0.005 and 0.01 mg/kg (6 replicates per level). The LOQ values are presented in Table 2. 3.4.3 Accuracy and precision Recovery was evaluated at three different spiked levels of 0.05, 0.1 and 0.2 mg/kg by spiking six blank samples at each level. Precision was expressed as the relative standard deviation (RSD) and was obtained from the six spiked samples at three spiking levels. Table 2 shows the recoveries and RSDs of all pesticides at all concentrations. The recovery of all the pesticides met the requirements of the pesticide residue determination. 3.4.4 Matrix effects (ME) In this study, some pest

The recovery of all the pesticides met the requirements of the pesticide residue determination. 3.4.4 Matrix effects (ME) In this study, some pesticides, such as mevinphos, propoxur, dicrotophos and carboxine, have better chromatographic peak shapes in matrix-matched blank solutions than in pure solvent solutions because of the ME. The ME was evaluated by the slope of the solvent calibration curve and the matrix-matched blank extract calibration curve according to the equation: ME (%) = [(slope in matrix/slope in solvent)−1] * 100 [29]. The ME results were grouped into 3 classes: a high ME (less than −50% or higher than +50%), a medium ME (between −50% and −20% or +20% and +50%) and a low ME (between +20% and −20%). Fig. 7 shows the ME of each pesticide. Among 133 pesticides, 53% showed low ME, 32% showed medium ME and 16% showed high ME. In order to avoid the ME, matrix-matched calibration standards were used for quantification to compensate for the ME. 3.5 Application to real samples Once the analytical methodology was validated, it was used for monitoring pesticides in chenpi samples. The established method was used for the simultaneous determination of the pesticides in twenty real samples and the results are summarized in Table 3. Chlorpyrifos, isocarbophos, methidathion, profenofos and fenpropathrin were found in eight batches, most of which were insecticides and fungicides. Insecticide clorpyrifos and methidathion were frequently detected pesticides, but no pesticide exceeded the maximum residue limits (MRL, the values of MRL for orange were taken as reference) prescribed by Regulation (EC) no. 396/2005 [30]. Clorpyrifos and methidathion are low toxicity pesticides, but the others are moderately or highly toxic pesticides, which are harmful to human health. Therefore, it is important to pay attention to the appropriate use of pesticides. 4 Conclusions A modified QuEChERS method for the determination of multiple pesticides by GC-MS/MS was developed. Several sorbents were evaluated in order to reduce the ME as much as possible. C18 and PSA were mainly used in the Original QuEChERS method. In our study, PSA had an effect on the pesticide ditalimfos, which showed an unsatisfactory recovery on increasing the amount of PSA. NH2, with a similar adsorption performance to PSA, is a substitute product of PSA for base-sensitive pesticides or pesticides which could be affected by PSA. The addition of GCB can remove pigment extracted with acetonitrile. A validation procedure was performed, which showed good results for suitability, recovery and repeatability. The developed method was applied to the determination of real samples, and some pesticides were detected, which demonstrated that it is essential to constantly monitor pesticide residues in chenpi. BACKGROUND: Traditional view considers that the long-t erm stored Chenpi (dried citrus peel)

remains obscure.

characteristics and intestinal immunomodulating activities were investigated and compared. Our 
results showed that CPP5 and CPP10 showed the lower dynamic viscosity and degree of 
methylesterification, as well as the higher mol ecular heterogeneity as compared with CPP1. The

Citrus peel is regarded as a by-product in the process of juice manufacture, but actually it contains 
a variety of bioactive compounds, such as phenolic acids,

coumarins,4 which is an exploitable biological resour ce. Dried citrus peel, known as Chenpi, has 
been used as a Chinese herbal medicine and functional beverage for promoting digestion of 
gastrointestinal tract in China and other Asian coun tries for centuries. Moreover, citrus peel is one 
of the main raw materials for pectin production.

MATERIALS AND METHODS 
Materials and reagents 
One-year, five-year and ten-year peels of C. reticulata were purchased from Xinhui region of 
Guangdong province, China. So far, the production of Xinhui Chenpi has still followed the 
traditional technology. In brief, the fresh citrus peel is dried in the sun and then stored in a 
ventilated and dry situation for maturing. 
Standard dextrans (5.0, 25.0, 80.0, 150.0, 470.0 and 610.0 KDa), monosaccharide (D-glucose, 
D-galactose, L-rhamnose, L-arab inose, D-xylose, galacturonic acid) and apple pectin were 
purchased from Sigma Chemical Co. (St. Louis, MO, USA). DEAE-cellulose D-52 was 
purchased from Beijing Solarbio Science & technology co., ltd (Beijing, China). 
Trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) and 1-pheny-3-methyl-5-pyrazolone (PMP) were purchased from 
Sinopharm Chemical Reageni Co., Ltd. RPMI 1640 medium and fetal bovine serum (FBS) were 
purchased from Gibco BRL Co. (Grand Island, NY, USA). Male mouse (Kunming) were provided 
by Bengbu Medical College. All other reagents were analytical grade or chromatographic grade. 
Sample extraction 
The dried Chenpi (50.0 g) were chopped into small pieces and dipped into 1.0 L of 95% ethanol 
for 24 h to remove the pigments and lipids. After dried, the peels were extracted with 1.0 L of 
distilled water at 95 ℃ for 2 h with constant stirring. The extract was filtered, centrifuged at 4500 
g for 10.0 min, and then concentrated to 1/3 of its initial volume using a vacuum rotary 
evaporation apparatus. The filtrate was precipitated by adding ethanol to a final concentration of

Preparation and characteristics of Chenpi pectins 
Chenpi has usually been used as a functional hot drink in China and other Asian countries, so the 
water-soluble pectic polysaccharides were the research focus. In this study, the three water-soluble 
extracts (CPP1, CPP5 and CPP10) were obtained from one-year, five-year and ten-year Chenpi, 
respectively, by the method of hot water extraction and alcohol precipitation. All the extracts were 
rich in carbohydrate and contained a certain amount of uronic acids, suggesting their pectic

extracts (1 mg mL -1, dissolved in distilled water) lowered with the extension of storage period of 
Chenpi. These suggested the solubility of pectic polysaccharides in Chenpi increased with the 
extension of storage period. The change of pectic solubility migh t be related to its molecular 
structure, such as the molecular weight and degree of methylesterification (DM).22 
In order to testify our assumption above, the relative molecular weight of the samples were 
investigated by high performance size exclusion chromatography (HPSEC) as shown in Fig.1. The 
three samples presented a similar main peak, and the retention time in the columns was about 21 
minutes. The relative molecular weights of CPP1, CPP5 and CPP10 were 4.18 ×105, 3.73×
105 and 4.02 ×105 Da, respectively, according to the standard curve of the dextrans. In 
comparison, the peak of CPP10 was broader, which suggested the depolymerisation of pectin. The 
FTIR spectrums of the three samples displayed the typical absorption peaks of carbohydrate, 
including the stretching vibration of O-H (3417 cm -1) and C-C (1108 cm -1) as illustrated in Fig.2. 
The peaks at 1743 cm -1 and 1630 cm -1 were attributed to the vibrations of esterified carboxylic 
group and free carboxylic group, respectively. 23 In this study, the DM of pectin was estimated 
based on the ratio of the peak area at 1743 cm -1 to sum of the peak areas at 1743 cm -1 and 1630 
cm-1 in FT-IR spectra.24 Hereby, the DMs of CPP1, CPP5 and CPP10 were 39.26%, 28.

Peyer’s patches are parts of gut-associated lympho reticular tissues (GALT) and play an essential 
role in uptake of antigen and initia tion of intestinal immune response. 26 Some exogenous 
substances, known as immunomodulators, can activate the plasmablasts and regulatory T 
lymphocytes that exist in the Peyer’s patches, and enhance the defense system of body. 27 Some 
natural immunomodulators are regarded as potential ingredients for body health. As shown in Fig. 
4, CPP5 and CPP10 displayed the significant stimulating effects as compared to the control group, 
however CPP1 showed the effective effe ct just at the concentration of 50 μg mL. Meanwhile, our 
work also proved that these pectic samples could not directly induce the proliferation of bone 
marrow cells (data not shown), which was in agreement with the previous research.11 
Natural pectin contains a variety of t ypical structural moieties, such as RG- I and RG- II. The 
backbone of RG-I is composed of repeating disaccharide [ →4)-α-D-GalpA-(1→2)- 
α-L-Rhap(1→], in which the C(O)-4 and/or C(O)-3 positions of α-L-Rhap were partially 
substituted with a variety of side -chains, such as arabinogalactan- I (AG-I), arabinogalactan- II 
(AG-II) and arabinan. 28 AG- I is an arabinosyl-substituted derivative of linear 1,4-linked 
β-D-galactosyl residues, an d the most abundant RG- I associated structural regions in some 
pectins.9 AG-II usually occurs in the proteoglycans known as arabinogalactan-proteins (AGP) or 
covalently linked to RG- I backbone.29 In addition to arabinose and galactose, AG- II also contains
